2.1 The First Chapter, titled "The Instruction of Nārada.
Now begins the latter half of the glorious Gaṇeśa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Śrī Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, Uttara-ardha, Krīḍā-khaṇḍa.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Salutations to the illustrious Great Lord of the Gaṇas.
Salutations to the feet of the illustrious Mahāsiddhi Mahābuddhilakṣalābha, the King of Nagnabhairava.
Salutations to all the Ganesha-gurus.
Now begins the Uttarakhaṇḍa.
The First Chapter. The Sages said: O Sūta of great intelligence, you have related this excellent narrative perfectly.
We have listened with reverence, yet we have not reached satiety.
Just as a living being is never satiated by eating food day after day,
tell us another story by which we may be satisfied.
Sūta said:
The section on worship has been told; now I shall speak to you of the section on divine play (krīḍākhaṇḍa), concerning how Gaṇeśa performed the destruction of various Daityas.
I shall now fully explain the protection of virtuous people, twice-born brahmins, and cows with the utmost care; listen with a steady mind. 4.
The sages said:
"To whatever extent that Purāṇa is narrated, to that same extent the desire to hear it increases.
Therefore, let it be told correctly, so that the entire world may be instantly liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra. (5)
Sūta said:
That which was previously spoken by Brahmā to Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor,
and by Bhṛgu to Soma’s beloved— that very thing I shall now tell you.
Vyāsa said: O lotus-born one, O Lord, tell me the auspicious life-story of Gaṇeśa—
whatever form the omnipresent one assumed and whatever he performed.
O Brahmin, may you, out of compassion, speak at my request;
for even after hearing this section on worship, I do not reach satiety. 8.
You should describe each of those deeds by which Vikaṭa slew whichever mighty Daitya he encountered through whatever means of approach.
Having heard from the lotus of your mouth his childhood deeds and various kinds of divine sports, my mind will attain peace.
Sūta said: Having heard various kinds of questions, the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā) related many divine stories to Vyāsa, who had inquired after them.
Brahmā said:
Well asked by you, O Vyāsa, who bring joy to the heart!
O Lord, the pleasure of the speaker increases when there is a respectful listener.

O you of virtuous fame, let it be told how even regarding that which is unspeakable, a most powerful capacity arises in me to speak of you, just as a speaker has power over a listener when something is being related. 13.
Now I shall relate to you the entire life-story of Gaṇeśa;
having assumed various incarnations, that omnipresent Lord removed the burden of the earth.
Having slain various kinds of Daityas, he established the gods in their own places;
he was devoted to the protection of the virtuous and capable of uprooting the wicked. 15.
O Sage, listen to this history concerning the narrative of Gaṇeśa, as proclaimed by Viṣṭaraśravas (Kṛṣṇa), which grants all desires upon being heard. 16.
Viṣṇu said:
In age after age, Gaṇeśa has different names, different vehicles,
different tasks, different qualities, and is the destroyer of different demons.
Mounted upon a lion, ten-armed, named Vināyaka, possessing a form of splendor and a massive body, he is the bestower of boons and the self-controlled master of all. 18.
In the Tretā Yuga, he was mounted upon a sacrificial grass mat (barhis), possessed six arms, and had the complexion of Arjuna;
he became renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Mayūreśvara.
In the Dvāpara age, he is red in color, mounted upon a rat, and possesses four arms;
known as Gajānana, he is worshipped by gods and men. || 20 ||
In the Kali age, however, he will be smoke-colored, mounted on a horse, and two-armed;
known as Dhūmraketu, he shall be the destroyer of the Mleccha armies.
O sage, I shall now describe each Daitya whom he slew.
In a city of the Aṅga country, there was a brahmin named Raudraketu.
He was a knower of the true meaning of all scriptures, one who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
he was impartial toward all living beings, a maintainer of the sacred fire-sacrifice, and a worshiper of the gods, cows, and elephants.
He was a constant devotee of the Lord, proficient in all the scriptures,
and his wife, named Śāradā, was adorned with beauty and grace.
Such a woman exists neither among the Apsarases, nor among the eight classes of celestial nymphs;
for the moon, having been vanquished by her face, has gone to its waning through anxiety.
Illuminating the surface of the earth with many divine ornaments, she shone like the vault of the sky with its garlands of stars. || 26 ||
Once, that Śāradā, whose eyes were like autumn lotuses,
became pregnant during the month of Śarada, which was as beautiful as the autumn moon.
By the brilliance of her body, nothing at all could be discerned;
yet this virtuous woman fulfilled every single longing she desired.
Thus, in her ninth month, she gave birth to twin sons,
both of whom were exceedingly handsome and brought joy to their respective mothers' hearts.
Seeing his two sons with arms reaching down to their knees and long eyes, their father said:
"Today I have become free from debt; today my ascetic merit has borne fruit."
"Blessed is my lineage, blessed is my birth, since two sons such as these have been beheld by me.
Having thus honored the best of the twice-born with offerings of water for the feet and other gifts, he likewise worshipped Gaṇādhipa.
Having quickly caused the benediction to be recited, preceded by the worship of the Mothers,
he performed the birth-rite (jātakarma) with devotion along with the brāhmaṇas, including the auspicious śrāddha ceremony.
Having honored the brahmins with devotion, he gave various gifts;
he also paid homage to his friends with garments, jewels, wealth, and other such things.
With the sounds of various musical instruments, he, being filled with joy at the births of his sons, caused sugar and betel-leaf to be distributed in every house.
Just as a yogi devoted to grain, having obtained the most excellent of true substances, then, after ten days had passed, summoned the foremost of the twice-born; || 35 ||
Having worshipped those experts in the science of astrology with supreme devotion, he asked them, "O best of the twice-born, what are the names of these two, and what is their purpose? (36)
"Having investigated through the knowledge of the past and the future, tell me.
They replied, "By means of our meditative concentration (praṇidhāna), [we shall know] Devāntaka and Narāntaka. || 37 ||
"O Brahmin, let us, in our opinion, give these two names that are true to their meaning.
Having heard those words, the twice-born man, who was devoted to the service of the twice-born, [acted accordingly]. (38)
He likewise bestowed two names according to the ritual prescribed in his own Vedic branch;
he then fed the Brahmins as well as all the citizens.
Then those two grew like Mount Meru and Mount Mandara;
by their strength, they were like two palm trees rooted in the marshlands or like two bamboo shoots.
Wherever those two place their feet by chance,
the head of Śeṣa, who dwells here in the netherworld, bows down.
A radiant mandala was seen shining, situated above the heads of the two as they stood; showing it to their parents, the two of them greatly delighted them with wonders. || 42 ||
Once, Nārada suddenly went to the house of Raudraketu;
having heard of the fame of the two boys, he took them both out of curiosity.
Placing them on his lap and smelling their heads, he spoke to the two parents.
Nārada said:
"Having heard of the wonderful and auspicious fame of the two sons, I have come here. (44)
O Sage, these two will also become even more wonderful in the future;
it is your great good fortune, O Sage, that you have obtained such sons.
"Upon seeing another, one feels joy; what then can be said of one's own kinsman?
Having heard these auspicious words uttered by Nārada, [the king spoke].
Then the parents, having bowed to the sage Nārada, said to him:
"By your grace, let there now be long life for our two sons. (47)
Grant your grace in such a way that these two may become even more heroic,
world-renowned, all-knowing, and punishers of their enemies.
Ka said:
Having observed the devotion of the two sons of Rudraketu and Śāradā, he instructed them both in the five-syllabled Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā). 49.
The enemy of Kama (Shiva) said to his two sons, "Let her be propitiated by this [act];
and placing his hand, which granted fearlessness, upon their heads, he commanded them to perform the rite.
Having spoken thus and taken leave of Raudraketu,
O Brahmin, the great sage Nārada, whose vision is divine, then vanished from sight.
When the Sage had vanished, the two of them joyfully said to their parents,
"Please grant us your permission so that we may carry out our religious observances."
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Instruction of Nārada," in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa. || 1 ||

2.2 Second Chapter. Vyāsa said:
O Brahmin, how was the performance of the rite conducted, and where did those two perform it?
Tell all of that in detail to me, who asks with reverence.
Brahmā said:
"Well asked by you, O Vyāsa; I shall now tell you everything.
Devāntaka and Narāntaka then performed their ritual observances. (2)
Having received their father's command,
they both went to the dense forest where even the wind cannot pass and which is filled with various trees and creepers.
It was adorned with ponds and lakes, beautified by flowers and sprouts,
and abounded in vast caves, mountains, and various rocky plateaus.
Remaining there, both of them began a great penance;
standing on a single big toe, they remained there with steady minds.
For a thousand years, they chanted the auspicious five-syllabled mantra proclaimed by Nārada and meditated upon the god Śaṅkara.
For two thousand autumns they remained without food, subsisting only on air;
for a thousand years, moreover, they ate only ripe leaves.
Thus ten thousand years passed as they performed their recitation;
then, by the power of their abundant asceticism, their splendor increased.
The sun’s rays grew dim before those two whose bodies were smeared with ashes;
they wore tiger skins and elephant hides, and carried rosaries of akṣa seeds.
O dear one, at the time of dawn, they both worshipped Śambhu with flowers and tender leaves in that penance grove; and by the wonderful splendor of those two, [the grove was illuminated].
Lions, elephants, and other creatures who were natural enemies became entirely free from enmity;
thus, the five-faced, three-eyed Lord was pleased by that austerity.
Having ten arms and no visible limbs, wearing a tiger skin and an elephant hide, and bearing a trident;
he carries the Gaṅgā upon his head and holds a hand-drum (ḍamaru) in his right hand.
Adorned with a necklace of serpents, his neck radiant with a garland of severed heads, mounted upon a bull, blue-throated, and illuminating the sky with his splendor. 13.
Adorned with various ornaments, white-limbed, and bearing the moon upon his crest—
seeing the God in such a form, the two attained supreme joy.
Thereafter, they both danced and prostrated themselves with the eight limbs touching the ground;
with palms joined in reverence, they addressed that God of gods.
Blessed are our parents, born of divine lineage, and blessed is our penance;
blessed is our family and our bodies, since Maheśvara has been beheld by us. 16.
He is beyond the scope of the Vedāntas and inaccessible to speech, from which [all words] have turned back;
where the scriptures are blunted, as are the six systems of philosophy and the mind.
Even he who possesses a thousand mouths is not capable of praising him; nor are Sanaka and the others able [to do so].
He is the creator, protector, and destroyer of the entire universe.
It makes a beggar a king, and a king indeed a beggar;
it makes a serpent a bracelet, and a bracelet indeed a serpent;
it makes the living dead, and the dead indeed dead. (19)
Having heard these words of theirs— how the one who was wealthy had become poor and the one who was poor had likewise become wealthy— the Lord of Umā spoke to them.
Excellent, excellent! I have heard the nectar of your words.
I, who am mounted upon my bull along with Umā, am well-pleased with your ascetic penance.
Having arrived through the perfection of their meditations, they requested their desired boons.
Ka said: Having heard these words from Andhakāri, the two then spoke. (22)
With a voice faltering with joy, he addressed Devāntaka and Narāntaka:
"If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, Lord of All, Sovereign of the Universe! (23)
If you would grant us boons, and if we are worthy of your favor,
then [grant them] from among gods, lords of men, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas.
It is superior even to humans, serpents, gandharvas, and apsarases, as well as to kinnaras;
it is also superior to all weapons and missiles, and even to domestic animals and the like.
Neither from the planets, the lunar mansions, nor from spirits; neither from Dānavas nor from Asuras;
neither by day nor by night; nor even from worms, insects, and the like. || 26 ||
O Lord of the Universe, by your grace may death never befall us;
grant us sovereignty over the three worlds and devotion to your feet as well. (27)
Ka said:
Then, having heard all their requests, the trident-bearer—the bull-bannered Lord whose feet are the wish-fulfilling tree for his own devotees—was pleased by their asceticism and spoke to them. 28.
Śiva said:
Whatever you both desire, all that shall be exactly so and not otherwise—
fearlessness from all sides, immortality, and even sovereignty over the three worlds.
"You two shall obtain, and indeed Antaka shall also obtain, fear from you both;
yet beneath their two heads, Śambhu held out his lotus-hand to grant them fearlessness."
Having thus obtained his desired objects, Śiva vanished;
then, having received permission, he returned home once He had disappeared.
Having circumambulated him, bowed down, and honored him,
the two parents, seeing him, were filled with great joy and prostrated themselves in delight.
Embracing their parents, the two recounted their own adventures;
smelling the tops of their heads, the father spoke joyfully to his two sons.
Through your attainment of heaven, through the sight of Śaṅkara, and through this [meeting],
your birth and lineage have been purified, and great fame has been earned.
O my two sons, having heard this news, my limbs have become cool;
there is no doubt that I have attained supreme satisfaction, as if from drinking nectar. (35)
Then, having been anointed with unguents, they both enjoyed various auspicious foods together with their father and with Brahmins who were experts in the Vedas and Shastras. (36)
Then she honored those two sons and the brahmins with various ornaments and decorations; having received many household instructions from them,
she bid them farewell after bowing down, and they both passed the night.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Boons by Devāntaka and Narāntaka," in the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.

2.3 Third Chapter. Who said?
Then, having risen at dawn, meditated upon their gurus, honored them,
and having remembered and bowed to all the gods, they departed toward the southwestern direction.
Having discharged urine and feces, and having cleansed their teeth and tongues,
they bathed, performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), and worshipped their desired deities.
Having worshipped the Brahmins with devotion, they gave them wealth and garments;
and beholding the clarified butter contained in a bronze vessel, they gave that to the Brahmin.
Having looked at a stainless mirror accompanied by ritual fees,
and having put on their garments, the two of them reflected as follows.
The elder brother said:
"By virtue of the boon granted by the Great Lord, I shall conquer the heavenly worlds;
you, however, must conquer the world of mortals and the netherworld through his grace. (5)
Ka said:
Having thus made their resolve and observed an auspicious day,
one of them, equal to the wind in speed, departed for the heavenly realm.
Having gone there to Amarāvatī, he shattered the circle of gardens;
girding his loins, the mighty one stood before Śakra.
A great clamor arose among the gods as they ran about frantically:
"Who is this? Who is this? How has he suddenly come into the presence of Indra? (8)
"Kill him! Bind him firmly! Drive this man far away!"—thus they all ran about, but were repelled by him.
Flying up again and again and suddenly swooping down repeatedly,
great trees fell from that flight along with the wombs of women.
The entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and mines, trembled;
by the radiance of his limbs, those best of the gods became dark-complexioned.
Just as a mortal who has been conquered by disease immediately turns pale,
even so did all the gods turn pale upon seeing him.
O Sage, even Indra then became agitated and pale;
some fled toward the ten directions, while others remained prepared for battle.
Some, exceedingly arrogant and the lowest of gods, sought refuge with him;
then Indra, thunderbolt in hand, mounted his four-tusked elephant.
He roared most terribly, and the three worlds trembled;
he said to those best of gods who were ready for battle, "What do you see? (15)
"Where has our manliness gone, now that the asura has arrived here?
Then, making preparations for battle, they went out before him.
Seeing the gods eager for immediate action, Devāntaka said to Hari:
"O Śakra, why do you weary yourself? Consider my boons. (17)
Antaka, terrified by fear, has fled intent on escape;
I consider your thunderbolt to be as insignificant as mere straw, by the command of Śaṅkara. 18.
"O Śakra, the gods who abide within your sight depart from all sides at the mere sound of my breath; listen to my words, let it be given to me in a conciliatory manner."
"Stay wherever you may be, keeping all your own steps under control;
otherwise, having abandoned everything, you will go to death in vain. (20)
"O god, how is it that you do not know my name, Devāntaka? Ka said:
Having heard these words of his, the heart of Hari broke. 21.
And from the mouth of Śakra, a powerful fire issued forth,
like what occurs when water is dropped into excessively heated oil.

Then, in the fourth year, he went beyond his own hermitage to a lake filled with aquatic plants and teeming with shoals of crocodiles and fish.

Devoid of qualities and free from ego, he is the supreme cause of both the existent and the non-existent;

Having bowed down to Kaśyapa, she related the entire account;

I believe he has assumed a human body as a mere sport;

Having heard those words of his, they, being questioned, said to him:
"Indeed, for us who were desirous of going to Kailāsa, the sight of you has now occurred."
Evil has gone to dissolution and our birth has become fruitful;

"Grant us leave; we are eager to go and see the Lord of the Mountain.
Having heard their words, the treasure-house of asceticism spoke again: || 9 ||

Having entered the inner house, he beheld five forms;

Then, all of them, filled with wonder, said to one another: "By which Daitya have our forms, the instruments of our actions, been carried away? (15)

Kailāsa and Śaṅkara with his attendants, Vaikuṇṭha and Viṣṇu himself,

Then Kaśyapa said to them, "Let it be eaten";

having ground it into a paste with his hands, he cooked it in leaf-cups and ate it day after day.
With that wealth being given by him, he brought garments, perfumes, unbroken grains, flowers, incense, and lamps of great splendor. || 51 ||
He set aside forest fruits and bark garments,
as well as pieces of dried āmalaka fruit for the purpose of cleansing the mouth.
Having spread a heap of darbha grass in his well-watered courtyard and raised a banner,
that sage, devoted to meditation, prepared his seat;
he first diligently performed the Vaiśvadeva offering and the presentation of food.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Devotion of Gaṇeśa Ending with Vidrumāśukla," in the Bālacarita of the Krīḍākhaṇḍa within the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa. || 22 ||
The total cumulative number of verses from the beginning is 5114 + 54 = 5168.
Chapter twenty-three, titled "The Bestowal of the White Boon," in the *Bālacarita*, ends here.
Ka said:
That boy, filled with curiosity, played among the other boys;
meanwhile, the king, seated upon his auspicious throne, watched the dance performed by all the people together.
Just as he was looking at the courtesans,
both Sanaka and Sanandana arrived from the world of the gods to that beautiful assembly hall.
That assembly hall was illuminated by their radiance like that of the sun and fire;
seeing them, the king rose from his seat along with his attendants.
Placing her head at their lotus feet, she prostrated before them with all eight limbs;
then, with palms joined in reverence, she said: "Today my family has become blessed."
"Kingdom, knowledge, body, wife, sons, and all else"—
having said this, he took hold of them with his hand and seated them upon his own seat.
He worshipped them with devotion using the sixteen types of offerings,
and he caused them both to rest by massaging their feet and other such services.
Bowing down again and again, he began to speak.
The King said:
"To the sages who have laid aside the rod of punishment and are forever free from desire—" (7)
I have no desire for any personal gain; nevertheless, I seek this command, being intent on making my asceticism, kingdom, lineage, and character meaningful.
The two of them said:
"This Blessed One, who has attained all desires, whose nature is that of the Supreme Brahman, and who descends through divine play (līlāvatāra), is your son, the offspring of Kaśyapa. (9)
"He performs various wonders in his home with marvelous prowess;
having heard of his heroic deeds, we have both come here to see them. (10)
Otherwise, what purpose would we have in abandoning the abode of Śakra? For he who has the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) in his own home—what else would he ask for? || 11 ||
"O King, having bowed at his lotus feet, let us go to our own place.
When they had arrived and heard these words, Vināyaka [acted].
Abandoning his play out of affection for those who spoke, he held a *modaka* in his hand,
effortlessly bearing that sweetmeat consisting of five kinds of edible foods.
To them, the king, smiling gently, showed him [the way], saying:
"This is that god whom you both were eager to behold; he has arrived."
"Whatever must be done now that he has arrived, do it as you please.
Having observed him, those two sages then spoke to one another.
"Surely that best of sages, Kaśyapa, has been defiled by him, who, having attained the status of his son, has utterly abandoned his own proper conduct. (16)
For him, there is no deliberation regarding what is touched or untouched, nor any rule concerning what is fit or unfit to be eaten;
indeed, a great fault would surely arise from seeing or touching him. (17)
How is it that he has abandoned his own restraints and stayed in the house of a Kṣatriya? But what would be gained by our seeing him while we remain established in our own duty? 18.
Then the god, who was seated near the king, heard that speech;
he, an expert in words, spoke these words like another Vācaspati.
"Where has your knowledge gone, O sages who have labored in vain?
Having abandoned heaven, how have you arrived here like two ordinary men? (20)
Having heard these words of his, those two then spoke to the king:
"We have been greatly deluded by the illusion of the Lord who consists of illusion. (21)
"Grant us permission; we shall go to our own hermitage.
Then the tiger among kings, impelled by his firm devotion, [spoke].
"Stay and listen to my words," he said to the two of them;
and having bathed and eaten, he entreated them with devotion, saying, "Please follow me."
Having heard his request, the two eminent sages said, "We do not eat the food of a king; therefore, we shall depart."
Having obtained his permission, they then went to Maṇikarṇikā;
Vināyaka, meanwhile, followed by all the children, went about joyfully playing.
Having bathed and gone to Śukla’s house, and perceiving his devotion, he went there with reverence,
just as a cow runs toward her calf, or as a mother rushes to her weeping child.
Just as Kṛṣṇa, seeing Draupadī brought into the assembly and having sought refuge,
those two, husband and wife, fell at the feet of the God.
Shedding tears of joy with voices faltering,
they embraced the Lord with delight and danced, overflowing with rapture.
They found nothing further to be done; as if their bodies had transcended the physical realm, their limbs bristling with horripilation, they shed streams of tears.
Regaining consciousness after a moment, the two of them bowed to the Lord of the World;
then the sage said to the God, "O Lord of the distressed, that which belongs to you... (30)
Your auspicious name, renowned throughout the three worlds and the destroyer of sins, has been made meaningful this very day by the sight of your feet; thus our birth has attained its purpose.
"Having abandoned a multitude of palaces, he has come to this hut of leaves;
blessed is my lineage today—blessed is my birth, my knowledge, my asceticism, and my age. (32)
Then that sage honored him as he sat upon a seat of kusha grass;
having washed his pair of feet, he took that water and held it to his head.
Then he offered fragrant unbroken rice, flower garlands, incense, and lamps;
as well as sprouts of dūrvā grass, leaves of śamī, excellent oil, and auspicious ketakī flowers.
Having placed a small amount of food before him as well as wild forest fruit,
and having offered a handful of flowers purified by mantras, he bowed down, feeling ashamed.
Thinking, "How can this poor food be given to him?",
the God of gods, Vināyaka, perceived his intention.
"O Mother, I beg you: what food is there in your house? Let that be given to me.
Even if it is poor food given with devotion, it would be more to me than even nectar. (37)

That which is given with hypocrisy and devoid of faith becomes poison; likewise, dry rice, even if it be extensive, or that produced from many grains for the sake of the Sun-god, [is ineffective]. 38.
Filled with shame, the sage’s wife set it down before him;
and seeing that all the oil was gone, the boys laughed at him.
He ate it with great reverence as if it were cooked food;
drinking water with every morsel, he devoured it most powerfully.
Then the entire alms-bowl was placed by that sage into Udana; that water surged out in all directions, and the boy was unable to restrain it. 41.
Then he became ten-armed and ate the rice with them;
the people, laughing and clapping their hands, beheld this wonder.
"This is indeed an unprecedented dish, cooked with water only knee-deep," said the children as they ate the milk-rice preparation with great relish.
Those who ate together with him attained a state equal to the gods;
others, however, later felt regret, those who had laughed with their teeth bared.
A great clamor arose in the city as to where Vināyaka was;
some said, "He is eating stale rice in the house of Śukla. 45.
The ten-armed one made them hold [the vessel] so that he could eat the rice;
when he had eaten and was purified, he gave him dry āmalaka fruit.
By that act, Vināyaka, the soul of the world, performed the purification of his face;
being pleased and delighted by your disposition, O sinless one, he spoke to Śukla. 47.
"O highly fortunate one, choose from me whatever boons you desire.
Śukla said:
"Having abandoned all those who live in cities, I have come here to eat coarse food. (48)
This alone is my greatest boon—that I have beheld you;
yet, in accordance with your command, I beg for firm devotion toward you. 49.
Grant me liberation beforehand, so that I shall not return again;
O Leader, my mind finds no delight in the pleasures of saṃsāra without you. 50.
Ka said:
Having replied to him, "So be it," the two-armed infant, as before,
gave him a house superior to Indra's abode, filled with excellent jewels and gold.
Bestowing his own supreme form, knowledge, and prosperity upon them,
he was permitted by the two of them to depart elsewhere, surrounded by the boys.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Granting of the Boon to Śukla," in the Bālacarita of the Krīḍākhaṇḍa within the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa. 23.
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning is 5168 + 52 = 5220.
Chapter twenty-four, titled "The Narration of the Feeding of Vināyaka," ends here.
Ka said:
All the great people in that city watched him,
having prepared the requisites for worship as well as various kinds of food.
Then, in every house, in the royal palace, and even in the houses of all the ministers,
the people searched for the son of Kaśyapa.
All people asked, "Has the Leader been seen? The Veda says, "No, no"; how then can He come within the range of anyone's eyes? (3)
"We did not see him," the people there said;
however, those who were at the edge of the city heard this from the reports of the people.
He had already arrived at the white house, so they went there;
however, they did not see him and asked about him, and he replied, "He has gone from here. (5)
But that child, composed of illusion and eager to deceive people, sent the other children away and then entered through the door and lay down as if asleep. || 6 ||
Some saw him sleeping like a lion in its cave;
others, overcome by anger, reviled him, saying, "He is but a child, a mere boy."
Why has he gone to the house of a pauper like a Piśāca?
If he were the Lord who knows the state of all beings, he would act for the welfare of everyone. || 8 ||
Raising him up and taking him by the hand, [he said]: "Go to the auspicious refuge;
make all that has been prepared for your sake fruitful for us. (9)
"Fatigue born of wandering has vanished upon seeing your lotus feet;
come, come to our home with your group of children to eat."
He said, "I have just eaten," but the people spoke to him again:
"What could you have eaten in the house of a poor man who subsists on alms? (11)
"O Lord, you do not even drink water; how then have you eaten food?
Gaṇeśa said: "My belly is completely full, and I have no power to go [anywhere]. 12.
Ka said:
Then all those people, having learned that he had been eaten in the house of Śukla, became hopeless, their resolutions shattered; they were enraged, dejected, and bewildered.
The provisions, accumulated for the sake of various necessities, have come to naught;
those wicked men, hypocrites devoid of devotion, have consumed them themselves. 14.
Those devotees remained abstaining from food, intent upon meditation;
thus, having perceived that all the worlds were established in meditation, he [proceeded].
Though one, he clearly became manifold in nature, like the space within jars;
just as the sun is seen as many when reflected in jars filled with water. || 16 ||
In one place he was reclining on a couch; in another, he was devoted to silent recitation;
in some places he was intent on giving gifts, and elsewhere he was eager for food.
In one place he teaches the students the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs and its meaning;
in another place he expounds the scriptures, and in yet another he studies them himself.
Thus, appearing in various forms as he entered various houses, they each thought, "He has come to our house first. || 19 ||
They gave him oil for anointing, a bath, worship, and food;
thus everyone rejoiced together with the King of Kāśī.
Having beheld the Lord, the guide of the virtuous, with supreme joy,
they worshipped him and fed the twice-born as well as their circles of friends.
They ate the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), cooked rice, side dishes, milk-rice, boiled rice,
and all other pleasing foods, according to their desire.
Thus, while the brahmins, the gods, the king of Kāśī, and his friends were all present and offering blessings,
the king of Kāśī addressed them with these questions.
Deluded in many ways by the illusory power of the sage’s son regarding his various forms, the king said: "It is clear that Vināyaka has gone to various houses to eat. (24)
"Even though he is near me, who indeed eats in every house?
And sometimes Vināyaka goes about mounted on a palanquin to eat. (25)
In one place he went mounted on an elephant, and in another place mounted on a horse;
thus it was in all the worlds while the boy remained intent upon receiving worship. 26.
Then the two of them went to the city; wherever they saw Vināyaka having eaten, they would turn back and come together. || 27 ||
Wherever they went in a house,
having always circumambulated Vināyaka there in its entirety, they wandered about for the sake of alms.
In one place he was reclining on a divine couch, eating fruits and chewing betel-leaf smeared with perfumes and other fragrant substances.
In one place he saw him watching a dance accompanied by a throng of courtesans;
elsewhere he was playing with dice, and in another place, by the power of his intellect.
In one place, they saw him adorned with various ornaments, clothed in divine garments, reciting, muttering prayers, and absorbed in meditation.
In some places he was being praised by devotees, and in others he was praising the Lord of the World; in many instances, through his devotion, he revealed his own divine majesty.
He delighted his own exceedingly beautiful young wives,
attended upon the aged with medical care, and partook of the most excellent flavors.
Somewhere in the courtyard, he was eating earth while running about;
exhausted, he was drinking water and playing with balls and other such toys. (34)
Thus, hungry and exhausted from wandering from house to house,
having searched everywhere for that god, they then spoke to one another.
"There is a stainless, pure, and clean brahmin in this city;
let us go to his house to eat," having said this, they both went there.
There too, they saw that Vināyaka had entered the courtyard;
"One must not eat here in the city until after Vināyaka has been appeased. (37)
Having spoken thus, they went outside and, seeing Vināyaka before them,
they assumed the state of animals and beheld him even from that position.
In the eastern and western directions, as well as all around,
below and above, they both beheld that same Vināyaka, who is omnipresent.
And they both saw the true form of Vināyaka as the universal form;
they beheld every single thing as consisting entirely of Vināyaka.
Then, as they meditated upon Śambhu and Viṣṇu, being greatly amazed,
they beheld both Him and Vināyaka within their hearts.
Closing their eyes, those two best of sages saw him within;
then, opening their eyes, they beheld him outside.
Wearing a diadem and earrings, adorned with pearl necklaces, garments, and armlets,
he was further embellished by a golden waistband and finger-rings.
Mounted upon a lion, ten-armed, auspicious, accompanied by Siddhi and Buddhi, with the crescent moon upon his forehead, a musk tilaka on his brow, and adorned with serpent ornaments. 44.

Having abandoned all sense of duality, those two knowers of reality bowed at the lotus feet of him who possesses the splendor of ten million suns and who effects the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.
Having praised Vināyaka, the God of gods, with supreme devotion, those two lords of sages attained awakening through his very compassion. 46.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Feeding of Vināyaka," in the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 5220 + 46 = 5266.
Chapter Twenty-five, titled "The Praise of Devotion" within the *Bālacarita*, ends here.
They both said:
You are the cause of all causes, yet you transcend all causes;
you are the very nature of Brahman, the pervasive and supreme cause of the cosmic egg.
O sinless one, you alone create the universe through your grace and you alone withdraw it;
though formless, you assume various forms, endowed with diverse powers of illusion and strength.
You alone are the five elements, the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas;
who would be capable of praising you, whose nature is both the moving and the unmoving?
"Neither this, nor that," thus the Śruti spoke out of ignorance of Your true form;
we two have been deluded, for we were not capable of knowing Your supreme nature. (4)
O All-pervading Lord, we do not know the full majesty of You who possess manifold forms;
yet, O Master, we have now accomplished our life's purpose through the sight of Your feet. 5.
"Through various incarnations, you remove the burden of the earth by means of your infinite power.
Ka said:
"Having heard their praise in this way, he spoke to them both with affection. (6)
Vināyaka, who takes the form of a child, is playful and even illusory;
yet by my grace, you two shall become knowers of reality and all-knowing.
Having thus granted the boon, the god vanished on that very spot;
then those two, having perfectly fashioned an incomparable image of Vināyaka, [worshipped it].
Having constructed an incomparable palace adorned with jewels and gold,
both Sanaka and Sanandana established it.
And they both gave it a name; "This Vināyaka is the granter of boons," they said, and thus the lake was named Gaṇeśakuṇḍa by them. 10.
Having bathed here, whoever worships that boon-granting Vināyaka, having attained all his desires and enjoyed manifold pleasures, [attains liberation]. || 11 ||
Having obtained sons and grandsons, great learning, long life, and extensive fame,
as well as wealth, grain, renown, and eternal knowledge of reality.
Beforehand, one goes to the abode of Vaināyaka; there is no doubt about this.
Ka said:
"Where the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and hosts of Apsarases [dwell]. (13)
Having beheld and worshipped the Lord of Gods, they vanished on the spot in an instant;
filled with wonder, the two of them departed for the highest heaven.
The King of Kāśī also arrived there with his ministers and subjects,
and honored him with various articles, ornaments, and garments of both superior and inferior quality.
With many kinds of cooked foods and various types of fruits, with jewels, pearls, flowers, and manifold sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās). || 16 ||
He worshipped with supreme devotion, together with the Brahmins, according to the sacred mantras;
he honored the Brahmins with garments, ornaments, and gold.
Having accepted their blessings, he returned once more to the city;
likewise, those subjects honored that leader.
In the same way, having honored the Brahmins, they received supreme blessings; thereafter, the subjects worshipped Vināyaka according to their ability. 19.
Then they all, with joyful minds, entered the city.
Thus has the entire conduct of Vināyaka been narrated to you. 20.
"This merit removes all sins; what else do you wish to hear?
The sage said:
"I have heard the life-story of Śukla, who was devoted to pure alms."
When the Guide had departed from his home, deprived of the touch of the [five] elements,
he took up the rice, which was softened by the waters, with his ten arms.
Having eaten and cast off his fatigue, being satisfied, he destroyed poverty;
he was given a house that surpassed the city of Śakra, the white one.
Likewise, such riches were bestowed upon the Lord of Alakā as do not even exist among the Lord of the Makara-bannered [Kāma]; and his very form was granted such that it has no equal even for him.
Such knowledge was bestowed upon him as does not exist even in the four-faced Brahmā;
O Brahman, you ought to explain to me the reason for this. || 25 ||
Ka said:
O Vyāsa, you have asked well, since the story of the Supreme Lord purifies the questioner, the listeners, and the speaker when heard with devotion. (26)
"O Lord, my mind is indeed set on speaking that which you have asked;
I shall tell you correctly the conduct of Him who is accessible through devotion. (27)
The God is omniscient, all-seeing, omnipresent, and the knower of all minds;
He is pleased by devotion alone, for it is indeed the cause of His satisfaction.
Even a Palāśa leaf, water, or a beautiful flower offered with devotion satisfies him;
indeed, he bestows his very self upon that very person.
Whether out of hypocrisy, or even with ease, or out of shame before another, [one may give] great wealth, vast riches, and various kinds of jewels. || 30 ||
Gold, silver, and pearls—all that is given becomes useless;
yet He, being pleased with a leaf of the śamī tree, granted the hunter residence in His own world.
Therefore, devotion is superior because it is acquired without effort, even when given incidentally, having been firmly established in the heart by making it one's own state of being. || 32 ||

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Devotion," in the *Bālacarita* (Account of Childhood Deeds) within the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* (Section on Play) of the *Śrī Gaṇeśa Purāṇa*.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 5266 + 32 = 5298.
Chapter Twenty-six, titled "The Liberation of the Bhima-rākṣasa," ends here.
The Sage said:
What deed did the hunter perform, and how was the leaf-offering presented?
What was his name, and how did he attain that same world [as the deity]? Tell me all that.
Ka said:
In the land of Vidarbha there was a city named Māhiṣmatī,
renowned throughout the three worlds and comparable to the city of Kubera.
In that city, there was a hunter named Bhīma who sold meat;
for although fault lies in speaking of the faults of others, he was so named. || 3 ||
When a question is asked, one must answer according to the truth and not out of malice:
"That Bhīma, who is full of faults and armed with arrows and a bow, is in the forest. (4)
Carrying quivers full of arrows, a sword, a bow, and a dagger,
he constantly killed living beings, being devoted to the maintenance of his family.
Once, while he was mercilessly killing travelers and even Brahmins in the lonely forest, a great festival commenced in that city. || 6 ||
Early in the morning, he went to the forest with a great desire to seize meat;
greedy for wealth and wishing to sell it, though he was the provider for his family.
Carrying a load of meat, he slaughtered those herds of deer;
just as he was entering the city, a great Rākṣasa arrived.
Delighted by the scent of humans, he whose eyes were tawny and who was named Piṅgākṣa— frightening to all— went to his presence in an instant.
Devouring both men and beasts like a fire that is difficult to satiate,
he trembled upon seeing him, and the hunter then fell to the ground.
Even though his eyes were forcibly covered, his weapons fell away;
opening his eyes, he beheld a śamī tree nearby.
Bhīma climbed it, and the Rākṣasa also climbed;
at that moment, a branch was blown by the wind and cast down upon him.
It fell upon the head of Gaṇanātha, who was established as a dwarf;
he was clearly pleased by that, having been worshipped by both.
He who became manifest as Gajānana (the elephant-faced one) to grant boons to Vāmana, that son of Kaśyapa, desiring to conquer Bali; he [is Śiva]. 14.
The Lord is exceedingly pleased with dūrvā grass and śamī leaves;
[an offering] combined with jewels and gold, and accompanied by divine garments, [is likewise pleasing]. 15.
Without a sprout of *durvā* grass, the worship of men becomes fruitless;
it may be fruitful with a leaf of *śamī*, but never otherwise. 16.
The God is not so pleased by sacrifices, gifts, vows, other rites, austerities, or even observances, as He is by heaps of gold and collections of jewels.
Just as the Lord is well-pleased by dūrvā grass and śamī leaves, the God of gods, gratified by those two, dispatched an excellent vehicle for them. 18.
They were joined by servants from their own world who had assumed their true forms;
by the mere sight of them, the mountainous heaps of sins of those [beings] were destroyed. (19)
And by the grace of Gaṇeśa, those two terrifying Rākṣasas perished, just as mountains of grass are destroyed upon contact with a spark of fire. || 20 ||
Having cast off their two bodies and assumed divine forms, they mounted a celestial vehicle,
honored by messengers with various garments, ornaments, and unguents.
Amidst the sounds of various musical instruments and accompanied by celestial Gandharvas, those two great beings were led into the presence of the God; there they both bowed down to Vināyaka.
Freed from all sins without exception, the two attained a form identical to his;
they were established by that Gaṇeśa in his own abode for the duration of a kalpa.
In this way, the God, who loves devotion, was pleased by the spirit of his worship;
likewise, being satisfied with merely a handful of food from the twice-born Śukla,
He granted him a divine residence resembling Alakā.
Therefore, worship without dūrvā grass and śamī leaves would be in vain; the Lord is not so pleased by grand, hypocritical worship as He is by these. || 25 ||
Just as this elephant-faced one was [pleased] by that very small act performed with devotion; || 26 ||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Bhīma Rākṣasa," in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa. || 26 ||
The total sum of the verses from the beginning is 5298 + 26 = 5324.
Chapter twenty-seven of the Bālacarita.
Vyāsa said:
O Nabhiga, tell me: who was this hunter in his previous birth, and who was that Rakshasa?
What was their character and what were their practices? Tell me that.
O Lord, how was the vow performed by that Vāmana?
And how was the boon granted to him by you in the form of Gajānana? || 2 ||
How does the world exist separately from Gaṇeśa elsewhere?
How is Śamī his beloved? Tell me all of this quickly. (3)
Ka said:
Listen, O sage, I shall tell you everything that you have asked.
In a previous birth, he was a king who had mastered the Vedas, yet he became a hunter.
He was an expounder of all the scriptures, endowed with all auspicious marks;
he was a performer of sacrifices, humble, modest, and a worshiper of the gods and guests.
The number of his elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry is unknown;
he is a donor, a hero, and wise, as prosperous as Maghavan himself.
And his two chief ministers, Dhvaja and Śatrujit, were the most intelligent;
by them, even Kāvya, the Lord of Speech, was clearly surpassed. (7)
Those two who were capable of conquering the surface of the earth by the power of their weapons had a wife named Madanāvatī, who possessed auspicious marks.
Devoted to her husband, virtuous, pleasant-faced, and all-knowing—there is no woman equal to her in the three worlds. 9.
He was compassionate toward the poor, the helpless, the elderly, and even toward guests;
likewise, he delighted in performing sacrifices, giving gifts, and honoring the virtuous.
The people of both the city and the countryside were satisfied with their conduct;
even their enemies adopted those six qualities esteemed by the virtuous. || 11 ||
Thus, being of virtuous fame, he ruled this earth for many years; then, by the power of fate, he succumbed to the law of time.
Knowing he was about to die, he offered a thousand cows according to the prescribed rites,
and he also gave eighteen other great gifts (mahādānas).
When he had died, the entire city then mourned for the king;
because he was childless, his wife likewise followed him in death.
The two ministers had all the funeral rites performed by the twice-born;
on the eleventh day, they gave various gifts with devotion.
When the month had passed, they deliberated upon finding a man born of noble lineage who was worthy of the kingdom—
intelligent, endowed with courage, heroic, and of truthful prowess.
Both of them were instructed by the king regarding that son of Durdharṣa, the heir of great strength, who was born of a wife (kṣetraja) and named Sāmba.
Having reached a firm decision, the two ministers, after consulting all the citizens, country-folk, and brahmins, resolved indeed to give the kingdom to him.
At an auspicious moment and under a favorable lunar mansion, both of them, together with the twice-born, had the consecration ceremony performed amidst a collection of various ritual materials.
The sage said:
O Grandfather, how was he born from the field (kṣetra), and of what lineage was he?
Tell me that regarding Sāmba; you are omniscient, O ocean of mercy. (20)
Ka said:
O sage, many efforts were made with great diligence by Dūrdharṣa for the sake of a son;
yet, despite being joined with adverse fate, no virtuous son was born to him.
He was begotten by his wife Pramadā, whose mind was attached to a fisherman;
he was born at an auspicious moment, yet it was not known that he was the son of an adulterer.
They both gave away as many royal insignia as there were,
having offered up the entire kingdom along with its realm and its treasury.
Those two were born as they had been before, established in the rank of ministers;

Neither misfortune, nor obstacles, nor untimely death, nor fever ever arises there, nor any fear of fire or thieves. || 28 ||
A Brahmin learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences shall become victorious; a Kṣatriya shall be a conqueror;

Ka said:

Having entered the womb of a Śamī tree, Aṅgiras, out of distress and through his firm yoga, became known as Śamīgarbha; thus was he born from the eater of oblations (Agni).
For this very reason, those who maintain the sacred fire churn the wood of the Śamī tree here;
and Śaunaka, having heard these words uttered by the elephant-faced god, [acted accordingly].
Having fashioned an image of the beautiful elephant-faced deity at the foot of a Mandāra tree,
he joyfully worshipped it with Mandāra flowers, Śamī leaves, and Dūrvā grass.
Being well-pleased, Gajānana granted boons to Śaunaka;

Gṛtsamada said:
From that time forward, Śamī became dear to that Gaṇeśa.
Thus everything has been told to you; I shall tell it to you again. 36.

Gṛtsamada said:
The Lord dwelt upon the Sahyādri mountain together with Girijā,
accompanied by his own attendants and sages, in that most powerful and meritorious sacred field.
Desirous of seeing him, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, set out for that place accompanied by his two wives and by gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras.

then Sadāśiva summoned the supreme ṛṣis. || 3 ||
Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Nārada;
Kapila, Pulaha, Kaṇva, Viśvāmitra, Trita, and Dvita. || 4 ||
Summoned by Śiva, all the others arrived, desiring to see him;
at the hour of dawn, having emerged for a moment, they began the sacrifice.
Then, O lords of sages, being in haste, they forgot the auspicious worship of Vināyaka and abandoned Sāvitrī, who was occupied with her household duties.
Having seated the Gāyatrī and having caused them to perform the recitation for an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana),
he performed the rite for prosperity (ābhyudayika), preceded by the worship of the Mothers.
While they were still establishing the sacrificial fire in the hearth,
Sāvitrī arrived, filled with rage upon seeing the commencement of the rite.
Looking at all the members of the assembly, she spoke with eyes red with anger.
Sāvitrī said:
"This sacrifice, undertaken in disregard of me, shall not succeed. (9)
The seer said:
Emitting flames from her mouth, desiring to burn all that is moving and unmoving, she cursed the gods and the sages: "You shall become dull-witted! (10)

Having thus appointed Gāyatrī, who was ineligible for that task, all the gods then bowed down and, filled with eagerness, made this fervent petition: 11. "Since all of us have appointed her, who is without authority, as Gāyatrī, therefore we pray to you with great urgency."
O auspicious one, because of the identity of the letters *ḍa* and *la*, we shall become Sāvitrī, the mother of all;
we shall take the form of water, appearing in the nature of rivers and streams.
When the goddess said "So be it," they assumed the form of rivers;
Maheśa became the river named Veṇī, and Kṛṣṇa became the river Kṛṣṇā.
All those deities became rivers, each bearing its respective name,
where formerly the Lord of Obstacles was not worshipped by those weak in knowledge.
In that matter, obstacles will arise for Śaṅkara just as they occurred in the past during the destruction of the three cities, due to his failure to perform worship. || 15 ||
When the obstacle to the sacrifice was at hand, Brahmā fell into deep anxiety:
"On my account, all the gods have assumed the form of rivers. (16)
By what karma was this celestial chariot sent to all the worlds?
And how has this insurmountable obstruction of my resolve been encountered today? (17)
The Lord of the World, the remover of obstacles, was neither remembered nor worshipped;
consequently, delusion overcame all the gods. (18)
"I shall make him propitious, and then the sacrifice will take place.
While Brahmā was thus reflecting, the celestial nymphs [arrived].
Having recognized the gods to be such as they were, Pulomajā, Girijā, Chāyā, and Kamalā also approached the presence of Brahmā.
All those others as well spoke to that lotus-faced one:
"How was the sacrifice commenced? How was our venerable lady not honored? (21)
Why was the elephant-faced remover of obstacles not worshipped first?
And how was it that the gods did not even remember you, or why was this forgotten by them? 22.
"What should be performed by us, or by the gods who have taken the form of water? To whom shall we go for refuge, O Lord, other than You, O Lotus-born One? (23)
Having heard their words, he said to them, "Do not fear," and spoke thus:
"I shall perform a sacrifice so that everything may become auspicious."
For what indeed is impossible for devotees when Gajanana is well-pleased?
Practice devotion to him all together; he will do everything that is dear to you.
I too shall propitiate Vināyaka, the Lord of the World,
the God who is without beginning or end, the cause of all causes.
Having been addressed thus, they went to the auspicious region of Karṇāṭaka;
directed by him, they stood at the foot of a Mandāra tree to meditate upon Vighneśa.
Formerly established by Rāma under the name Vakratuṇḍa,

And the renowned Daśānana went with his wife to his own abode;
there, all those celestial women performed severe austerities.
One performed the recitation of names, another likewise the recitation of mantras;
one remained in the lotus posture, meditating upon the Supreme Lord.
One sat in the vīrāsana posture without food, while another likewise remained fasting while sweeping the doors, courtyards, and houses.
Performing supreme devotion through circumambulations and prostrations,
one woman stood with her gaze fixed on a single toe, meditating upon Vināyaka.
Then, closing her eyes, one woman recited hymns of praise;
yet even after a long time had passed, Vināyaka was not satisfied.
Then, overwhelmed with distress, they fell into deep thought, wondering, "What shall we do?
Thereupon, some brought loads of flowers, while others brought loads of dūrvā grass.
Having offered [the oblation], they honored the deity with incense, lamps, food, and gold;
some with Mandāra flowers, and others with Śamī leaves.
Then, having heard the voice from the sky, the Lord thought, "He will not be satisfied without a leaf of the Śamī tree," and so [he provided] all [the leaves] with Śamī foliage.
He worshipped the god of gods, Gajānana, with supreme devotion;
thereafter, being exceedingly compassionate, he was well-pleased by the śamī leaves.
Before them appeared the radiant Lord with four beautiful arms,
wearing a crown and armlets, and adorned with necklaces and earrings.
With long ears, shimmering cheeks, and adorned with two tusks,
he is joined by Siddhi and Buddhi, has a mouse as his vehicle, and wears yellow garments.
They all beheld the god, whose splendor was equal to ten million suns;
closing their eyes, they prostrated themselves like staffs upon the surface of the earth.
With palms joined in reverence, their faces exceedingly serene and filled with supreme bliss, they praised that gentle one of great vows.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of His Own Form by Vināyaka, who was pleased by the offering of Śamī leaves, to the gods and the celestial nymphs," in the Bālacarita of the Krīḍākhaṇḍa within the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa. || 36 ||

Chapter thirty-seven, titled "The Greatness of the Śamī and Mandāra Trees," in the Bālacarita section.
Kīrti said:
"O great sage, tell me how that praise was offered by them.
The sage said:
"Listen, O Kīrti, hear that praise with an attentive mind. (1)
They said:
"Salutations to You who possess all forms; salutations to the inner controller of all.
Salutations to You, the doer of all, the compassionate giver of everything at all times. (2)

Salutations to the destroyer of all; salutations to you of infinite power! Salutations to the awakener of all; salutations to the source of all, the beginning of everything, who is present in every worthy recipient.

Salutations again and again to the one whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, who is devoid of attributes; salutations to the one whose nature is consciousness and bliss, who is beyond the reach even of the Vedas. 4.
Salutations to You, who have Māyā as Your support, who are immeasurable, who transcend all qualities (guṇas),

O destroyer of all enemies, who holds many weapons in your hands;

"O Lord, grant to the gods who are in the form of water their own true forms. 8.
"Your lack of mindfulness shall not persist forever; you ought to act accordingly here.

"Quickly satisfied by this praise, let your word be so.
By the word of Sāvitrī, the auspicious gods were born as water-beings.

they shall return to their own true nature, remaining in such states through their portions (aṃśa).

"Having abandoned our eldest sister and you, we began that sacrifice;

"We have been born anew; we have attained supreme bliss through your grace.
Having spoken thus, they worshipped Vināyaka with leaves of the śamī tree.

The Blessed One, being pleased with him, will grant all desires—whether through salutation, remembrance, or even prostration; of this there is no doubt.
Taking that great image fashioned from a mandāra tree which was there,

Even now, the Lord, together with his consort, worships her with devotion;

Having fashioned an image of Gaṇeśa, they worshipped it with śamī leaves;
they attained great joy and, together with their wives, experienced unsurpassed pleasures.
Having performed most intense penance for twelve years and having propitiated Vighneśa, Brahmā again performed a sacrifice.
He too worshipped with great reverence the form of the Lord of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa), the bestower of boons, with many kinds of Śamī leaves. 26.
With golden leaves, dūrvā grass, mandāra flowers, and also ketakī flowers,

Thus, O auspicious mother, the greatness of Mandāra and of Śamī has been described to you in brief; it destroys sin upon being heard. 28.
From that time forward, the auspicious Śamī tree, which is exceedingly dear to the God, was worshipped by you out of ignorance; because of that, this son has been restored to life. || 29 ||

Kīrti said:
O Brahmin, you have duly and with devotion described the greatness of the Śamī tree;
the Mandāra has also been mentioned, and by this my mind is satisfied. || 1 ||
"O Lord of Sages, although this prince has been taught the six-syllable mantra, he is unable to recite it due to his childhood. (2)
O Sage, this mantra is easy to understand, brings great clarity, and leads to the attainment of one's own sovereignty;
it can be recited even by a child—teach it to him now.
The Sage said:
Your intellect has been rightly directed toward the lotus feet of Gajānana;
therefore, I shall bestow upon you my own mantra, which bestows happiness. 4.
The four-syllabled name which is the cause of the entire world, the witness of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, and the destroyer of the wicked Daityas—[that name is "Hari"]. 5.
Of him who was the protector of all beings, the benefactor of Divodāsa,
who, though assuming the form of a twice-born, resided in Vārāṇasī.
Of him who was making every effort to attain Avimukta, the Lord of the Universe, and who was himself praised by Viśveśvara—the inner controller of all—[he spoke]. 7.
For the sake of protecting the world and for the gratification of Janārdana,
he was meditated upon and worshipped by Brahmā for the purpose of creation.
He who was worshipped even by Śiva for the sake of the universal dissolution,
and who was honored with great devotion even by the husband of Pulomajā (Indra).
For the sake of the destruction of the Daityas and for the attainment of the happiness of the kingdom of the gods,
[he was sought] by Sūrya, Varuṇa, Śaśin, and Yama.
He was honored by Agni and Vāyu for the sake of the excellence of their respective qualities,
and he was honored by Bṛhaspati and Uśanas for the sake of their own excellence.
With the remainder [of his merit], he propitiated Dhuṇḍhi for the sake of supporting the earth:
Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Rākṣasas; sages, animals, and all auspicious beings, both stationary and moving. 12.

"A son shall be born to you who will share in the kingdom and be a destroyer of enemies.

"O Brahman, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely.
The sage said:
"O auspicious lady, O blessed one, you have asked well, owing to your excellence in knowledge. (17)
This doubt of yours has been presented with devotion; I shall dispel it for you, just as the Daitya was slain by him, though he was difficult to overcome, and likewise the Rākṣasa.
Through the manifestation of his illusory power, he went to delude King Divodāsa,
just as Hara, the Lord of the Universe, was brought to Avimukta.
O queen of kings, I shall relate everything concerning how his name "Dhuṇḍhirāja" came to be, exactly as it was heard by me from Skanda.
"O auspicious one, listen with a single-minded focus as I relate it to Agastya.
Skanda said:
"Listen attentively, O Brahmin, to this narrative concerning the refuge of Avimukta."
Merely by hearing it, one is liberated from all sins;
Hari spoke it to Kaśyapa, saying, "Create various kinds of progeny."
Then, through his fully developed ascetic power, he created a body and produced jarāyuja (viviparous) beings;
at that time, there were twenty-one thousand aṇḍaja (oviparous) and svedaja (sweat-born) beings.
There are as many [beings] born from sprouts, and among them, human birth is difficult to attain;
one obtains that through merit, and the status of a Brāhmaṇa through great merit.
If that [sacrifice] is properly protected by the established rules of dharma and adharma,
it bestows the supreme station, having gone to which one does not return.
If not [liberated] during eighty-four lakhs of births,
men of evil conduct surely fall into the torments of Yama.
Then, when their karma has been exhausted after a long time,
they return once more to the world of mortals, born one-eyed, hunchbacked, and destitute.
Therefore, out of compassion for them, the gods beginning with Brahmā and Īśāna, as well as the highly fortunate sages, established various sacred fords (tīrthas). || 28 ||
And at that time, the celestial sages remained there, dissolving their own sins in those highly precious fields which remove the evil of living beings.
Wherein the dissolution of the sins of living beings occurs;
the celestial sages always remain there to protect creatures from sin. 30.

Then Viśveśvara created this auspicious [city], the most excellent of all, possessing every virtue, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and granting release to those who meditate upon it and those who know it. (31)
The beautiful city named Vārāṇasī, which embodies all sacred fords (tīrthas),
is where the powerful Viṣṇu created the famous lake.
While performing penance, he performed a beautiful bath that grants liberation merely by being seen;
at the sight of it, the jewel from Śiva’s earring trembled upon his neck.
Having fallen there, she became known by the name Maṇikarṇikā;
thereafter, being summoned by Bhagīratha, she became the river Bhāgīrathī.
Here, even for insects and moths, liberation occurs through death;
by remembering [the Name] three times, it bestows the fruit of residing in Kāśī. 35.
Blessed are those creepers, vines, grasses, and trees that do not go elsewhere;
for the tortoises and fish leave that earthly Kailāsa and depart no further.
Where Śambhu is eternally stationed, assuming various forms as well as a singular form—he who is the Sun, the Moon, Hari, and Brahmā, he alone is the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain. || 37 ||
Vināyaka is the embodiment of Śakti and he is the cause even of the universe;
for even at the time of dissolution, Kāśikā is held by him upon the tip of his trident.
This one [Lord], desiring to show grace to the worlds, has become fivefold;
whatever form a devotee meditates upon, that very form is assumed by Him in an instant. (39)
In this regard, the person who perceives a distinction between them—whether by offering praise in one place or criticism in another—attains the Avīci hell. (40)
He went to twenty-one hells for many years;
therefore, he became known as Bhasmāsura’s son, Durāsada by name. 41.
Having approached Śukra, he acquired the five-syllabled lore;
for a thousand divine years, he remained standing on the tip of a single big toe.
Without food, like a piece of wood, covered by an anthill and reduced to mere bones, he remained with only his eyes visible and chanted the supreme mantra. || 43 ||
Pleased by his suffering,
he whose ten arms and five faces were adorned with a garland of skulls came to grant him that boon.
Wielding a trident and a hand-drum, adorned with a mass of matted hair, bearing the Gaṅgā, possessing three eyes, and his body smeared with funeral ashes; 45.
The bull-bannered god, mounted upon his bull, adorned with the crescent moon,
and filled with compassion for Aparṇā, spoke to the preeminent Daitya.
Śiva said:
Arise, arise! May it be well with you; you have been greatly exhausted by your ascetic penance.
I shall grant you your desire; choose that which resides in your heart. 47.
Ka said:
Then, opening his eyes and joining his palms in reverence, the Asura bowed down and praised that Great Lord, the bestower of boons, with great satisfaction. 48.

O Lord, you are the cause of the universe, whose form is supreme bliss; your body transcends the perishable and the imperishable, and you are the creator of the transformations of the three qualities.
Transcending all qualities, consisting of pure knowledge, and knowing the arrangement of both the manifest and the unmanifest;
his body is the object of meditation for sages, and he bestows grace upon all devotees. || 50 ||
You are the cause of infinite universes, the benefactor of the virtuous,
filled with indivisible bliss, and the bestower of unfailing fruits.
He is the support of all, the endurer of all, augmented by all powers,
and possesses the essential nature of earth, air, water, fire, and light.
Today my eyes have become blessed by penance, and my birth has borne fruit, since I have seen Your true form directly; my sin has gone to its ultimate dissolution. 53.
"O Lord, that which is never within the range of the hearts of yogis or the words of the Vedas—I now entreat you; it behoves you to grant that to me.
Śiva said:
Choose without hesitation; I shall give you everything, even that which is most difficult to obtain.
Highly gratified by his hymn of praise, his asceticism, and his devotion,
the sage spoke;
then he chose freedom from fear from the exceedingly gracious Lord Sadāśiva.
"May death not come to me from those born of the four wombs—neither from Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, or Piśācas, nor from Devas, Dānavas, or Kinnaras. (56)
For sages, men, gandharvas, and serpents wandering in the forest would surely tremble upon seeing my form at the forefront of battle. || 57 ||
"O illustrious one, let all the gods grant me sovereignty over the realm of the Suras;
may I have constant mindfulness of your feet and unwavering devotion. (58)
Śiva said:
"Without one particular Śakti, I cannot grant fearlessness to all the gods.
Someone born from the splendor of Śakti, having conquered him, will restore [the world] to life."
Placing his foot upon your head, he will hold it there incessantly;

Gṛtsamada said:
Having thus granted those boons to him, Śiva vanished;
though difficult to approach, he returned to his own abode filled with intense joy.
Whoever recites this hymn shall obtain all their desires.

The Sage said:
Then, due to the pride of excellence acquired from Śiva, that king of the Daityas, being utterly deluded, could not endure his own self. || 1 ||
In former times, desiring to conquer the earth, he mounted his horse;
with his locks of hair tied back and his ear-rings shining, he set forth. || 2 ||
With sword in hand and bow in grasp, adorned with two quivers,
he wore a most costly garland composed of jewels, pearls, and gems.
Adorned with a musk tilaka, clothed in divine garments and a fine bodice,
his face radiant with betel-leaf, he was accompanied by two female attendants.
By the prowess of their own arms, they have repeatedly conquered many heroes;
endowed with great strength, they marched on both his flanks.
That fourfold army, intent on conquering the earth,
covered the vast sky with dust as if it were the expanse of the ocean.
Whichever hero was prosperous, him alone he conquered;
then, taking thousands of jewels and riches, [he departed].
The powerful king, having brought everyone under his control, appointed his own trusted and mighty men to those positions in various offices. 8.
And those who were unarmed, having surrendered their taxes, went to him alone for refuge;
while those who were exceedingly timid protected the kingdom even after abandoning it.
Even though he was difficult to overcome, he brought them under his control through messengers alone;
having thus conquered the circle of the earth, he desired to conquer Śakra.
Having learned of the power of that wicked one, the king of the gods suddenly set out with his army toward the city protected by Śakra.
Having fled, he went to a cave together with the gods and his family;
at that very moment, Viṣṇu departed from his abode and went to the Ocean of Milk.
Having placed his head upon the lap of Lakṣmī, Madhusūdana lay asleep;
while the wielder of the trident, having abandoned the peak of Kailāsa, had gone to Kāśī.
The four-faced Brahmā went along with him;
wherever the king of the Daityas left his footstep, there he followed.
He stationed his own powerful messenger, a most intimate friend;
thus, having conquered the gods through sheer arrogance, the one of great strength [remained]. 15.
He dwelt in the city of Bhasmaka within the territory of the fishermen, which was renowned everywhere in the worlds by the name Mukundapura. || 16 ||
In that city formerly dwelt the powerful King Bhasmasura,
to whom Śaṅkara had granted a wondrous boon.
"He shall die on whose head you place your hand.
Thus was the boon granted to the Daitya, who was impelled by his wicked intent.
Then the wicked one went to place his hand upon the head of the bridegroom, who was out of sight, as well as that of the giver of the bride; however, the Lord of Girijā protected him.
Having seen him, the powerful Viṣṇu, who holds the discus in his hand,
assumed the beautiful form of Mohinī and went into his presence.
He said, "O best of men, if you abide by my word, then I shall become your wife. He replied with joy, "So be it."
She then began to dance at his word, and he indeed danced;
as she displayed her expressions, he likewise displayed his.
She placed her hand upon his own head, and at that very moment,
the Daitya of wicked conduct was reduced to ashes, bringing about his own end.
Mukunda also remained there, and the city became renowned by his name;
it grants immediate supreme perfection to men who perform their religious observances.
That deluding power bestows all desires upon men through devotion;
remaining there, he rules the three worlds, difficult to approach due to his pride.
Out of pride, he said to his ministers: "How has the three worlds been conquered by my own prowess as I triumph over the enemies of the Asuras?"
Then those ministers said: "It has been released, not conquered by you;
for there is no equal to that tenth section anywhere. (27)
As long as that city, which was not conquered even by Śaṅkara when he was aided by all the gods and is served by them, remains unconquered by you, your manliness is in vain.
