accompanied by mantras from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Having gratified other Brahmins with gifts of sacrificial fees and jewels,
he himself took the initiation for dwelling in the forest and made his inquiries.
The king, remaining with his own forces, dismissed them all;
thereafter, he, whose arm bore the battle-axe, ruled over this earth.
And according to the principles of the Dharmaśāstras, he acquired fame through renunciation;
by virtue of his prowess and strength, he became renowned throughout the three worlds. || 15 ||
Having fashioned an image of Mandāra from the clay of Ḍhuṇḍhi, he wore it around his neck;
he never performed worship without śamī wood and dūrvā grass.
He enjoyed various pleasures and many women according to the law;
having begotten sons and given gifts for a thousand years, he [departed]. || 17 ||
Afterwards, he ruled the kingdom through his son and went to heaven;
remaining in the celestial realm for many kalpas, he took on the form of Dhuṇḍhi.
The sage said:
Thus has the power of the śamī tree been described to you in brief,
as well as the merit of its worship, in connection with the mandāra.
Therefore, O sage, you too should worship me with flowers from the Śamī or Mandāra trees;
a flower or leaf offered with devotion becomes as sweet as nectar.
Having offered prohibited leaves, flowers, and so forth, one shall go to hell.
Whichever deity is one's primary object of worship, that alone is acceptable; others may be offered as well.
By offering [the senses] without distinction, the devotee incurs no fault;
having thus worshipped all five deities, one should attain total absorption in them. 22.

The one of sattvic nature merges into the Divine; the rajasic attains similarity of form; the tamasic, through both of these, attains proximity, while the one of purely tamasic nature attains residence in the same world.
One who worships him shall attain [his grace]; indeed, devotion is never in vain.
Vyāsa said: What is the world of Vināyaka, and in which world does he abide? (24)
O Brahmin, you ought to sever this doubt of mine right now;
whom else should I question, setting aside you who are omniscient? O sir! 25.
Brahmā said:
"I also spoke it to Nārada, and he to Mudgala;
and it was narrated by him to the King of Kāśī—the auspicious world of Vaināyaka."
Formerly, he was created by that very power which grants all desires;
Vināyaka himself gave him the name Nijaloka. || 27 ||
The King of Kāśī, situated in his celestial chariot, beheld with his physical eye him whom,
having attained, neither woman nor man experiences suffering or the pairs of opposites.
Having attained a form of light, he dwells there for a Brahmā-kalpa;
remaining there, he enjoys the ocean of sugarcane juice.
That which remains imperishable even at the time of the great dissolution—
that is the eternal seat of that God, the place of his sleep.
Success and wisdom serve him; the Sāmaveda sings of him;
and the wish-fulfilling tree grants whatever is desired by that man. 31.
By the power of that [merit], unimagined riches arise here;
all the worlds of the gods have been described by me many times over. || 32 ||
The power of Gaṇeśa’s own world is beyond my capacity for description; therefore, it has been told in brief. What else do you wish to hear? 33.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits Arising from the Offering of the Śamī and Mandāra Trees," in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa. || 49 ||
The total number of verses from the beginning: 6224 + 33 = 6257.
Chapter Fifty, titled "Description of the Verses on Gaṇeśa," ends here.
The Sage said:
And how did the King of Kāśī attain that supreme state through the instruction of Mudgala? You should explain that to me. || 1 ||
Ka said:
In the course of his pilgrimage to sacred fords, Mudgala went to that king;
having honored him, the king questioned that omniscient sage.
The king said:
"What is the world of Vināyaka, and how can it be attained by me?
The sage said:
"‘The world of one's own bliss’ and ‘one's own world’—these two [expressions] are thus [synonymous]. (3)
There exists a world of Vaināyaka known by its famous name;
it shall come into being when the two Daityas, Devāntaka and Narāntaka, are born.
Vināyaka also will descend into a human womb to slay them;
he, in the form of a child, shall perform wondrous deeds of marvelous prowess.
When he is born in the house of a poor man devoted to Śukla, that one of great strength will act according to his own will in this world of men.
Having bestowed upon Indra the unerring prosperity that is difficult to attain even for the White One (Brahmā),
he will display his prowess when brought here for the sake of the marriage.
O King, O mighty-armed King of Kāśī, when he comes to your house, you shall attain your own world through devotion to him. 8.
Ka said:
Having spoken thus, when he had departed, the high-minded King of Kāśī, practicing devotion to Gaṇeśa, remained awaiting the appointed time. 9.
Then, after a long period of time, that omnipresent Vināyaka,
who indeed possesses a form for his divine play, descended into the house of Kaśyapa.
Various kinds of Daityas were slain and various sports were performed;
he immediately dispelled the poverty of Śukla and then took food at his house.
The mighty one returned once more to the palace of the King of Kāśī,
after the two immensely powerful Daityas, Devāntaka and Narāntaka, had been slain.
Having departed for his own realm of bliss situated in the midst of the Ocean of Milk,
the King of Kāśī, however, constantly brooded over him due to the pain of separation.
Thinking, "This very Vināyaka is embracing some man," he perceived the entire world within the assembly hall as being of that same nature.
Day and night he beheld it, and he too attained absorption in that [vision].
At times, the king remained there without food. || 15 ||
Sometimes he would eat only a single mouthful according to his whim;
at other times, the king would laugh or even dance about.
Seeing Vināyaka in his dream, he slept for a long time;
while the king remained thus, the ministers fell into a most grievous anxiety.
"If the people were to find out, then a foreign army would descend upon us.
While the ministers were thinking thus in the royal palace, (the king spoke). 18.
At that very moment, Mudgala emerged from his meditation and approached the king;
having attained awakening upon seeing him, the king bowed down to the sage.
Having seated him on a seat and worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, he then spoke with palms joined in reverence: "Blessed is my lineage, blessed is my birth! (20)
O Sage, our parents and our eyes have become blessed by the sight of you;
for by your grace, the supreme state that delivers men from the cycle of worldly existence has been attained.
"Great was my sorrow from that insult; yet I have seen you through my merit.
Then the brahmin, highly gratified by his words, spoke to him.
The sage said:
"A self-restrained soul such as you has never been seen nor heard of before.
I am well-pleased by your worship; I shall grant you your desire."
Ka said: Satisfied by those words, the King of Kāśī spoke to him:
"O Sage, by this very body, [one reaches] the world of one's own bliss. (24)
"And I wish to remain there for a long time, yet I have no wealth at all.
Then Mudgala, being highly pleased by those words, spoke.
O King, by means of this inert body, you shall attain the realm of your own bliss belonging to Gaṇeśa, from which there is no return. 26.
Having enjoyed the abundance of food here for five thousand years,
you shall thereafter attain your own bliss for the duration of a Brahma-kalpa.
The king said:
"O sage, tell me truly, what is that world like and what is its name?
By what merit can it be reached? I have heard of all the worlds. (28)
Mudgala said:
Listen, O King, to the greatness of the sage Kapila as it was heard by me;
those things which are generally well-known throughout all the worlds have already been heard by you. 29.
The course of this world is exceedingly difficult to fathom, O King;
its name is "the divine world," and another is "one's own world. (30)
O Mahāmati, that Vināyaka resides upon the seat of Kāmadāyinī, which extends for five thousand yojanas.
This divine one, named Svānanda, shines upon the ground of precious gold, illuminating the directions; he dwells in the midst of the ocean of sugarcane juice.
Neither by the Vedas, nor by gifts, nor by vows, nor by sacrifices, nor even by recitations,
nor by various kinds of austerities, is this ever attained at any time.
Through the grace of Vināyaka, [this state] is attained by constant devotion;
here the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnarāja), existing both as the collective whole and as the individual, ever abides. 34.
With his feet he pervaded the seven netherworlds and the heads of Śeṣa; with his two ears he pervaded the tortoise Kūrma and all the directions.
Having obstructed even the sky with his hair, he stands upon the foundational lotus;
the merit-maker meditates upon him within the fire-wheel at the center of the brows, in that two-petaled [lotus]. 36.
Joined with the khecarīmudrā, one is unable to meditate on anything else;
[one beholds] the thousand-petaled lotus of the universe, radiant with splendor. 37.
Therein, the nature of fire exists within the heart;
the navel-cakra has ten petals, and the auspicious one at the genitals has six petals.
In the region of the throat is a sixteen-spoked [wheel], where everywhere Vighnarāja shines in the form of radiant energy, like the Creator in the world of truth (Satyaloka). || 39 ||
The twelve-spoked Vaikuṇṭha is there, where Viṣṇu is eternally stationed;
he who has five faces resides in the lotus of the throat, just as [Śiva] dwells on Kailāsa with his attendants. 40.
He has the moon, sun, and fire as his eyes; the circle of the earth is his vast belly;
he pervades the twenty-one heavens; and he possesses medicinal herbs as his body hair.
He whose single drop of dharma shines as the rivers and oceans,
and within whose very being the entire cosmic eggs appear like mere motes of dust— 42.
Thirty-three crores of gods and thousands of living beings appear like gnats that have entered the Udumbara tree.
O King, I shall describe the creation of that world in brief:
its lofty peak, which rivals the summit of Mount Kailāsa. (44)
There, in a void extending for a thousand yojanas, inaccessible even to the foremost of sages, there is a single power known by the name Bhrāmikā (the Whirling One). 45.
Where bees indeed wander from what is approved, yet remain bright;
there the Support-Power (Ādhāra-śakti) is situated upon his head, seated in the lotus posture. 46.
That [energy] on her head, resembling gold, is the bestower of desires;
upon her head is a most magnificent seat, radiant like ten million suns.
Bearing a formidable mass of matted hair and likewise a face,
she shone like a thousand suns, illuminating the ten directions.
It was ten thousand yojanas wide and as many long;
in its center, it was one yojana in length and possessed a brilliance equal to countless suns.
The world of its own bliss shines forth, wherein countless radiant houses made of gold and jewels gleam, adorned with ivory and pearls. 50.
Only through his grace is that which is free from suffering and delusion attained;
beyond that shines the supreme, like a sea of sugarcane juice.
In its center was an auspicious lotus-pond endowed with a thousand petals;
upon it shone a thousand-petaled lotus like the moon.
O King, upon the pedestal situated at its pericarp, fashioned from jewels and gold and draped with divine garments, Vināyaka lies there. 53.
Siddhi and Buddhi always joyfully perform the massaging of his feet with supreme devotion; likewise, the Sāmaveda, embodied in three forms, does the same.
The scriptures sing his praises, the personified treatises offer him hymns of praise, and all the Purāṇas describe his excellent qualities. 55.
There he appeared in the form of a young elephant, adorned with a trunk like a staff, with tender limbs, the hue of dawn, large eyes, and tusks. (56)
Wearing a crown and earrings, with a shining musk tilaka, he is the self-sovereign lord;
he wears divine garlands and garments, and is anointed with divine perfumes.
He was holding a garland adorned with clusters of pearls and precious gems.
Possessing the splendor of infinite millions of suns and having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
he instantly destroys the sins of men through mere remembrance, just as the Gaṅgā is remembered.
O King, the two Śaktis, Tejovatī and Jvālinī, always stand by the sides of his couch, resembling a thousand suns in brilliance.
There is neither cold nor old age there, nor fatigue, perspiration, or even lassitude;
neither hunger, thirst, nor suffering ever arises.
Those who were there due to their great merit became immersed in the lake of bliss, where the all-pervading Knower of the Universe dwells in the form of a child. 62.
Mudgala said:
Thus has the world of Gaṇeśa been described to you according to my understanding;
therefore, O Lord, worship him alone with undivided devotion. 63.
Ka said:
Having spoken thus, the sage Mudgala departed for his own abode;
the King of Kāśī became entirely devoted to the worship of Gaṇeśa.
Having ruled the kingdom for fifteen thousand years,
he indeed ascended a celestial vehicle with this very body and departed for that abode of his own bliss.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "Description of the World of Gaṇeśa," in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa. || 50 ||
The total number of verses from the beginning: 6257 + 65 = 6322.
Chapter Fifty-one (2.051).
Vyāsa said:
How was Vighnarāja propitiated by that King of Kāśī, and how did he, possessing a body of skin, attain the unsurpassed station? || 1 ||
"Tell me this, O Blessed One; hearing it, I am never satiated.
Ka said:
"Listen well, O one of great intelligence, to this story that destroys all sin. (2)
O Great Sage, I shall relate an ancient history of how the king,
free from all taints, attained the realm of his own bliss.
Having fully realized the greatness [of Gaṇeśa] from Mudgala, that ocean of knowledge,
he became devoted to Gaṇeśa in body, mind, and speech.
With great devotion, he gave gifts of cows, numerous gifts of elephants,
as well as chariots, horses, houses, grain, and even goats— these ten kinds of gifts.
Day after day, for the pleasure of Vināyaka, he indeed gratifies the Brahmins with meals of sweet foods and with wealth and other gifts.
Day after day, on the auspicious occasion of the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Māgha falling on a Tuesday, he prayed for firm devotion to Gaṇeśa.
At dawn, he performed his bath, the ritual of twilight, and the daily duties;
then, having adorned himself with various ornaments and garments, [he set out].
Having summoned all the worlds, the brahmins, and other friends,
he honored them with various jewels and heaps of fine garments.
Again and again the king watched their arrival in the celestial chariot; he repeatedly tried to dissuade them as they desired to depart from the assembly hall.
Then Vināyaka, knowing the time of that high-souled one had come,
dispatched two messengers with a most resplendent celestial chariot.
Gaṇeśa said:
"O Pramoda and Āmoda, go to the surface of the earth and bring that devotee of mine here, seated upon his excellent celestial chariot."
Ka said: Having received that command and bowed to him, the two of them then took a celestial chariot from the world of heaven and approached the King of Kāśī. 13.
The worlds, scorched by that radiance, thought it was the fire of universal destruction;
some, moreover, thought it was like the falling of lightning in a cloudless sky.
Others conjectured that he was falling toward the solar disc,
while others heard the sound of bells, musical instruments, and the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Having heard this, others recognized that the vehicle had arrived through the grace of Gaṇeśa,
having emerged in the courtyard of the King of Kāśī, resplendent with glory.
The two hosts named Pramoda and Amoda arrived in the presence of the King,
wearing divine garments and resplendent with celestial ornaments.
Adorned with divine garlands, unguents, and the like, and possessing a divine radiance like two Smaras,
the king bowed to those two who were the very embodiments of Vināyakas and sat upon his own throne.
Having quickly seated and honored them, while the king was about to question them,
those two messengers then spoke as all the world listened.
Listen, O King, I shall speak these auspicious words concerning Vaināyaka:
"In the three worlds, there is no king more devoted or more pleasing to him than you;
they meditate upon you day and night and speak of your virtues incessantly. (20)
You are blessed; you, being meritorious, have made your birth fruitful.
By the sight of you, my great darkness of sin has been destroyed most swiftly.
"We do not know what penance you performed in previous births;
this Vināyaka, who is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, has appeared here in the form of a child. (22)
Having come to your home, he displayed various divine sports;
for the greatness of the God, the devotee of God, is not within the range of perception. || 23 ||
Since the god Vināyaka contemplates you at all times,
a divine vehicle endowed with great majesty has been sent for your sake.
"O Yavas, since you have not brought you under the power of our command, bring the King of Kashi here quickly; thus did the Lord speak to us. (25)
While all the worlds were listening, he heard those words of the two of them;
submerged in the ocean of nectar, he shed tears of joy again and again.
Having regained his bodily state and bowed to them, he said:
"O parents, my birth is blessed; my steadfastness, devotion, and prosperity are complete. (27)
That these two auspicious feet of yours, which are difficult for me to behold, have been obtained by me in the form of Vināyaka to lead me to the supreme state. || 28 ||
Situated in the midst of the ocean of sugarcane juice, it is difficult to perceive for those with physical eyes—
that which is devoid of qualities, consisting of consciousness and bliss, the supreme, eternal Brahman.

That which is the cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, which is beyond the reach of the senses, which is subtler than the subtlest atom and yet vaster than the vastest; (30)
All-pervading and unattached, possessing form yet the enjoyer of qualities; having manifold forms and yet formless, it is intent upon removing the burden of the earth.
"Thus, this great compassion has been shown toward me, who have become a pauper.
Having said this, he paid homage, embraced them all, and looked upon them.
The messenger said, "Ascend first, preceded by a prostration;
afterwards, I shall ascend this celestial chariot, which is difficult for mortals to attain."
Having paid homage to the two ministers and placed his son in their hands, he said:
"The protection of the subjects must be carried out by you both through righteousness and through force."
"This was spoken by Mudgala, and this has been experienced by me";
having said this, he ascended the supreme vehicle with his physical body.
But once it was presided over by the two honored messengers in manifold ways,
his body, as he ascended there, became radiant like the sun.
Honored by them with divine perfumes, ornaments, and garments,
the two departed with the speed of the wind, making themselves visible to the king.
The world of those of evil deeds— of bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas—
is there, where they, with deformed shapes, have their feet upward and their faces downward.
Some had their backs facing forward and others had eyes in their heads;
some had eyes in their chests and others had eyes in their backs; they had narrow throats and large bellies.
Just as atoms whirl within a sunbeam passing through a lattice, so too do those in great suffering wander in the sky in manifold forms. 40.
"O best of messengers, tell me, who is this person in the world? He replied: ||| 41 ||
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Abode Named Svānandabhuvana," in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning: 6322 + 41 = 6363.
Chapter Fifty-two (2.052).
The two messengers said:
O best of kings, O lord of the earth, this world belongs to the pretas, bhūtas, and piśācas;
those who commit slander, calumny, and theft go here.
Then he beheld before him the worlds of the Asuras and Rākṣasas,
where those beings of various forms, with hair standing erect, were terrifying.
Seeing those two, who had terrible faces, protruding tongues, voices like thunderclouds,
and countenances resembling mountains or sacrificial fire-pits, he questioned them again.
"To whom does this city belong? O messengers, tell me as I ask you. They both replied, "This world belongs to the wicked Dānavas and Rākṣasas."
There stood sinners who were devoid of Vedic and Smārta rites;
then, in front of that, he beheld a world frequented by Gandharvas.
There, the houses were made of silver and gold, and the ground was of jewels and gold;
the men and women delighted in sensual pleasures and were skilled in dancing and singing.
Seeing that city which brings such exceeding happiness, he questioned them again: "O messengers, tell me who this city belongs to, as I ask you. (7)
The two of them said:
"O singers, it is by great merit that one attains this unsurpassed city, which is like a city of the Gandharvas found among the abodes of the gods. (8)
The great city of the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, and Guhyakas is accessible through various vows, gifts, and the accumulation of merit.

And those two messengers subsequently showed the king the most magnificent city of Indra, beautiful and earned through a hundred horse-sacrifices. (They both showed the king that most magnificent and lovely city of Indra, acquired by means of a hundred aśvamedha sacrifices. || 10 ||

[The state] attainable through the gift of gold, jewels, cows, chariots, horses, and elephants, as well as by various merits such as bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) and other rites, [is not equal to this]. 11.
There, they showed him the delightful and auspicious abode of Indra;
having observed it, the king said to them, "That which was heard has now indeed been seen."
Then, showing the auspicious world of Agni first to the king,
they showed him that place where many performers of the Agnihotra sacrifice, possessing the brilliance of fire, shine forth in great numbers.
Then they showed the king the world of Yama, both auspicious and inauspicious,
where those who have performed meritorious deeds go, as do those who have committed sins.
That Dharma shines for those of good deeds, yet it is cruel to those of evil deeds;
the well-performed leads to all enjoyments, while the ill-performed leads even to the hells.
Living beings experience the fruits of their respective karmas in manifold ways;
they are boiled in the Kumbhīpāka hell and cut by sword-leaved trees.
They are beaten with iron hammers and even pierced by thorns;
they dwell in the Tāmisra and Andhatāmisra hells, as well as in the Pit of Worms filled with pus.
Those evil-doing creatures are cast into a terrible hell;
seeing them, he closes his eyes, saying, "Go, go! (18)
Then the two of them showed him the supreme world of Kubera,
which was most wonderful and far superior to the world of Śakra.
Resplendent houses endowed with jewels and gold were obtained by him through the gift of jewels and gold,
as well as through millions of gifts on the scales.
Those highly fortunate ones attain the supreme world of Kubera;
thereafter, those two showed him that supreme world of Varuṇa.
Obtainable through visiting sacred fords and the giving of food, surpassing even the abode of Kubera,
all dwell within the waters with dried bodies, yet they enjoy happiness.
There they see givers of water from step-wells, wells, and tanks;
beyond that, the two show them the world of Vāyu, which brings great happiness.
Those who offer fans in the summer, along with sandalwood paste and water scented with camphor,
dwell in the world of Vāyu, sporting there according to their own will.
Then those two showed him the world of the Sun, which is difficult to attain;
they were devoted to the practice of the five fires and dedicated to the worship of the Sun.
Having attained their desires, all those sages, possessing the splendor of the sun,
dwell free from affliction for a hundred kalpas of Brahmā.
Then, through the gift of pearls and gold resulting from the Soma sacrifice, they both showed the king the world of the stars and the world of the moon.
Those great-souled ones attained this world through their supreme merit;
thereafter, they both showed Goloka to the king.
Those who give thousands of cows to Brahmins according to the prescribed rite indeed dwell in Goloka for as many kalpas as there are hairs on those cows. 29.
Then they showed them the ancient Satyaloka,
where those of true vows, knowers of the Vedas, and devoted to the study of the Vedas reside.

Those who follow the conduct of the virtuous, those who know the scriptures, those who recite the Purāṇas, those devoted to the gift of food, performers of sacrifices, and those who frequent sacred fords; || 31 ||
Those Brahmins who do not accept gifts, who perform services for others,
who are devoted to austerity, and who are intent on giving— such as these go to the world of truth (Satyaloka).
It was eight thousand gavyūtis in width and extended for the same distance in length;
there Brahmā dwells with hosts of sages and eminent royal seers.
Being praised day and night by the celestial sages, the Dānavas, and the Gandharvas and Apsarases, he is served by those devoted to him with great piety.
Seeing that city where houses gleaming on all sides bore the names of Indra’s abodes, the king was struck with wonder and then spoke to those two.
The king said:
"I am blessed and I am graced by the compassionate Gaṇeśa,
and by you both, since the heavenly realms so difficult to attain have been seen."
Ka said:
"Those two should show him again that renowned Vaikuṇṭha, which exists in the three worlds;
there indeed go the Vaiṣṇavas who are intent on devotion. (37)
He is the most excellent in all the worlds, for whom no comparison exists;
neither Śeṣa nor the self-born Brahmā with his many mouths is capable of describing him.

One who bathes with vigor, one who bathes with fish-skin, one who bathes with sheep-skin, one who gives food with sesame seeds, one who gives cows, one who studies songs, and he who is helpful to living beings; || 39 ||
He quickly goes to the world of Viṣṇu, which extends for five thousand yojanas and is fashioned by Viśvakarman, radiant with the splendor of the sun and moon. 40.
The temples shine with jewels, gold, and silver, wherein darkness never enters at all due to the rays of the gems. 41.
Where the slayer of demons dwells, accompanied by his retinue and endowed with splendor,
that best of kings rejoiced upon seeing it, owing to his accumulation of merit.
Then they both showed him Kailāsa, the abode of the Lord of the Mountain,
situated upon the delightful peak of Meru, which extends for ten thousand yojanas.
There, palaces shine with the brilliance of the sun and moon;
there, those who perform the recitation of the five-syllable mantra and the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya reside.
The meritorious ones, devoted to many means of practice, go there;
having seen him, the king spoke by the grace of Vināyaka.
Having seen all the celestial worlds, which bestow merit upon men by the mere sight of them,
neither the sun nor the moon shines beyond that point for a distance of ten thousand yojanas.
He proceeded by means of the splendor of his celestial chariot, and they could see nothing at all;
the king, however, heard an unbearable sound resembling the roar of clouds.
The king asked them both, "Whose sound is this that is heard on all sides from the bees, which shine like the finest mountains?"
"When shall I behold the lotus-feet of the Lord?"—while he was thus clearly thinking, the king saw before him a firm spear capable of producing whirling motion. 49.
Seeing her, who resembled many suns, who was capable of swallowing thousands of cosmic eggs,
whose mouth was wide open, and who was terrifying, the king would have fainted.
Then the two messengers, having comforted him, led the king forward;
from there, he [went] to Ādhāraśakti, who was even more terrifying than the former.
Upon seeing her standing upon his head— a Bhrāmarī with formidable hair, protruding lips, a long tongue, and radiant with splendor— the king trembled.
Reassured, as he proceeded forward, he beheld the Wish-granting One (Kāmadāyinī), the Supportive Power (Ādhāraśakti), lying down and extending for ten thousand yojanas. || 53 ||
That city stands firm even as its mountains whirl about from the turning of the wind of its breath,
despite its bodies being as hard as adamant.
The two messengers spoke to the king: "Behold your own city of Ānanda, auspicious and resembling ten million suns, in which you find such complete satisfaction through meditation. (55)
There, other houses shine, interspersed with jewels and gold,
and constructed by the thousands from pearls, silver, and sun-stones.
Where the floors were paved with blue sapphire, where the men possessed the luster of fire,
and where there shone ponds, wells, lakes, and reservoirs.
Its waters are clear, cool, and blue, with banks of yellow jewels;
by drinking its water, men suffer neither old age, nor hunger, nor disease. (58)
The pleasure gardens are pure, adorned with various trees and creepers,
and where divine medicinal herbs shine by day with the brilliance of ten million suns.
There, on the surface of the moon— which is free from spots and always descends downward during the night— women of playful charm behold their own faces.
Having reached the shore of the ocean of sugarcane juice, where the fragrance of the Yātrā-flower groves dispels the fatigue of those who wander there, they emerged with great joy.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of the World of Self-Bliss," in the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The total number of verses from the beginning: 6363 + 61 = 6424.
Chapter fifty-three, titled "Description of the Attainment of Royal Bliss," ends here.
Brahmā said:
In the midst of that [lake] was a white lotus-pond endowed with a thousand-petaled lotuses, where the juice of the *papuri* fruit—attainable only through a mass of merit—is easily found. ||1||
In that [lake] was an excellent lotus, resembling the thousand-rayed sun;
in its center sat the most enchanting couch of that god.
It was furnished with celestial coverings, well-perfumed with divine incenses,
possessed of various divine flowers, and filled with heaps of jewels that shone with their own radiance.
Illuminating all the cardinal and intermediate directions with his splendor,
that Vināyaka lay there while being fanned with whisks.
Resembling ten million moons, adorned with various ornaments and decorated with serpents,
his trunk was like a plantain pillar and beautiful with its tusks.
Clad in divine garments, with an eye upon his forehead and wearing a crown,
he bore earrings, armlets, a seal-ring, and a costly waist-thread.
His two feet, which are the cause of accomplishment and wisdom, were indeed massaged;
he was fanned with white whisks by the powers of *aṇimā* and *garimā*.
Jvālinī and Tejinī were stationed on both sides, blazing;
his limbs were smeared with divine fragrance, and he was adorned with celestial garlands.
Māhīmā stood nearby, holding a vessel for rinsing the mouth and a parasol adorned with gold and jewels, while Prathimā held the water. 9.
Then, holding the two messengers by the hand, they stood before that king and awaited an opportunity to speak; thereupon, the Lord perceived their intention.
Those two messengers said to the god: "This person has been brought here by your command;
having prostrated, we both stand at a distance awaiting your further orders. (11)
When he had awakened, the king bowed to him with palms joined in reverence and said with supreme affection: "Truly, my lineage is blessed today! (12)
My parents, my birth, my learning, my austerity, my vision, and my sons and others—
by whom all this was shown to me, that Brahman, your pair of feet worthy of meditation.
Such majesty was never seen by me in the world of Brahmā, nor on Kailāsa, nor even in the realm of Śakra; indeed, it was not seen anywhere else in any other world.
The messenger said, "Please be seated," and so they both sat down.
Then he beheld Vināyaka in the form of a child, possessing two arms. 15.
By whom those two Daityas, Devāntaka and Narāntaka, were slain—he who was exceedingly fair, with delicate limbs, resembling snow and camphor. 16.
At that time, his great throat being choked with tears, he was unable to speak;
instead, he drenched those two feet with the overflowing streams of tears of joy.
Recognizing his great devotion, the Lord of Obstacles raised him up and embraced him;
having smelled the crown of his head like a father, he treated him as a son who had been away for a long time.
The god also became choked with tears; both were covered in horripilation.
Both were submerged in an ocean of bliss like two sages who have transcended the body.
Then Vināyaka, in the form of a child, spoke these words:
"O father, whatever was done by me while playing in many ways in your house," (20)
For you have indeed forgiven everything, whether it was auspicious or inauspicious;
many Daityas have been slain and the burden of the earth has been removed.
The virtuous people have been protected and the bridges of dharma have been established;
by your command, I have returned once more to Kaśyapa, the creator of the world.
Having bowed to him, I reached my own world and this one of universal splendor;
yet, reflecting only upon you, I find no rest anywhere. 23.
Having understood your initial disposition, I sent Mudgala, the bull among sages, to your home; and through his grace, you [attained this]. || 24 ||
This state, which is inaccessible even to the gods led by Brahmā and to the foremost of sages, has been attained by Mudgala through his devotion, and now by you as well. (25)
Ka said:
Having drunk that nectar of his speech and having bowed down again and again, the king, summoning his fortitude, spoke and praised him according to his understanding. (26)
The King said:
O Lord, I bow to your lotus-feet, the most worthy of meditation for Brahmā and the other gods, for the sake of auspiciousness;
those feet, marked with excellent signs such as the lotus, noose, sword, and axe, remove all obstacles for your own devotees. 27.
That which is worshipped by Viṣṇu, Śiva, and other gods, as well as by men who perform manifold tasks—
that which is repeatedly capable of destroying obstacles and brings the rain of nectar to those scorched by the cycle of worldly existence— 28.

I bow to your lotus-face, O Lord, which possesses three eyes—the fire, the sun, and the moon as its pupils—and whose power is seen to uproot the threefold suffering by the sprinkling of the nectar of your compassionate side-glance. 29.
I bow to you, O Lord, to your lotus-hand which has struck down hosts of Daityas with many weapons;
O Lord of the Gods, it grants fearlessness to countless devotees and serves as a supporting hand for crossing the well of saṃsāra. 30.

O Gaṇeśa, you alone sustain all things through your nature as Sattva; having attained the state of Rajas, you create; and by being the substratum of the quality of Tamas, you destroy the moving and the unmoving—all of which remain under your control. 31.
He who, with a pure mind, worships you incessantly—you run away from him after having overcome all obstacles;
indeed, he brings you under his control and sleeps in happiness, while you run toward him like a cow toward her calf. 32.

Others who worship [the gods], having encountered various miseries and wandering manifoldly on the wheel of saṃsāra, may at some time obtain grace; they too, having attained human birth, worship [the Lord]. (33)
Someone might measure the host of stars in the sky or the torrents of rain-clouds;
yet even Śeṣa, the Creator himself, is not capable of enumerating your multitude of virtues, even over many series of years.
If, according to your view, there were no form (ākṛti), then the injunctions for worship and ritual action would be in vain;
likewise, how could the manifold expansion of qualities, the play of primordial nature (prakṛti), and the enjoyment of living beings exist? (35)
If there is association with the virtuous, there will be their favorable grace, dedication to righteous action, and constant remembrance of the Truth;
through your great compassion, the purification of the mind, knowledge, and liberation will not be difficult to attain. (36)
Ka said:
Having heard this hymn of praise, Vināyaka was thoroughly pleased and said to the King of Kāśī, "Choose a boon that resides in your heart. (37)
The king said:
"The purpose for which I have come has been accomplished by you;
let that be ordained whereby there may be no more birth or death from this point forward. (38)
Ka said:
Pleased by the hymn of praise, he said "So be it" to that one of divine body and established him nearby for a duration of ten million kalpas and yugas.
O Sage, this hymn was obtained by me through his grace;
it was spoken by me to Nārada, and Nārada [spoke it] to Gautama.
He too spoke to all the sages about that which bestows the fruits of all desires,
which grants knowledge and liberation, which destroys obstacles, and which is supremely purifying.
The man who recites this shall obtain devotion in the presence of Gaṇeśa;
and the man who recites it at the three junctions of the day shall obtain knowledge if he desires knowledge.
One desiring a son shall obtain sons; one desiring victory shall obtain victory.
Thus everything that was asked by you, O sage, has been fully explained.
[This was] the narrative of the King of Kāśī; what else do you wish to hear?
Bhṛgu said:
Having heard these words of Brahmā, Vyāsa became free from doubt and [uttered] these words. 44.
Sumati again asked for another account in detail.
Vyāsa said:
"The poverty of Śukla, who was exceedingly destitute, was removed through diligent effort. (45)
Tell me what that god did after eating poor food in his house and meeting the King of Kāśī, and what the King of Kāśī did. 46.
How were those two Daityas slain, how was the burden of the earth removed, and how was dharma established? Tell me that according to the facts.
Ka said:
O Sage, I shall relate in brief the life of him who appeared in the form of a child, and whatever was accomplished by him through his efforts to remove the poverty of Śukla. 48.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Self-Bliss by the King of Kāśī" (or "The Vision of Śrī Gaṇeśa by the King of Kāśī who has Attained Self-Bliss"), in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa. || 53 ||
The cumulative total number of verses from the beginning is 6426 + 48 = 6472.
Chapter fifty-four in the Bālacarita.
Ka said:
Having eaten in the white house, while the god was playing in the courtyard, he slept for a moment in its midst; then the citizens [arrived]. || 1 ||
Having made preparations for the meal of the sage’s son,
they came to summon the King of Kāśī to his palace.
The King of Kāśī said to them: "He has gone from here while playing, playing.
Then people saw Vināyaka in every house.
"Some said, 'He has gone to the house of Śukla,' and then the people reviled that god Śukla, who possessed nothing. (4)
The people said:
"The camel eats thorns, having abandoned tender sprouts;
leaving us who are wealthy, it has gone to the house of the poor. (5)
If this boy were truly a lord, he would have been brought to lordship by the king in vain;
for if he were a lord, he would bring satisfaction to the hearts of all.
"How will the child eat even that meager, poor-quality food?
Some virtuous men among them were eager to bring him there. (7)
They ran hither and thither to find Vināyaka;
they asked the people on the road, "Has Vināyaka been seen anywhere? || 8 ||
Being questioned again and again, the people devoted to his worship continued on their way;
some said to them, "He must have gone to the white house."
Having learned that Vināyaka was asleep, those virtuous ones went quickly to his house and remained silent, waiting for the time when the lord would awaken.
"Therefore, let us entreat him," said the rajasas;
but he replied to them, "Rise up and go! Alas, the food will have become stale. (11)
"On your account, the people in the city are raising a clamor against this poor Śukla, who is devoted to receiving alms from those of pure character. (12)
He never obtains sufficient alms, nor does anyone drink water in his house; how is it that you, though being the son of Kaśyapa, have eaten such contemptible food? 13.
Some reviled him with various words, while others praised him;
having heard all these words, the sage, the son of Kaśyapa, spoke. 14.
The god said:
"Today I have eaten the food offered with devotion according to my desire;
yet, being satiated, I do not have the strength to move even a single step."
"O people, I have no desire now even to eat a single morsel. Someone said: "Having perceived such cruelty, those people then became despondent. (16)
Some said to one another, "What indeed must be done for this child?
And he, perceiving the agitation of the city-dwellers, [remained silent].
In an instant, the one attained infinity, like the space within a jar;
yet it appeared as if possessing many forms, like the sun reflected in various water-pots. || 18 ||
Having gone from house to house, the Lord became intent on various sports;
sometimes he was on the stairways, and sometimes he was even seated upon a swing.
In some places he sits upon a couch, and in others he is even atop a palace;
in one place he plays and laughs with the children of the house, and in another he partakes of food.
He studies the scriptures in one place and teaches them in another;
having seen him returning to his own home accompanied by the King of Kāśī, [the people were amazed].
That master of the house rejoiced and said, "I am blessed!
In this manner, that Vināyaka, accompanied by the King, visited every house.
In one place he is anointed with oils; in another, he bathes in auspicious waters;
and in yet another, his feet are washed with the utmost reverence.
In some places, he is worshipped with devotion by means of the sixteen services;
in others, he is fed with exquisite food, just as one would do out of childish affection.
In some places, he is worshipped with various fragrances such as musk and sandalwood, with flowers, and with diverse food offerings;
he is attended by housewives, children, and even servants. || 25 ||
Having eaten as much as he desired, he slept while his feet were massaged and so forth;
devoted to the Vedas, he was at times intent on singing.
Sometimes he heard virtuous stories, and at other times the story of Hari;
and occasionally he watched the dancing of women along with the king.
In some places the Lord is honored with various waving of lights (ārārtika), and in others he plays with small children, holding a noose in his hand. || 28 ||
In some places the Purāṇas are recited, and likewise the Dharmaśāstras and Smṛtis;
having thus eaten in every house, he fulfills the desires of all. (29)
Whatever each person desired, the omnipresent Mahādeva, being well-pleased, fulfilled it accordingly, just as a wish-fulfilling tree does.
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem or the cow of plenty grants all desires,
so too did the name "Protector of the Wretched" (Dīnanātha) become truly meaningful at that time.
Divine drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell in every house;
seeing this, the King of Kāśī became bewildered and spoke to his own people.
This Vināyaka is a fool who stays in my very presence;
how can he, who dwells in every house, be worshipped by all men? 33.
But how is it that he remains here now in every single house?
He who summons me, I speak to him again and again.
"How can I go to eat in your house without Vināyaka?
I shall eat the food situated in the middle of the house, accompanied by Kāśyapa. (35)
Then, seeing him having finished eating and having left the food outside, the people, their minds filled with great astonishment, spoke here and there: || 36 ||
The omnipresent Lord, accompanied by the King of Kāśī, ate at various houses;
having heard their words, that king spoke to them while smiling.
"How did he go to various houses to eat without me? Thinking thus, the king went to two or three houses and indeed saw him there.
In the meantime, having bathed, those two best of sages arrived at every house where their own son and the son of Kaśyapa had already eaten.
Wandering for the sake of alms, Sanaka and Sanandana reached that auspicious city, which was filled with great festivities and presided over by Vināyaka.
Whenever they entered a house and saw a Vināyaka there,
as soon as they looked at it and remembered [the mantra], the two of them would go right back outside.
They saw him eating and having eaten, sleeping and even playing, as well as muttering prayers, reading, and teaching others to read.
Seeing this everywhere, they then said to one another:
"O friend, no clean place for eating is to be seen here. (43)
"Whoever builds a white house shall receive various forms of hospitality with respect.
Having said this, he went to that house, and there too he saw Kāśyapa.
Afflicted by hunger and with their faces turned downward, the two went outside the city;
there they beheld a supreme, manifest, and auspicious form of Vaināyaka.
Again, having closed or opened one's own eyes within the heart,
[one should contemplate] below, above, in between, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions.
Thereafter, with their gazes stilled by meditation,
they both stood for a moment with their eyes opened, beholding him who possessed the form of Vināyaka.
Sanaka looked at him, and he too looked at Sanaka; they both beheld that Vināyaka, the very deity whom they had been meditating upon.
Pervading all, possessing all forms, he appeared before the two of them—
ten-armed, seated upon a lion, and resplendent with Siddhi and Buddhi.
He wore a brilliantly shining crown, earrings, and armlets;
he bore celestial fragrance, a garland, a serpent, and even the crescent moon.
With a musk tilaka on his forehead, wearing divine garments that shone like the luster of his teeth,
he possessed a gentle splendor, yet was difficult for wicked-minded people to behold.
Having abandoned their delusion, those two knowers of reality bowed down to Vināyaka;
with palms joined in reverence, those two of great intelligence offered him praise.
The two of them said:
"The supreme, eternal Brahman is the non-dual reality beyond all;
one should worship that all-pervading Lord, who consists of the five elements, with the highest devotion. (53)
The Supreme Lord, who possesses all forms and pervades all that is moving and unmoving—he upon whose pores millions of cosmic eggs revolve. || 54 ||
How can he be praised, being beyond the scope of the Vedāntas?
O Lord, having understood our desire, it has been fulfilled by you. (55)
We do not know the full extent of your greatness as you have assumed the form of a child;
for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth, you have taken this most excellent form of Kāśyapa.
Ka said:
"While the two were thus praising him, that form vanished before their eyes;
when they no longer saw the form, they were freed from fatigue. (57)

Having constructed a supreme palace and an auspicious image of Vaināyaka, he performed the rites on a favorable day, accompanied by the sounds of Vedic recitation and instrumental music, exactly as prescribed.
Varadada Vināyaka established the name of that excellent lake there as Gaṇeśatīrtha. || 59 ||
That place was indeed named after him, and it became renowned there;
[it is known] for the merit gained through bathing, giving gifts, and the worship of Gaṇeśa. (60)
Having cast off his ancient sins, he attains all desires;
there all the sages and the gods, together with the lords of the quarters, assemble.
Having seen the God, having worshipped, praised, and bowed to him, they departed once more.
The sage said:
"Thus those two came to behold the power of the one in the form of a child. (62)
Having witnessed their power and being highly gratified, the two returned to their own abodes.
Whoever listens with devotion to this auspicious account of the Child’s deeds [shall attain the highest state]. 63.
One obtains all desires and, after death, becomes composed of Brahman;
there shall be no affliction from child-seizing spirits, and one shall be victorious everywhere. 64.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise by Sanaka and Sanandana," in the Bālacarita of the Krīḍākhaṇḍa within the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa. || 54 ||
The cumulative total of the verses from the beginning is 6472 + 64 = 6536.
Chapter fifty-five, titled "The Release of the Messenger," ends here.
The Sage said:
After those two had departed, the great king, the ruler of Kāśī, overcome by delusion,
wandered from house to house mounted upon his horse.
"Without informing Vināyaka, where has he gone to eat?
Having abandoned me, how could he have gone off alone to eat sweet food? (2)
In every house he inquired, "Where has that Vināyaka gone?
He has now come outside, having eaten, and is eager to play. || 3 ||
"How is it that you ask this in vain, accompanied as you are by the King of Kāśī?
Thus was he rebuked by all the inhabitants of the city. 4.
Having undergone the utmost hardship like a destitute householder, some said: "This Vināyaka is playing in the White House. || 5 ||
Then, filled with joy, the king went to the white palace;
there, in its courtyard, he beheld the Lord as a child mounted upon a bull.
Seeing him mounted upon the bull, like another three-eyed deity,
he bowed with supreme devotion and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke.
The king said:
"O child, you possess neither the conduct of the virtuous, nor knowledge, nor even affection;
how is it that you have eaten various kinds of sweet food while leaving me behind?"
Ka said:
Having heard those words, Vināyaka replied:
"Wherever I have eaten, there you have also eaten. (9)
"You speak falsely, you dull-witted man; in intellect, you are but a child.
All people will say, 'Ask him with witnesses. (10)
Having heard the words of Vaināyaka, the people then said to the king:
"Indeed, you have now eaten in the presence of Vināyaka."
"How can you speak falsely, being an elder, O best of kings?
Thereupon, having returned to his natural state and come to know the truth, that king spoke.
This supreme illusion of yours is unknowable, deluding even the yogis;
you are blessed in every respect, for you are honored everywhere. 13.
Ka said:
With his body bristling with horripilation, he entered into meditation;
then he himself assumed the form of Vaināyaka. 14.
Just as water poured into water attains the state of being water,
so too did that best of kings, through the power of illusion, again assume a divided form.
He led him, mounted upon the palanquin, to his own palace with the sounds of various musical instruments and with numerous dances and songs.
The boy shone exceedingly like Madana among the gods;
his devoted father, Śukla, followed him slowly along with his wife.
Turning his face away, he was seen by the boy, who was deeply ashamed:
"How have you departed without granting him a boon, and what [boon] could not have been pleasing? (18)
Thus, with his mind, the Lord bestowed upon him supreme prosperity—
the most excellent wealth of Kubera, which was wondrous in every respect.
Pale, shrouded, dejected, accompanied by his wife, and high-minded, the god was angry due to eating poor food and wondered, "What is this? || 20 ||
He did not see that leaf-hut and fell into the deepest anxiety;
then his servants [anointed him] with massages using white, fragrant oil.
Having bathed him, they adorned him with ornaments and golden garments; likewise, they adorned his wife as if constrained by force.
Filled with great wonder, they both beheld all manner of riches:
walls of gold and jewels, couches, and various seats.
In various places there were many diverse objects adorned with clusters of pearls and gems,
as well as golden vessels, garments, and coverings.
Having thus seen all these various kinds of foods and diverse types of edibles, the two of them spoke to one another.
"How has this humble dwelling become like the palace of Indra?
Then Śukla said to his wife, "By the grace of Vināyaka... (26)
"Know this, O fortunate one: the Great Lord does not bestow everything in our presence;
rather, He gives behind our backs, satisfying us with only a small measure. (27)
The All-pervading Lord considers even a great deal that is given by oneself as indeed small;
yet He regards even a tiny thing offered with devotion as abundant.
Therefore, out of fear, desire, affection, or even from a sense of enmity,
he should be remembered, bowed to, praised, and honored for one's own welfare.
The sage said: Then those two messengers, Śūra and Capala, dispatched by Narāntaka, remained concealed in the city for a long time.
At his fierce roar, the three worlds tremble like the leaves of an ashvattha tree;
and at the shaking of his head, the gods, including Indra, undergo a trembling.
In prowess, strength, and voice, there is no one equal to these two in the three worlds;
yet this one, born from the body of a sage, must be slain within the middle of the palanquin.
"Since the powerful Daityas who previously arrived have been slain by him, we must take revenge upon them," they said to one another. (33)
Assuming the form of lightning, they roared with a great sound;
their eyes struck by that brilliance, the hosts of heroes cried out in extreme agitation, "What is this? What is this? || 34 ||
In the meantime, when those two had reached the vicinity of the palanquin,
all the draft animals fled, abandoning that Vināyaka.
With both his powerful hands, Vināyaka forcibly attempted to uproot the two from the earth by their strength; he whirled them both around.
With a heart moistened by compassion, he then placed him upon the ground, saying, "This man must be slain by one who is superior in prowess. (37)
"What purpose for a man could there be when a mere gnat has been killed? Then he asked them, "Tell me, whose messengers are you? (38)
"But when an effort has been made according to one's own power, there is no fault on the part of the man.
Having heard these words, the two who were standing before him spoke.
"You are renowned as an ocean of compassion; you are our father, the lord of the day (the sun).
You are the one who performs the consecration, the initiator, the giver of knowledge, and another who grants fearlessness. (40)
"The five ancestors known as the Annadas are renowned throughout the three worlds;
we two are their messengers, sent by Narāntaka and disguised in form. (41)
O Lord, those two who caused obstacles for you were protected by you out of compassion;
you, the all-knowing one, know everything—past, future, and present.
"Whosoever have come against you with enmity, they have been slain in a mere moment. In the meantime, the citizens then spoke to Vināyaka: || 43 ||
"O Lord, why have these two wicked ones, who cause terror to the world, been protected? Any benefit rendered to them would only result in harm. (44)
"Indeed, milk given to a serpent turns into poison.
The sage said:
"Then the God spoke to them: 'Long ago, I [declared] this very same thing for these two.'"
"Protection has been granted now; how could it become otherwise?
Having said this, the king released them and spoke again.
Having forgiven their innumerable offenses, those two enemies were released;
for it is held that the desire of a living being regarding death or life is the determining cause.
Having spoken thus, the King of Kāśī and Vināyaka reached the temple;
after bowing down, they and all the people returned each to their own abode. 48.
They praised the king and the leader who possesses various forms.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Release of the Messenger," in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa. || 55 ||
The cumulative total of the verses from the beginning is 6536 + 49 = 6585.
Chapter Fifty-Six, titled "The Departure of Narāntaka," ends here. The Sage said:
The two of them went to the beautiful assembly hall of Narāntaka in Raudrapura,
which was resplendent with a thousand pillars and adorned with jewels and pearls.
It was frequented by many heroes, auspicious, and possessed of various wonders;
it was a hundred yojanas in width and equal in length.
At that time, Narāntaka was seated upon a beautiful throne made of various jewels,
while his two ministers were seated on excellent seats beside him.
Having bowed down to those two best among the strong, whose heads touched the sky,
Śūra and Capala spoke many words of praise regarding their virtues.
The excellent messenger must speak that which is beneficial and most appropriate;
otherwise, there would be fault on the part of the messenger and terrible wrath from his master. (5)
Having heard that, his master reflected upon his own welfare and what was auspicious;
he then went to that city to create obstacles for us at Vināyaka’s shrine. 6.
Then Vighaṇṭa and Dantura, appearing first in the form of children, stood there in a most secret place, waiting for the boy.
Embraced by those two, Vināyaka turned them into ashes;
they then became Pataṅga and Vidhūla, assuming the form of wind.
Having gone there to lift up the boy, they stepped upon his head and were destroyed;
the powerful demon, who had taken the form of a stone, was shattered into a hundred pieces. || 9 ||
The two asuras, Kāma and Krodha, having assumed the form of donkeys,
were crushed upon the surface of the earth on the path while attempting to kill the boy.
Then Kuṇḍīyāstuvara, assuming the form of an elephant,
stood blocking the path in order to shatter Kumbha’s frontal globes.
He was slain in a mere moment by the powerful Kumāra;
thereafter, Jṛmbhiṇī arrived to destroy the house of Dharmadatta.
Struck on the head with a coconut, she met her death;
the third was the demon Jvālāsura, who had the face of a tiger and was a rending one.
The first [fire] blazed up to consume that city when it arrived to destroy the child;
the last [fire], moreover, rendered assistance to him by assuming the form of wind.
Tearing open their mouths, Vyāghratuṇḍa devoured all the people;
yet even those three were slain by that boy of infinite illusory power.
The great Daitya named Meghanāda, having assumed the form of an astrologer, was slain by a blow from a signet ring; that indeed seemed like a marvel.
Both Kūpa and Kandara, those two masters of illusion, have been slain by force;
Ambhāsura, Andhaka, and Tuṅga have also been destroyed. They came to kill the child. || 17 ||
One created darkness, while another rained down torrents;
yet another, with its lofty peak, fell upon the boy. (18)
Having cast all three of them far away in the form of a great bird,
the Rākṣasī named Bhramarā set about making their likeness.

When his army had been destroyed in many ways, that king of the Daityas mounted his horse;
sword in hand and filled with rage, he went forth to fight Mayūreśa.
Upon seeing that, Mayūreśa mounted his own peacock;
and seeing him approaching swiftly, that king of the Daityas [prepared] the serpent-missile (pannagāstra).
Having respectfully recited the mantra taught by Bhārgava and others a hundred times,

The god rejoiced at that Daitya of exceeding heroism and prowess, saying:

Having spoken thus to his enemy, the god discharged the Garuḍa weapon;
thereupon the serpents fled, and the soldiers of the army rose up.
The Lord discharged the discus weapon, which destroys the army of the Daityas;
by it, some Daityas were killed, while others had their limbs and heads severed.
Others fell with their knees and shanks shattered and their ankles severed;
they cried out, "Roar! Run! Run! Father! Mother! Son! || 8 ||
Those who attained liberation upon seeing Mayūreśa and those who gave up their lives—thus was his army routed; thereupon the Daitya rushed forward in a rage.
With sword in hand, roaring in rage, he rushed with speed toward Gajānana;
seeing his enemy in such a state, the Lord seized his axe.
He went toward the Daitya and hurled that axe of great velocity;
it scorched the sky with its brilliance, as well as the quarters and the flocks of birds.
He swiftly cut off the Daitya’s hand and his sword into a hundred pieces;
then, suddenly seizing his bow and stringing it, he took up many arrows.
Forcefully piercing countless soldiers, he shrouded them;
with a roar like a thundercloud, he filled the sky and all the directions.
Having warded off the cage of arrows with a powerful downpour of shafts,
no one could discern anyone else in that darkness consisting of arrows.
Then Mayūreśa quickly threw that horse to the ground;
standing thereafter in the sky, he spoke to the leader of the Gaṇas.
Behold my great wonder: this horse has been struck down;
O Lord of Virtues, you shall see me slay Śikhaṇḍin while you look on.
He cast both quivers full of arrows upon the ground;
drawing his bow back to his ear, he discharged a multitude of shafts.
Slaying all the soldiers in Mayūreśa’s army,
he rained down nets of arrows like clouds during the rainy season.
"How many gods have lost their lives, their entire bodies mangled?"—while the heroes were thus perishing, this peacock was filled with rage. || 19 ||
Leaving aside the peacock that had been pierced by the arrows of the demon Kamala,
he took up his noose with his hand, weighing it with respect.
Roaring and making the sky resound, he abandoned his own brilliance;

And it fell upon the throat of that Daityasena commander;
having assumed another form, that Daitya obstructed his breath.
In that very instant, he completely covered the orb of the sun with his head;
in the most terrible darkness, nothing at all could be discerned.
Filled with rage, he came face to face with Mayūreśa and said:
"O child, why do you fight with me? Go and drink from your mother's breast! (24)
"Play with the children, otherwise you shall die before me;
by my mere roar, the three worlds tremble. (25)
When my foot is placed upon the ground, even Śeṣa trembles below;

"With the tip of my claw, I shall send your head to the netherworld.

One who reviles the gods and the twice-born never attains victory anywhere;

Filled with joy, I fight in this world to proclaim your fame;

Seeing the prowess of that Daitya, the god, filled with haste, came before him and struck him with showers of arrows. || 1 ||

Having placed a forest garland around his neck, I gave him the name "Vanamālī" (Garlanded with Forest Flowers),
which is renowned throughout the worlds and brings all auspiciousness.
Having completed the ritual of worship, I then performed a circumambulation of him;

"My water-pot, filled with the waters of various sacred fords, has been placed here;

Mayūreśa said: This hymn composed by Brahmā destroys all sins;

O Creator, the release of those imprisoned within the jail shall occur after seven days; it removes mental anguish and physical disease, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"Be firm, O Viriñca; this river, which purifies all, shall become famous in the world by the name Kamaṇḍalu. (22)

"When that boon had been granted by him, the lords of the sages bathed there."

Ka said:
"O child, you have asked well; it brings joy to the heart.
I shall describe all of that, which destroys sin, according to the prescribed method."
When that night had dawned, Puṣpikā beheld her son, who had four arms, was red in color, possessed the face of an elephant, and was adorned with ornaments. || 3 ||

"Never before has such a fool among men been seen or heard of anywhere.

"Having abandoned the child, she has come back; he might have been devoured by the forest-dwellers.

Parāśara, the best of sages and a treasury of compassion,

O God, you alone are the Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pannagas, Apsarases, and Kinnaras; you are indeed this entire world of the moving and the unmoving.
"We are blessed, for we have directly beheld the means to liberation;
O Lord, when Sindūra was slain, the foremost of the gods attained happiness. (33)
Kings, sages, and the worlds will take delight in their respective duties;
all ritual acts will be performed in reliance upon the utterances of Svadhā, Svāhā, and Vaṣaṭ.
Through various incarnations, you especially perform the protection [of the world],
the immediate destruction of the wicked, and the fulfillment of the desires of your devotees.
Ka said:
Having spoken thus, all those gods indeed constructed a palace with a beautiful pinnacle and installed the elephant-faced one there.
By the mere sight of whom a person is liberated from sin, by remembering him a man delivers seven generations of his lineage. (37)
Having worshipped and bowed down to him, the gods attained complete satisfaction;
thereafter, all the sages honored him with the utmost reverence.
Because he had destroyed the sindūra, they gave him the name Sindūrahā;
with exceedingly joyful minds, they bowed and departed for their own hermitage.
Then all the excellent sages, having bowed with great devotion to the God,
worshipped the Supreme Self many times with various ritual substances.
"This field shall become renowned as Rājasadana.
Upon seeing him, Vareṇya realized he was his own son. 41.
Since you, O Lord, have swiftly struck down that most terrible Daitya, a thorn to the world, and bestowed these footprints upon the kings along with vermilion; 42.
"He shall attain renown by the name Daityavimardana (the Destroyer of the Daityas)";
then, having witnessed his prowess, he affectionately honored his son. 43.
He shed tears born of affection and was unable to speak;
with his throat excessively choked, he wept, overwhelmed by intense grief.
Vareṇya said:
"Abandoned by that sinful one through delusion and fear of obstacles,
you are the one whom Brahmā, Śakra, and the others have gone forth to worship."
Like a fool who would abandon the wish-fulfilling cow, a treasure-trove, or the celestial tree, we do not recognize you, the leader of infinite millions of universes. 46.
"Deluded by Māyā, I abandoned you as well as my home.
Ka said:
"Having heard those words of his, the Supreme Lord, out of compassion," (47)
The Lord affectionately embraced that most excellent king with his four arms and,
with supreme devotion, spoke to the preeminent monarch.
The god said: "In a former kalpa, in the great forest, a most severe penance was performed by both of them, subsisting only on the ripe leaves of the banyan tree. (49)
After a thousand divine years, I then became pleased.
For a son has been chosen by you two; liberation is not possible through such deluded behavior.
Thus, I have attained the state of being your son for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth.
To effect the slaying of Sindūra and likewise for the protection of the virtuous. || 51 ||
"Otherwise, I have no body, for I am the formless witness;
yet my word has been made true, bringing satisfaction even to the three worlds. (52)
"I shall now go to my own abode; do not set your mind on grief.
Vareṇya said:
"In this cycle of existence, many sufferings have been seen that are difficult to endure. (53)
Now, O Destroyer of Suffering, out of compassion show me the path to liberation;
O Elephant-faced One, how could there be bondage for you even upon direct realization? (54)
Tell me that instruction by which I shall attain liberation—that yoga by which I may cast off desire, anger, and the fear of death. (55)
Ka said:
Having heard those words, that elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa), out of compassion, seated him upon his own seat and placed his hand upon his head. 56.
Having dispelled all doubts and having revealed his universal form, he began to instruct him in the Gaṇeśagītā.
Having understood the essence of the Gītā through the instruction of Gaṇeśa,
he entrusted the kingdom to his ministers and went to the forest for asceticism.
Endowed with supreme dispassion, he meditated upon that elephant-faced deity;
virtuous and having no other object of focus, he constantly recited the Gītā.
Just as water poured into water becomes indeed water itself,
so too, through that meditation, he attained identity with it.
The Sage said:
O Lord of Gods, four-faced one, please speak out of your supreme compassion.
That Gītā of Gaṇeśa, which destroys all ignorance. || 61 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Instruction of Vareṇya," in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa.
The total number of verses from the beginning: 10,350 + 61 = 10,411.
Chapter One Hundred and Thirty-Eight, titled "The Yoga of the Essential Meaning of Sāṅkhya and Yoga.
Chapter Two Hundred and Thirty-Eight.
Ka said:
"In this very manner, having been questioned in the past by the high-souled Śaunaka, that Sūta recounted the Gītā as he had heard it from the mouth of Vyāsa. (1)
Sūta said:
"I have consumed the nectar spoken of in the eighteen Purāṇas;
now I desire to drink the most excellent nectar that is even more flavorful than that."
O highly fortunate one, please tell me out of compassion that nectar of yoga, by which a person, having become composed of nectar, attains the nectar of Brahman. (3)
Vyāsa said:
Now, O Sūta, I shall proclaim the Gītā which illuminates the path of Yoga, which was composed for the King who questioned it by means of the elephant-faced god. 4.
Vareṇya said:
O Vighneśvara, O mighty-armed one, you who are proficient in all branches of knowledge and know the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures; you ought to explain the Yoga to me.
Gajanan said:
"O King, your intellect has rightly resolved through my grace.
Listen, O monarch, for I shall proclaim the Gītā, which consists of the nectar of Yoga."
They do not call yoga "yoga" [in the common sense]; yoga is not the acquisition of prosperity, nor is yoga union with sense objects, nor likewise is it union with one's mother and so forth.

O lord of men, that which is attachment to father, mother, and so forth is not true yoga; nor is that yoga which consists of attachment to kinsmen, sons, and the like, or that which is joined with the eight supernatural powers.
That union with a woman of wondrous form is not true yoga;
nor is our union with sovereignty, nor is our union with elephants and horses.
For one who seeks yoga, even union with the status of Indra is not dear;
that yoga which belongs to Satyaloka is not true yoga for me when one is dead.

O King, the yoga of a Śaiva is not true yoga, nor is that which belongs to the station of a Vaiṣṇava; O King, yoga is neither the state of being the sun, nor the state of being the moon, nor the status of Kubera.
Therein is neither the state of wind nor the state of fire, neither the state of immortality nor the nature of time;
there is neither the domain of Varuṇa nor that of Nirṛti, neither yogic power nor universal sovereignty.
O King, the wise practice that manifold yoga which is praised;
they become free from thirst in this world, having conquered their food and their semen. 13.
Having brought the three worlds under their control, they cause all people to drink [the nectar of the Dharma];
with hearts full of compassion, they awaken some few. 14.
The liberated-while-living are immersed in the heart that consists of supreme bliss;
closing their eyes, they behold the Supreme Brahman residing within the heart.
Meditating upon the Supreme Brahman, which has been brought under control by yoga within their minds, they regard all beings as equal to their own selves. 16.
By whomsoever they were cut down, by whomsoever they were struck, by whomsoever they were dragged away, and by whomsoever they were taken refuge in; || 17 ||
With hearts full of compassion, they wander upon the surface of the earth for the sake of favoring all beings, having conquered anger and subdued their senses. 18.
O King, those who sustain only their bodies, for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal—such highly fortunate ones, my dear, may come within the range of your vision. 19.
I shall now declare that; listen to this unsurpassed yoga, by hearing which a living being is liberated from sins and from the ocean of worldly existence. 20.
O lord of men, that state of mind which perceives no difference between Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śakti, Sūrya, and myself—that is yoga; in my view, it is considered perfect yoga.
Since I alone create and protect the universe,
having assumed various forms, I withdraw it through my own divine play.
I alone am Mahāviṣṇu; I alone am Sadāśiva;
I alone am Mahāśakti; and I alone, O beloved, am Aryaman. 23.
In former times, I was born as the fivefold lord of men;
yet, due to ignorance, they do not know me, the cause of the cause of the world.
From me come fire, water, and the earth; from me come ether and wind;
and from me come Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the world-protectors, and the ten directions.
The Vasus, Manus, cows, sages, and even animals;
the rivers, oceans, Yakṣas, trees, and even flocks of birds. || 26 ||
Likewise, there were the twenty-one heavens, the Nāgas, the seven forests, humans, mountains, Sādhyas, Siddhas, and hosts of Rākṣasas.
I am the witness, the eye of the world, untainted by all actions;
I am changeless, immeasurable, unmanifest, all-pervading, and imperishable.
O King, I alone am the supreme Brahman, whose nature is imperishable bliss;
it is I who cast this entire world, including these excellent men, into illusion. 29.
At all times, one should diligently apply oneself to those six transformations;
for by abandoning the veil of ignorance, a living being gradually attains [liberation] over many births.
Having become dispassionate through perfect awakening regarding sense objects, one attains Brahman—
that which is indestructible by the multitude of weapons and unburnable even by fire.
It cannot be moistened by the earth or the waters, nor can it be dried up by the wind;
it is indestructible, O lord of men, even while this body is being destroyed.
Those fools who delight in the discourse of the three Vedas praise this flowery speech proclaimed in the scriptures, and do not consider anything other than that. || 33 ||
Those whose consciousness is destroyed and whose intellect is fixed on enjoyments, being devoted to heavenly sovereignty, constantly perform actions that yield the fruits of birth and death.
Those dull-witted men, devoted solely to ritual action, further bind themselves by their own selves; they set the wheel of worldly existence in motion. (35)
Whatever action is prescribed for one, that should be performed as an offering unto Me;
thereby, the great sprouts from the seeds of his actions shall be utterly destroyed.
Great purity of mind becomes the means for accomplishing higher knowledge;
for by means of higher knowledge, the Supreme Brahman has been realized by the lords of sages. || 37 ||
Therefore, O lord of men, one should perform actions endowed with wisdom;
for no one can exist without action, nor can one who abandons their own duty.
If one abandons actions, then one does not attain perfection;
in the beginning, there is no qualification for knowledge—one is joined only to action. (39)
With a heart purified by action, he shall attain non-dual consciousness;
that indeed is declared to be Yoga, for it leads to immortality. 40.
O King, listen as I shall proclaim another yoga, the most excellent one:
[to maintain equanimity] toward an animal, a son, a friend, an enemy, a kinsman, and a well-wisher. (41)
With an outward gaze and with equanimity residing in the heart, a man should observe;
he should remain the same in pleasure and pain, as well as in indignation, joy, and fear. 42.
Upon the onset of disease, and likewise upon the attainment of enjoyments; in victory or even in defeat; in the absence of prosperity and in its presence; in gain and in loss, and even in death. (43)
Beholding me as equal within and without among all classes of things—
whether in the sun, the moon, water, fire, Śiva, Śakti, and likewise in the wind— 44.
In the twice-born, in the heart, in the great river, in sacred fords, in holy fields that destroy sin, in Viṣṇu, in all the gods, as well as in the Yakṣas and the Uragas; || 45 ||
He who should constantly behold me among the Gandharvas, among humans, and likewise among the states of animal existence—he indeed is called a knower of Yoga. 46.
Having withdrawn the senses from their own objects through discernment, and possessing a mind of equanimity toward all things—that, O King, is what I consider to be yoga. 47.
The wisdom that arises through the discrimination of the self from the non-self by the power of destiny, belonging to one whose mind is attached to its own duty—that is called yoga, that is yoga. 48.
By means of that [knowledge], one abandons both merit and demerit here;
therefore, one should apply oneself to yoga, for yoga is skill regarding the Vedic injunctions. 49.
Having abandoned the fruits of merit and demerit, the wise man who has conquered his senses is liberated from the bondage of birth and attains the state that is free from all ailment.
For when the turbidity of ignorance departs from the intellect of a living being, then he gradually attains detachment toward the Vedic statements and other such teachings. 51.
When the intellect of one who has been confused regarding the three Vedas becomes unshakable in the Supreme Self, then he shall attain Yoga. 52.
O dear one, when the wise man abandons all mental desires and is satisfied within his own self by means of himself, he is then said to possess steady intellect. 53.
Free from craving for all pleasures, undisturbed by the onset of suffering,
with fear gone and passion subdued, one is then said to possess steady wisdom.
Just as this tortoise withdraws its limbs from all sides, so should one intent on yoga draw back the senses from their objects. 55.
The objects of the senses turn away from this radiant one who has renounced food;
and even passion, upon seeing the Brahman, perishes without leaving a trace of attachment.
O King, even a wise man who exerts himself by adopting the stability of a yogi finds that his mind is forcibly carried away once he has churned his senses. 57.
One who is disciplined should always bring these under control and remain intent on Me;
he whose senses are restrained here is considered wise. 58.
For one who contemplates sense-objects, attachment to them arises;
from that, desire is born, and from that, anger increases. (59)
From anger arises ignorance, and from that comes the loss of memory;
from the loss of memory comes the destruction of the intellect, and with its destruction, even that [anger] perishes.
He who moves among sense-objects with his senses, free from both hatred and attachment, attains contentment through self-mastery over his heart and the subjugation of his faculties. (61)
There shall be the casting off of all three kinds of suffering through contentment;
and established in wisdom, he becomes one whose heart is serene.
Without serenity there is no wisdom; without wisdom there is no meditative cultivation;
