without that, O King, there is no peace; and without that, whence can there be happiness? (63)
The mind follows after the objects as the horses of the senses roam;
one should destroy that mind with the intellect, just as the wind destroys a boat upon the waters. (Or: as a horse [destroys] a boat).
He does not sleep at all during that night which belongs to all living beings.
O lord of the earth, those nights do not truly sleep here where she is.
Just as forests from all sides flow toward the lord of rivers, so do desires flow toward him;
he shall never find peace.
Therefore, a man should restrain those openings here on all sides.
Just as they run away from their respective objects, so too does his intellect [run away] from that which is stable.
Having abandoned possessiveness and egoism, and whoever renounces all desires, should remain constantly devoted to knowledge; through knowledge, he shall attain liberation. 68.

O King, he who understands this divine wisdom of Brahman attains liberation through his character, even after reaching the fourth state (turiyāvasthā). (You shall attain liberation through your character. Om Tat Sat. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Essential Meaning of Sāṅkhya and Yoga," in the *Śrīmad Gaṇeśa Gītā*, which contains the essence of the Upaniṣads, a treatise on the nectar of yoga, within the *Śrīmad Ādi Śrīman Mahāgāṇeśvara Mahāpurāṇa*, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, the *Bālacarita*, in the dialogue between the illustrious Gajānana and Vareṇya.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Essential Meaning of Sāṅkhya and Yoga," in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa.
The total number of verses from the beginning: 10,411 + 69 = 10,480.
Chapter Two, titled "Karmayoga," the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter.
Vareṇya said:
O All-pervading Lord, you have spoken of two paths: steadfastness in knowledge and steadfastness in action. Having considered them, tell me which one alone truly brings about the highest good.
Gajanaṇa said:

"O beloved, these two states previously mentioned by me regarding this world of the moving and the unmoving— namely, through the yoga of discernment of the Sāṅkhyas and through the yoga of action of the Vedas— " || 2 ||
By the non-commencement of ritual acts, O King, a person becomes inactive;
yet one does not attain perfection through mere renunciation of actions born of duty.
No one ever remains inactive even for a moment;
being dependent on the qualities born of nature, one is driven to action.
Restraining the group of organs that perform actions, a man should remain mindful;
yet he whose mind is dull regarding their objects is called one of wretched conduct. (5)
Having first restrained those senses, one should begin action with the mind;
he who, free from craving, engages the senses in the yoga of action, O King, is supreme.
Action performed without desire is indeed the most excellent of all actions;
for even the maintenance of one's physical body would not be possible through inaction alone.
By not surrendering their actions to Me, people become bound by those very deeds;
therefore, one should always perform action without attachment, for that is the offering unto Me.
Those actions which are performed for my sake do not bind one anywhere;
however, this action, together with its latent impressions (vāsanā), forcibly binds the embodied soul.
O beloved, having created the social orders (varṇas) in the past, I declared that they should perform sacrifices;
may this [sacrifice] prosper through sacrifice, for it is the granter of desires like a wish-fulfilling tree.
"Gladden the gods with this, and may the gods gladden you;
through this mutual gratification, may you attain a supreme and stable station."
The beloved gods, being well-satisfied, will bestow desired enjoyments;
the man who enjoys those things given by them without first giving to them is a thief.
Those who eat what remains after the offerings have been made shall be liberated from all sins;
whereas those great sinners who cook for their own sake alone eat only their own transgressions.
Beings arise from energy; the origin of food is from the gods;
the origin of the gods is from sacrifice; and the production of that [sacrifice] is from the Veda. 14.
From me was born the Veda of Brahman, and from me arose Brahman;
therefore, O protector of the earth, know that I am established in the sacrifice and in the entire universe. 15.
The wise should traverse the great wheel of worldly existences;
that base person, however, breathes with joy, sporting with the senses and the objects of the earth.
(He breathes with joy) in his inner self—he who is delighted within, who delights in the Self, and who is dear to all.
For the man who is satisfied with the Self, no worldly purpose whatsoever exists.
He incurs neither merit nor demerit from actions performed or not performed;
for him, there would never be anything to be accomplished among all living beings at any time. (18)
Therefore, O King, actions should be performed by living beings without attachment; one who is attached meets with a miserable end, whereas one such as that [who is unattached] attains Me. 19.
O twice-born ones, in ancient times the royal sages attained supreme perfection;
indeed, for the sake of gathering people together, they undertook such deeds.
Whatever superior action one performs, all people perform that very same thing; whatever he regards as authoritative, everyone else follows that alone. 21.
"O lord of men, there is no purpose in my world that remains unaccomplished;
yet, even regarding what has not been attained and is yet to be gained, I shall still perform my duty."
O high-minded one, when I, being independent yet characterized by indolence, do not perform my duty,
all the social orders will direct their meditation toward me.
Consequently, the worlds that transmit the tradition will be destroyed;
I shall be the destroyer of this world and the creator of its confusion. (24)
For those who desire always perform actions out of ignorance due to their desires;
therefore, a wise man, with a mind unattached, should perform this [action] for the sake of maintaining the world.
One should abandon the notion of diversity held by the ignorant who act out of worldly motives;
disciplined in yoga, the performer of action should offer all actions unto Me. 26.
Assisted by the qualities of ignorance, performing actions without weariness, that person of dull intellect who, out of egoism, declared, "I am the doer," [is the one described]. (27)

But he who knows the reality of the self through the distinction between the qualities and their functions, and realizing that the instrument has operated upon its object, does not become attached. || 28 ||
Deluded by the three qualities, those who do not know the universe act with fruitless deeds and are enemies of their own selves; one who knows the universe should never transgress [this truth]. 29.
Therefore, the wise person should offer all obligatory and occasional rites unto Me;
having abandoned the notions of "I" and "mine," he shall attain the supreme goal. 30.
Those who are free from envy and full of devotion, who practice all this auspicious teaching spoken by me—
they are all liberated from all karmas.
Know those to be my enemies who do not practice [this], whose minds are struck by impurity, who are envious, greatly deluded, and ruined. 32.
Even one possessed of knowledge performs action that is identical by nature [to that of others];
and since he follows that very same [nature], his [claim to] being a "grasper" (graha) therein is considered vain. 33.
Lust and likewise anger arise regarding the objects of the senses;
one should not fall under their sway, for they are the destroyers of this [body]. || 34 ||

One's own duty, even if devoid of merit, is praised over the duty of another, even if accompanied by all its constituent parts; for death while performing that own duty is better, whereas another's duty brings fear in the next world.
Vareṇya said:
By what is a man impelled to commit sin, even though he does not desire it, as if driven by Heramba with great force? (36)
The illustrious Gajānana said:
Know that desire and anger are great evils arising from two qualities;
they bring the worlds under their control—know these two to be the foremost of enemies. (37)
Just as illusion conceals [reality], just as mist [conceals] water, and just as a rain-cloud [conceals] the sun, so do desire and anger [conceal] all [virtues]. 38.
The knowledge of one who possesses right practice is constantly obscured by the enemy consisting of desire, which is swift, difficult to nourish, and fierce. (39)
Resorting to the intellect and the mind, it abides through the senses;
veiling wisdom by means of those very senses, it deludes the man of knowledge. 40.
Therefore, having first restrained those senses, a person should conquer the mind;
for the sin born of the mind brings an end to both knowledge and realization. 41.
Since they say those [senses] are superior, and the mind is superior to them;
and since the intellect is indeed superior even to that, the Self is considered superior to the intellect.
Having thus realized the Self by means of the self, and having steadied the self by means of the self,
one should slay the enemy whose form is desire and attain the supreme state.

Om Tat Sat. Thus ends the second chapter, named "Karmayoga," in the *Bālacarita* (The Childhood Deeds) within the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the *Śrīmad-Ādi-Śrīman-Mahāgāṇeśvara-Mahāpurāṇa*, a scripture concerning the nectar of Yoga and the essence of the Upanishads, contained within the *Śrīmad-Gaṇeśagītā*, in the dialogue between the venerable Gajananavarēnya.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Karmayoga," in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa. || 139 ||
The total number of verses from the beginning: 10,480 + 43 = 10,523.
Chapter 140 (the one hundred and fortieth), titled "The Yoga of Offering to Brahman," the third chapter.
Śrī Gajānana said:
Formerly, at the time of the beginning of creation, I, who possess three bodies, having fashioned this triple-guṇa yoga, declared it as the supreme yoga to Viṣṇu.
He spoke it to Aryaman, and he too to his own son Manu;
thereafter, the great seers have received this [knowledge] through successive tradition. || 2 ||
Over the course of much time, O lord of the earth, this [teaching] will perish in the final age; for it will be met with lack of faith, mistrust, and public censure.
You have heard from my mouth this Yoga of the former existence, which is more secret than all secrets, the essence of the Vedas, and supremely auspicious. 4.
Vareṇya said:
O Gajānana, you have now descended from the womb;
how did you proclaim this supreme yoga to Viṣṇu? 5.
The illustrious Gajānana said:
"Many births have passed for you and for me as well;
I remember them all, yet your memory does not persist."
O mighty-armed one, from me alone are born the gods, beginning with Viṣṇu;
and into me alone they go to their dissolution during the dissolutions at the end of every age.
I alone am the supreme Brahmā, and I alone am Mahārudra;
I alone am the entire universe, both the stationary and the moving. 8.
I am the unborn, the imperishable Self of all beings, the beginningless Lord;
yet, by resorting to my threefold Māyā, I manifest in many wombs.
When there is an accumulation of unrighteousness and a depletion of righteousness, I manifest myself in order to protect the virtuous and to strike down the wicked. 10.
Having eradicated the accumulation of unrighteousness, I establish the Dharma;
joyfully performing various divine sports, I slay the wicked Daityas.
Assuming many forms, I protect the castes, the stages of life, the sages, and the virtuous;
thus does one who knows my divine manifestation in age after age [attain me]. 12.
Having abandoned that various karma and vigor, as well as my form— in short, having abandoned the notion of "I" and "mine"— he is not born again.
Free from desire, free from fear and anger, devoted to Me, taking refuge in Me,
and purified by knowledge and austerity, many have come to Me.
For by whatever disposition the best of men serve me, in that very manner I, the imperishable, clearly bestow the fruit upon them. 15.
O King, let other people be followers of my path;
likewise, they conduct their affairs among their own kin and others in that same manner.
Those who desire the fruit of their actions perform what pleases the deities;
they indeed swiftly attain in this world the success born of ritual action. || 17 ||
O King, the four castes were indeed created by me in the world of mortals through the blending of the qualities of passion, goodness, and darkness, as well as through the influence of past actions.
The wise know me, though I am their creator, to be their non-creator; they know me as the beginningless Lord, eternal, and untainted by the qualities born of action. 19.
He who understands that action is devoid of agency does not bind himself by karma;
having realized this, those seeking liberation have performed their actions from time immemorial.

Having understood this, a living being is liberated from the entire firm bondage of ignorance—the primordial cause of transmigratory existence which is accompanied by latent impressions (vāsanā). || 21 ||
Now I shall describe to you that which is both non-action and action,
wherein even the wise sages have fallen into silence out of delusion.
The seeker of liberation must understand the true nature of action, inaction, and mis-action;
for here, O lover of the goal, these actions are of three kinds. 23.
He who possesses the knowledge of non-action in action, and the perception of action in non-action—
he indeed is liberated in this mortal world and accomplishes all purposes.
The wise call that man wise who, being free from the sprout of karma, undertakes actions with his activity burnt away by the vision of reality. 25.
Having abandoned thirst for fruits, he should always remain content and free from effort;
though intent on performing action, he does nothing at all. (26)
Free from worldly desire, with the self restrained and all possessions renounced,
one who performs his domestic duties solely as such incurs no sin.
Having become free from duality and envy, being equanimous toward success and failure, and content with whatever comes to him here, one who performs action is not bound. 28.
Even one who is liberated from all objects of the senses and possesses both theoretical knowledge (jñāna) and realized wisdom (vijñāna),
all his performed action dissolves when it is for the sake of sacrifice.
I am the fire, the oblation, and the invoker; whatever is offered and deposited within me is the Brahman to be attained, for I am devoted solely to that Brahman. || 30 ||
Some other yogins, moreover, declare that destiny is the sacrifice.
Some indeed considered that Brahmā was the fire and the sacrifice itself. || 31 ||
O supreme king, they offer their senses as oblations into the fire of self-restraint.
Others offer those objects, such as sound and the rest, into the fires of their own organs. || 32 ||
They offer the vital breaths and the senses, along with all their functions,
as oblations into the fire that is their own self, which is of the nature of the vital essence and kindled by knowledge.
Neither by material wealth, nor by austerity, nor even by Vedic study, nor by those who practice intense vows, do any yogis worship Me through knowledge alone. (34)
Those who, being devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma), block the two paths and cast the apāna into the prāṇa, and likewise the prāṇa into the apāna; || 35 ||
Having conquered the vital breaths, they offer the movements of the life-force into those very breaths;
thus, various devotees of sacrifice, having destroyed their sins through sacrifice, [attain liberation].
These who eat the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice go eternally to Brahman;
for those who do not perform sacrifice, what other world could there be? (37)
O King, having understood all those sacrifices established in the Vedas as being of three kinds—bodily and so forth—you shall be liberated from every bond. 38.
O King, among all sacrifices, the sacrifice of knowledge is considered supreme;
for all action is dissolved in knowledge, which is the means to liberation.
O tiger among men, that which is to be known has been bowed to by your question;
the virtuous ones, who are experts in the truth, will speak of it out of a desire to serve you.
A person, forming various attachments but never a single association with the virtuous, thereby incurs bondage within this cycle of existence. || 41 ||
From association with the virtuous arises the development of good qualities and the very dissolution of calamities;
everyone attains their own welfare both in this world and in the next. 42.
O King, everything else is easily obtained, but the company of the virtuous is exceedingly difficult to find;
having known that, one does not again incur bondage—therefore, that alone is what should be sought from all other sources.
Then one perceives all beings within one's own self alone;
thereafter, even a creature devoted to great sin is liberated from that.
Even various kinds of actions the fire of knowledge consumes in an instant, just as a well-known fire reduces everything to ashes in an instant. 45.
O King, there is no other purifier that attains equality with this knowledge;
through yoga, over time, yogis realize it within their very own selves. 46.
One who is devoted, has conquered the senses, and is intent upon that [knowledge] shall attain wisdom;
having attained that supreme liberation, he goes [to the goal] in a very short time. 47.
But for one who is devoid of devotion, lacking faith, and full of doubt regarding everything—neither in this world nor in the next is any well-being known for him. 48.
O King, those [actions] do not bind one who delights in self-knowledge, whose every doubt has been destroyed by knowledge, and for whom all karmas have been stilled through yoga. 49.
Having forcibly severed internal doubt by cutting away ignorance with the blow of the sword of knowledge, a person should therefore become disciplined in yoga. 50.

Om tat sat. Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Yoga of Offering to Brahman," in the *Bālacarita* (Childhood Deeds) of the *Śrīmad-Ādi-Śrīman-Mahāgāṇeśvara-Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Uttarakhaṇḍa*, in the dialogue between the venerable Gajananavarēnya, contained within the *Yogāmṛtārtha-śāstra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Gaṇeśagītā* that embodies the meaning of the Upaniṣads. || 3 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Offering to Brahman," in the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*. 140.
The total number of verses from the beginning: 10,523 + 50 = 10,573.
Chapter Four, titled "The Yoga of Renunciation of Action" (Karmasaṃnyāsa), being the one hundred and forty-first chapter.
Vareṇya said:
You describe both renunciation and the yoga of actions;
tell me, O Lord, which one of these two is definitely superior? || 1 ||
The illustrious Gajānana said:
Both the yoga of action (kriyāyoga) and disjunction (viyoga) are means for attaining liberation;
between these two, the yoga of action is superior because it leads to renunciation.
He who endures the suffering of dualities, who is free from hatred, and who does not long for anything—
being ever established in renunciation— he is immediately liberated from bondage and dwells in happiness.

The ignorant, due to their limited understanding, speak of the abandonment and the undertaking of action as being distinct; however, the wise man should unite them as one. (For the ignorant and those of little knowledge [should practice] one of these two:
Whatever fruit is obtained through renunciation, that very same fruit is obtained through yoga.
He who understands the application of the integration of action, he truly understands.
The wise do not understand renunciation (saṃnyāsa) to be merely the abandonment of actions;
rather, by performing action without desire, the practitioner of yoga becomes Brahman itself. 6.
Stainless, with mind and self controlled, having conquered the senses and being intent on yoga, he who perceives the Self abiding in all beings is not tainted by action. 7.
The knower of reality, whose self is disciplined through yoga, does not think "I am doing";
it is the eleven organs that perform actions according to their respective functions.
He who performs action while offering all of it to Brahman is not smeared by merit or sin, just as the sun moving through the sky is not smeared by clouds. 9.
Having abandoned hope, those who know yoga perform actions— whether physical, vocal, pertaining to the Buddha, sensory, or mental— for the purification of the mind.
A man devoid of yoga performs actions excessively out of a desire for their fruits;
he is bound by the seeds of karma and consequently experiences suffering. 11.
Having mentally renounced all action, the yogi may dwell in happiness, neither acting nor causing others to act, like one who has reached his own excellent city on a mountain peak. 12.
Neither action nor agency is created by me for anyone;
nor is there a conjunction of action and its seed; rather, all this is brought about by Śakti.
O King, I do not touch the merits or sins of anyone;
yet those deluded by ignorance become bewildered, their intellects shrouded by delusion. 14.
For those whose knowledge of the Self has been destroyed by the self through lack of discrimination, their supreme knowledge shines forth like the sun. 15.
With their minds fixed on Me, their thoughts entirely absorbed in Me, intent on Me, and having had their sins destroyed by knowledge, they attain the state from which there is no rebirth. 16.
The great-souled wise ones look with equanimity upon a twice-born man endowed with knowledge and discernment, a cow, an elephant, and so forth, as well as upon a dog-cooker and a dog.
Heaven is under their control; they are liberated while living and possess equal vision.
Since that [object] is faultless and equal to Brahman, it has been made an object of experience by them. (It has been mastered by them.
Those who, upon encountering the pleasant and the unpleasant, do not experience joy or hatred—
Taking refuge in Brahman, undeluded, knowing Brahman, and possessed of equal intellect. || 19 ||
Vareṇya said:
"O Blessed One, O master of knowledge, tell me out of compassion: what happiness exists in the three worlds, even among the classes of gods and Gandharvas? (20)
Gaṇeśa said:
One who is attached to his own self, delighting in his own soul within himself, experiences bliss. 20.
For that indeed is imperishable happiness; there is no such happiness in sense objects and the like.
The pleasures arising from sense objects are themselves the causes of sufferings.
Those things characterized by arising and destruction—one who is unattached to them is a knower of reality.
He who endures desire, anger, and even cold when the cause for them is present.
Because he is free from physical exhaustion, he enjoys victory over those two with ease for a long time.
One whose focus is within, whose light is within, whose happiness is within, and whose delight is within, shall attain [the Self]. 23.
He is the indubitable, imperishable Brahman, who acts for the welfare of all living beings.
Those who are conquerors of the six enemies, and who are likewise peaceful and self-controlled; ||| 24 ||
Then, for those who have realized their own self, the Brahman shines forth equally; oh, how wonderful!
Seated upon his seats, he abandoned these external sense-objects. || 25 ||
Having fixed his frown, he remains devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Prāṇāyāma, however, is the restraint arising from the prāṇa and apāna breaths. || 26 ||
And the wise sages declare that it is threefold in nature.
Know that the measure differs according to its divisions: inferior, middling, and superior. || 27 ||
Prāṇāyāma performed with twelve syllables is known as light (laghu).
That which consists of twenty-four syllables is declared to be the medium one. || 28 ||
That which consists of thirty-six short syllables is called the "excellent" (uttama).
Just as one might bring a lion, a tiger, or even a rutting elephant to a state of gentleness.
In the same way, one should properly regulate the prāṇa and apāna breaths, which lead living beings [to their destination].
O King, having come under your control, they do not oppress the deer, nor do they harm the worlds.
In the same way, that wind burns the sinner, yet it does not consume its own body.
Just as any man might ascend a flight of stairs step by step.
In that very manner, the knower of yoga should indeed bring the prāṇa and apāna under control.
Then one should practice inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
Consequently, he shall become a knower of the past and the future upon the surface of the earth.
Twelve supreme breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) are considered equivalent to one concentration (dhāraṇā). || 33 ||
Yoga consists of two types of concentration; the Lord of Yogis should practice these constantly.
O King, he who acts in this manner becomes a knower of the three periods of time.
O King, by this means, the three worlds will surely come under his control without effort.
He perceives the entire world as the form of Brahman within his own inner self.
Thus, yoga and renunciation yield the same fruit.
The benefactor of living beings and the bestower of the fruits of actions.
By knowing me, the all-pervading Lord of the three worlds, one attains liberation.

Om Tat Sat. Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Renunciation of Action," in the *Śrīmad-Gaṇeśagītā*, which contains the essence of the Upaniṣads; in the treatise on the meaning of the nectar of Yoga; in the *Śrīmad-Ādi-Śrīman-Mahāgāṇeśvara-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the *Bālacarita*, within the dialogue between the illustrious Gajānana and Vareṇya.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Yoga of Renunciation of Action," in the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning: 10,573 + 37 = 10,610.
Chapter 142: The Fifth Chapter, named "Praise of the Practice of Yoga" (Yogānuṣṭhāna-praśaṃsā-yoga).
Śrī Gajānana said:
One should perform the rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis without desiring their fruits;
O King of kings, such a yogi is praised as superior to one who relies on yoga while remaining inactive.
O mighty-armed one, it is my view that action alone is the cause for attaining yoga;
for one who has perfected yoga, tranquility and self-restraint are considered the causes for final perfection.
One who acts while forming conceptualizations regarding the objects of the senses becomes his own enemy;
however, the yogi who performs these same actions without desiring them attains perfection.
In friendship and in enmity, in liberation and in bondage, it is by oneself that one's own self becomes either a self or a non-self. 4.
In honor and dishonor, in pain and pleasure, toward friends and the virtuous,
toward a friend, an enemy, or one who is indifferent, and toward the hateful, a clod of earth, or gold— 5.
One who is self-controlled, possessed of discernment, wise, and who has brought his senses under mastery, should practice yoga constantly; for then he is indeed the most disciplined.
Whether heated, fatigued, agitated, or hungry, yet with an undistracted mind,
one should eat at a time that is neither too cold nor too hot, nor when the air is disturbed by wind, fire, or water.
On a road, in a very dilapidated cow-pen, near a fire, at the edge of a well, in a cremation ground, by a river, or in a place where the vital parts are pierced; || 8 ||
A yogi devoted to meditation should not practice the yoga of yoga in a place containing a shrine, in a region infested with vermin, or in a place surrounded by piśācas and other such beings. 9.
Loss of memory, muteness, deafness, blindness, fever, and dullness arise immediately for the yogin due to ignorance of the defects [of the elements]. || 10 ||
These defects must be abandoned by one who is devoted to the practice of yoga;
for if they are disregarded, the loss of mindfulness and other such faults will certainly follow.
O King, a yogi who practices yoga constantly attains perfection by neither eating too much, nor not eating at all, nor sleeping excessively, nor remaining overly awake. 12.
Restraining his group of senses with the intellect, one who is restricted in diet and wakefulness should abandon desires born of volition and gradually cease from them. 13.
Therefore, wherever the mind wanders, one should diligently bring it under control through steadfastness, making that flickering mind subject to one's own will.
Practicing in this way, the yogi always attains supreme bliss;
he beholds his own self within the universe and the universe within his own self. || 15 ||
Whosoever approaches me through yoga, him I approach with reverence;
I liberate him, I do not abandon him, and he shall not forsake me. 16.
He who perceives all beings with equanimity as himself, and likewise perceives me, who am omnipresent, in pleasure, pain, aversion, hunger, satisfaction, and thirst—[he knows. 17.
That lord of yogis is liberated while living, being united with me alone;
he shall be worthy of worship by Brahmā and the other gods throughout the three worlds. 18.
Vareṇya said: "O Lord, even this twofold yoga is, in my opinion, impossible for me, because the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is wicked, restless, and difficult to restrain. (19)
Śrī Gajānana said: He who devises a means for the restraint of the mind, which is so difficult to grasp, shall attain liberation from this wheel of worldly existence, which is like a water-wheel. 20.
This firm wheel of saṃsāra, joined with the saws of sense-objects and well-fastened by the bolts of karma, people are unable to cut asunder. || 21 ||

Extreme suffering, detachment, and indeed the absence of thirst for enjoyments, as well as the grace of the guru and association with the virtuous—these are the means for conquering that [desire]. 22.
Or, through practice, one should bring the mind under control for the sake of achieving yoga;
O most excellent one, yoga is difficult to attain without the conquest of this mind. 23.
Vareṇya said:
O All-knowing Lord, bearer of the wheel of wisdom, please sever my doubt: for one who has fallen from yoga, what world is there, what is his destination, and what fruit shall he obtain? 24.
Śrī Gajānana said:
One who possesses a divine body through yoga, having fallen from it after enjoying supreme celestial pleasures,
shall obtain birth in a family of yogis or in a family of the wise.
Furthermore, this yogi becomes such again due to the residual impressions born of his previous karma;
for no one who has performed meritorious deeds ever falls into hell. || 26 ||
O lord of men, among those established in knowledge, those established in austerity, and those established in action,
the yogi who possesses devotion to Me is the best, indeed the most excellent of all.

Om Tat Sat. Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Practice of Yoga," in the *Śrīmad-Ādi-Śrīman-Mahāgāṇeśvara-Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Uttara-khaṇḍa* (Latter Section), the *Bālacarita* (Childhood Deeds), in the dialogue between the venerable Gajananavarēnya, contained within the *Yogāmṛtārtha-śāstra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Gaṇeśagītā* whose essence is the meaning of the Upaniṣads. 5.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Yoga of Praise," in the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The cumulative total number of verses from the beginning: 10,610 + 27 = 10,637.
Chapter 6, titled "The Yoga of Wisdom" (Buddhi-yoga), the one hundred and forty-third chapter.
Gajanana said:
Know this to be my true nature, with your inner self absorbed in me;
having known this, you will know me without doubt and shall be liberated from that which pervades all. 1.
Listen, O King, as I shall tell you that for the sake of the welfare of the worlds;
there is no other thing to be known than this, nor any other means for liberation.
First, my primordial nature (prakṛti) should be known; thereafter, it becomes the object of knowledge.
Then, once I am known, there arises for men the perfection of higher realization (vijñāna). || 3 ||
Kva, na, la, u, kha, ma, haṅkāra, kaṃ, citta, dhī, and samīraṇa; Ravi, Indu, and Yāgakṛt—thus my Prakṛti is elevenfold.
The sages declare that there is another, aged Prakṛti of mine;
likewise, heaven is pervaded by this [Prakṛti] which has attained the state of being a living soul.
From these two, this entire world consisting of the moving and the unmoving is produced;
through attachment to them comes the origin of the universe, and I myself am its preservation and dissolution.
Indeed, only some person strives to understand this reality of mine,
owing to the karma performed in former lives by men belonging to the various castes and stages of life.
Even while they are striving, someone perceives me directly;
seeing nothing other than me, he beholds everything within me.
On the earth, he exists in the form of fragrance; in fires, in the form of heat;
in the lotuses of the sun, in the form of light; and in the waters, in the form of taste.
I am the intellect of the powerful, and wisdom as well as austerity are my strength;
I abide within the threefold transformations born from me.
The wicked ones, their minds deluded by illusion, do not find me;
my nature, characterized by the three transformations, deludes the three worlds. 11.
He who understands my true nature abandons all delusion;
having known me thus through many births, he is then liberated from it.
Others worship various other deities and go to them;
in whatever way a person forms their resolve, in that same way they worship me, O All. 13.
In whatever way I fulfill that disposition of his, I alone am he;
I know everything, yet no one perceives me.
Deluded by desire, they do not recognize that the Unmanifest has attained manifestation;
I do not reveal Myself to those of sinful deeds who lack knowledge. 15.
O King, he who, endowed with faith, remembers me at the end and gives up his life-breath, goes by my grace to the state from which there is no return. 16.
O lord of men, remembering whichever deity with devotion while casting off one's own body, one attains the same world as that deity through such devotion.
Therefore, O King, you should remember me in my manifold forms day and night;
for I am accessible to all, just as the ocean is the goal of all rivers. 18.
Having reached the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Indra, and others, one may fall again;
but for him who approaches me with unwavering resolve, there is no falling anywhere. 19.
O protector of the earth, for him who worships me with devotion, having no other refuge,
I always provide for his acquisition and preservation.

O King, two kinds of paths have been described: the white and the black. By the one [white path], one goes to the supreme Brahman; by the other [black path], one enters the cycle of worldly existence.

Om, Tat, Sat. Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Intellect," in the dialogue between Śrī Gajananavareṇya and [the Goddess] within the *Bālacarita* of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa*, in the *Śrīmadādi-Śrī-Mahāgāṇeśvara-Mahāpurāṇa*, which is a treatise on the meaning of the nectar of yoga, containing the essential meaning of the Upaniṣads, known as the *Śrīmad-Gaṇeśagītā*. Chapter Six.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Yoga of Intelligence," in the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning: 10,637 + 21 = 10,658.
Chapter 144 (the seventy-fourth chapter of the second part), titled "The Yoga of Devotion" (Upāsanā-yoga). Chapter 7.
Vareṇya said:
O Elephant-faced One, what is declared to be the white path, and what is the black?
What is the cycle of worldly existence for Brahman? Out of favor toward me, you should explain this to me. (1)
Gajanana said:
Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the northern solstice, and its course;
likewise, the lunar light, smoke, night, and the southern solstice. || 2 ||
O Kṛṣṇa, these two paths are the causes for attaining either worldly existence or Brahman;
resolve that all this, whether visible or invisible, is indeed Brahman alone. (3)
Know the perishable to be composed of the five elements; that which is beyond it is remembered as the imperishable.
Know that which transcends both of these to be the pure, eternal reality.
The cycle of rebirth through many births is proclaimed to be "saṃsṛti";
those who do not reckon me, however, undergo this cycle of rebirth. 5.
Those who worship me correctly attain the Supreme Brahman;
they do so through services such as meditation and likewise with the five nectars and other offerings.
Whoever worships with bathing garments and other ornaments, fragrant incense, lamps, food offerings, fruits, betel leaves, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā); || 7 ||
With a single-minded heart through devotion, I fulfill his desire;
thus, day by day, my devotee shall offer himself to me with devotion.
Alternatively, one should perform mental worship with a steady mind;
or else, one should worship me with effort using fruits, leaves, flowers, roots, water, and so forth. By doing so, one shall obtain those respective desired fruits.
Among all three types of worship, mental worship is considered the most excellent;
even that mental worship is deemed supreme when it is performed for me without desire.
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic— indeed,
anyone else who performs even a single act of worship attains perfection.
O King, even he who, out of devotion, hates me while worshipping another deity, worships me alone; however, he does so in an improper manner.
For he who, hating me and another deity, worships that other,
goes for a thousand kalpas to hells, constantly experiencing suffering.
Having first performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and likewise the stabilization of the vital breaths (prāṇasthāpana),
one should withdraw the activity of the mind and then commence the ritual placement (nyāsa).

Having performed the internal placement of the Mātṛkās (antarmātṛkā-nyāsa) and then the external six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa), as well as the placement of the root mantra (mūlamantra-nyāsa), one should then meditate and recite the mantra. 15.
With a steady mind, one should recite the mantra as it has emerged from the mouth of the Guru;
having offered the recitation to the deity and praised him in manifold ways with hymns of praise. || 16 ||
Thus, whoever should worship me shall obtain imperishable liberation;
but fie on that man who is devoid of such worship—he partakes in a birth in vain.

I am the sacrifice, the medicinal herb, the mantra, the fire, and the kingdom; I am the oblation poured into the flame, meditation, the object of meditation, praise, the hymn of praise, salutation, devotion, and worship. 18.
He is the three Vedas, the object of knowledge, the purifier, the father, and the grandfather;
He is the syllable Om, the sanctifier, the witness, the Lord, the friend, the refuge, and the dissolution. 19.
I am indeed birth, the nourisher, the seed, the refuge, and the dwelling; I am death that is non-existent, the immortality that is existent, the Self, and Brahman.
Whatever he performs—be it charity, fire-offerings, austerity, devotion, silent recitation, or even Vedic study—all that he should offer unto Me and dedicate within Me. 21.
If even women of wicked conduct and sinful members of the three higher castes are liberated by taking refuge in me, why then should the twice-born and others not be so through devotion to me? 22.
My devotee does not perish after knowing these manifestations of mine;
neither the gods nor the seers know my origin or my manifestations.
Pervading the universe with various manifestations, I abide therein;
learn from me those manifestations which are the most excellent in the world. 24.

Om Tat Sat. Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Yoga of Devotion" (*Upāsanāyoga*), within the *Śrīmad-Gaṇeśagītā*, which contains the essence of the Upaniṣads; in this treatise on the nectar of yoga, within the *Śrīmad-Ādi-Śrīman-Mahāgāṇeśvara-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Uttarakhaṇḍa*, in the *Bālacarita*, in the dialogue between the venerable Gajānana and Vareṇya.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Devotion," in the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The cumulative total number of verses from the beginning: 10,685 + 24 = 10,709. Chapter 8, titled "The Vision of the Cosmic Form," is the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter.
Vareṇya said:
"O Blessed One, Nārada has described to me your various manifestations;
I know them, yet he too does not know them all. (1)
O elephant-faced one, you alone know all those [goddesses] in their true essence.
"Now, reveal to me your own form, which is all-pervading and beautiful."
The illustrious Gajānana said:
Behold this entire universe, with all that is moving and unmoving, within me alone.
In former times, various divine wonders were seen by someone.
Today, by my own power, I shall create for you the eye of knowledge.
How could one with the eye of flesh behold me, the all-pervading, unborn, and undecaying?
Vyāsa said:
Then that excellent king, possessing divine vision,
beheld the supreme and most wonderful elephant-headed form of the Lord.
He has countless faces, is graceful, possesses innumerable feet and hands, is great,
is anointed with fragrant scents, and wears divine ornaments, garments, and garlands.
With eyes beyond counting and bearing weapons like the rays of ten million suns,
the three worlds were seen by him in their various forms within that body.
Having beheld that supreme form of the Lord and having bowed down, that king spoke. The Excellent One said:
"I behold within this body of yours the gods, the hosts of ṛṣis, and the ancestors."
Of the netherworlds, the oceans, the islands, and indeed the mountains.
And the group of seven great seers, O Lord, crowded with various purposes.
The earth, the atmosphere, and the heavens, as well as humans, serpents, and rākṣasas; || 9 ||
The gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and Indra, as well as various kinds of living beings.
Without beginning or end, the origin of the world, possessing infinite arms and heads.
Resembling a blazing fire, immeasurable, and ancient.
Wearing a crown and earrings, he was difficult to behold, yet he brought joy.
And I behold you, my lord, of such a form, with a broad chest.
By the excellent Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, sages, and humans. || 12 ||
And with dancing Apsarases and Gandharvas intent upon singing.
[He was] accompanied by the hosts of Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, and by the Siddhas and Sādhyas, who were filled with joy.
He was being served with great devotion and gazed upon by those filled with wonder—
the knower, the imperishable, the object of knowledge, the protector of dharma, and the Lord.
Pervading the netherworlds, the directions, the heavens, and the earth, it remains encompassing everything.
The worlds, as well as I myself, are terrified upon seeing you thus embodied.
He was formidable with various fangs and proficient in various branches of knowledge.
With a face blazing like the fire of universal destruction, he had matted hair and reached up to the sky.
O Gaṇeśa, having seen your form, I became as if bewildered.
Gods, humans, nāgas, and others—even the wicked—all lie within your belly.
Having experienced various births, they finally enter into you alone. || 17 ||
Just as drops of water from clouds arise from the ocean.
You are Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, and Marut.
Likewise, Guhyakeśa, Īśāna, Soma, and Sūrya are the entire world.
I bow to you, O Lord; therefore, grant me your grace now.
"O gentle one, show me that innate form of yours which was previously beheld;
who, O Infinite One, can know your pastimes being performed by your own will? (20)
By your grace, I have beheld such a divine form,
since you, being well-pleased, have granted me the eye of knowledge.
The illustrious Gajānana said: "O mighty-armed one, yogis such as Sanaka and others, as well as Nārada and others, do not behold this form of mine; they behold it only through my grace. (23)
Those who know the true meaning of the four Vedas, those who are proficient in the four branches of knowledge,
and those devoted to sacrifice, charity, and austerity— they do not know my form.
I can be seen, known, and entered through the state of devotion;
abandon both fear and delusion, and behold me in my gentle form. 25.
My devotee, who has me as his supreme goal, who is free from all attachments, who acts for my sake,
who is devoid of anger, and who is equal toward all beings— such a ruler of the earth attains me.

Om Tat Sat. Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Vision of the Universal Form," in the *Śrīmad-Gaṇeśagītā*, which contains the essence of the Upaniṣads, within the *Yogāmṛtārtha-śāstra*, the *Śrīmad-Ādi-Śrīman-Mahāgāṇeśvara-Mahāpurāṇa*, in its *Uttara-khaṇḍa*, in the *Bālacarita*, within the dialogue between the venerable Gajāsya and Vareṇya. 8.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Vision of the Universal Form," in the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning: 10,682 + 26 = 10,708.
Chapter 9, titled "The Yoga of Discrimination between the Field and the Knower of the Field," is the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter.

The Exalted One said: "Between those two—one who worships you with undivided devotion as the manifest embodied form, and one who worships the supreme, unmanifest Imperishable—which of them is considered by you to be superior? (1)
You are the all-knowing witness, the creator of beings, and the Lord;
therefore, I question you. Speak to me out of compassion, O All-pervading One.
The illustrious Gajānana said:
That devotee of mine who, with devotion, serves me as the possessor of form, is worthy of my honor, for he possesses exclusive devotion and has fixed his heart upon me. 3.
Having brought the host of birds under his control, he acted for the welfare of all living beings;
he meditated upon the imperishable, unmanifest, all-pervading, stable essence that resides in the peak of existence.
Even he who, devoted to Me, worships Me as the one to be pointed out—
him too I lift up from this ocean of worldly existence.
Greater suffering is obtained from the worship of the Unmanifest;
that very same [result] which is accomplished through the worship of the Manifest is attained through devotion to the Unmanifest.
Devotion and respect alone are my supreme criteria here;
for among all learned men, even one who knows nothing is the best if he is devoted. (7)
He who worships devoid of devotion is called a cāṇḍāla;
yet even a cāṇḍāla who worships with devotion is, in my view, superior to the Brāhmaṇas. 8.
In ancient times, Śuka and others, as well as Sanaka and others, were indeed liberated through devotion;
and by devotion alone did Nārada and others attain long life and reach me.
Therefore, with devotion, fix your mind and your intellect upon me;
worship me with devotion, O King, and then you shall come to me alone. 10.
O lord of men, you are certainly unable to surrender your heart to me;
therefore, strive to reach me through practice and yoga.
If you are unable even in that, then perform action dedicated to Me;
and by My grace, you shall thus attain supreme peace.
If you are unable to practice even in this way, then perform with effort the renunciation of the fruits of the three kinds of actions. 13.
The intellect that turns away from worldly involvement is superior; therefore, meditation is considered better than that.
Hence, the renunciation of everything is superior, and peace is the most excellent of all. 14.

He who is free from the notions of "I" and "mine," who is without hatred and is compassionate, who is equanimous in gain and loss, in pleasure and pain, and in honor and dishonor—he is dear to me. 15.
He whom people do not fear upon seeing, who himself does not fear anyone,
and who is free from agitation and terror— he is dear to me.
He who is the same toward enemy and friend, as well as in blame and praise, and who remains equanimous in sorrow;
who is silent, steady-minded, devoted, and free from attachment—he indeed is dear to Me. 17.
He who practices this instruction given by me is to be honored in all worlds; he is one whose self is liberated and is always dear to me. 18.
He who feels no hatred upon encountering the undesired, nor rejoices upon attaining the desired, and who knows both the field and its Knower—he shall be most dear to Me. 19.
Vareṇya said:
"O Gajānana, ocean of compassion, what is the field (kṣetra), who knows it, and what is that knowledge? Tell this to me as I ask you. (20)
Śrī Gaṇeśa said:
The five elements, the five subtle essences (tanmātras), the five organs of action,
the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the mind (manas), the intellect (buddhi), and the five organs of perception.
Desire, the unmanifest, resolve, aversion, as well as pleasure and pain; || 21 ||
This aggregate, accompanied by volition, is called the field;
know me, O King, as its knower, the all-pervading Lord who dwells within all. 22.
O King, this assembly and I myself are the objects of that knowledge;
[the means are] straightforwardness, service to the guru, and detachment from the objects of the senses. (23)
Purity, forbearance, absence of deceit, perception of the defects of birth and other worldly conditions, equanimity of vision, firm devotion, single-mindedness, tranquility, and self-restraint. (24)
O Bāhujā, know that knowledge which is endowed with these [qualities] to be true knowledge;
O King, listen as I describe to you the object of that knowledge. 25.
Having known that, one goes to Nirvana, leaving behind the ocean of saṃsāra—
that which is beginningless, devoid of the senses, the enjoyer of the qualities, yet free from the qualities.
Unmanifest, distinct from both being and non-being, the illuminator of the objects of the senses,
the sustainer of the universe and all-pervading, it is one, yet appears as if manifold.
It is full both internally and externally, unattached, beyond darkness, difficult to know because of its extreme subtlety, and the illuminator even of luminous things. (28)
Know that this which is to be known is such as this: ancient, attainable through knowledge;
this alone is the supreme Brahman, the object of knowledge, the supreme, imperishable Self. 29.
The Puruṣa, though beyond Prakṛti, experiences the qualities born of Prakṛti;
by means of these three qualities, this [Prakṛti] binds the Puruṣa firmly within the body.
When illumination and forbearance predominate, then goodness (sattva) is superior;
greed, lack of tranquility, longing, and the undertaking of actions are the qualities of passion (rajas). 31.
Delusion, inactivity, ignorance, and negligence are the qualities of tamas;
happiness and knowledge predominate in sattva; and attachment to action predominates in rajas.
And when tamas predominates, one obtains sleep, sloth, and that which is other than pleasure.
When these three are intensified, there arise liberation, worldly existence, and miserable states.
Men go [to their respective states], O King; therefore, be endowed with sattva.
And so, O lord of men, worship me with your whole being. 34.
And through unwavering devotion, it is established everywhere—
in fire, in the sun, in the moon, and that which is established in the stars.
"Know, O King, that the splendor residing in the wise Brahmin is mine;
I alone create and withdraw this entire universe. (36)
By my splendor, I nourish all herbs and the entire universe;
presiding over all the senses and the digestive fire within the stomach, O Dhanañjaya.
Devoid of both merit and sin, I enjoy all pleasures;
so too do I, as well as Viṣṇu, Rudra, Brahmā, Gaurī, and Gaṇeśvara. 38.
Indra and the other guardians of the worlds have likewise arisen from my own portions;
for in whatever form people worship me, [I appear in that very form]. 39.
In whatever way [a person] possesses excellent devotion, in that very way do I manifest My form to him.
Thus have I described the field, as well as the Knower, knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
O lord of the earth, [this has been told] in its entirety to you who have approached with proper conduct and inquire [about it]. 41.

Om Tat Sat. Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Discernment between the Field and the Knower of the Field," in the *Bālacarita* (Childhood Deeds) of the *Śrīmad-Ādi-Śrīman-Mahāgāṇeśvara-Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Uttarakhaṇḍa*, in the dialogue between the venerable Gajānana and Vareṇya, which is the essence of the meaning of the Upanishads and a treatise on the nectar of Yoga, known as the *Śrīmad-Gaṇeśagītā*. 9.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Discerning the Field and the Knower of the Field," in the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning: 10,708 + 41 = 10,749.
Chapter 10, titled "The Yoga of Instruction" (Upadeśayoga), the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter.
The illustrious Gajānana said:
"The nature of men is threefold—divine, demonic, and rakshasa.
I shall now describe to you briefly their fruits and characteristics."
O King, the first [of these powers] accomplishes liberation, while the other two result in bondage. I shall describe the characteristic of the first; listen as I speak of it. || 2 ||
Absence of backbiting, compassion, freedom from anger, lack of fickleness, fortitude, straightforwardness, vigor, fearlessness, non-violence, forgiveness, purity, and humility; || 3 ||
Now hear the characteristics of the first, the demoniacal nature:
excessive speech, arrogance, pride, ignorance, and anger. (4)
O King, such signs as these belong to the demonic nature:
cruelty, intoxication, delusion, egoism, and pride.
Hatred, violence, lack of compassion, anger, restlessness, ill-behavior, performing malevolent rites, and likewise delighting in cruel deeds; || 6 ||
Lack of faith in the words of the virtuous, impurity, deficiency in ritual action, and reviling the Vedas and the devotees of the Enemy of the Asuras; || 7 ||
Trust in the words of sages, Vedic scholars, and Brahmins, as well as in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas, and association with those of impure soul—these are [the causes of downfall]. 8.
Performing evil deeds, coveting the possessions of others, being possessed by manifold desires, and always speaking untruths—these are [the characteristics of the tamasic mind]. || 9 ||
Intolerance of the excellence of others, the sabotage of the undertakings of others, and many other such qualities are the characteristics of the demonic nature. 10.
Wandering between the earth and the heavenly world,
those people who are devoid of devotion to me dwell having resorted to a demonic nature.
O King, those who have resorted to the quality of darkness (tamas) certainly go to the Raurava hell;
remaining there, they experience unspeakable suffering.
O King, having emerged from hell by the power of fate, they are born on earth as hunchbacks, those blind from birth, the lame, and the wretched among low castes. 13.
Furthermore, those of evil conduct who lack devotion to me fall;
whereas my devotees, having entered whatever womb they may have taken, indeed rise upward.
O protector of the earth, they attain the heavenly realm through other sacrifices and religious duties;
yet that devotion to me, which fulfills all desires, is easily obtained by some but extremely difficult for others to attain.
Deluded and bound by the net of ignorance through their own karma, they speak thus:
"I am the taker, I am the doer, I am the enjoyer. (16)
"I alone am the lord, the ruler; I am the knower, I am the happy one"—such a mindset causes men to fall downward in this world. 17.
Therefore, having completely abandoned this, take refuge in your divine nature;
practice devotion to me with a steady mind, without ceasing. 18.
That devotion also, O King, is threefold: sattvic, rājasic, and the other (tāmasa).
That which worships the gods with devotion is considered auspicious and sattvic. (19)
That devotion which consists of sacrificing to yakṣas and even to rākṣasas with their whole being should be known as rājasic; it bestows rebirth and death. 20.
They resort to cruel rites not ordained by the Veda, characterized by egoism and hypocrisy;
they worship spirits, ghosts, and the like, performing actions driven by desire. || 21 ||
Those who, with firm resolve, emaciate their own bodies while dwelling within me—such devotion of men to the quality of darkness (tamas) leads to hell. 22.
Lust, greed, anger, and hypocrisy—these four are the great gateways to the waves [of worldly existence]; therefore, one should avoid them. 23.

Om Tat Sat. Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Instruction," in the *Upadeśayoga* within the *Bālacarita* of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa*, in the *Śrīmad-Ādi-Śrī-Mahāgāṇeśvara-Mahāpurāṇa*, which is the *Yogāmṛtārthaśāstra* containing the essence of the meaning of the *Śrīmad-Gaṇeśagītā-Upaniṣads*, in the dialogue between the venerable Gajananavarēnya.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Yoga of Instruction," in the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The cumulative total number of verses from the beginning: 10,749 + 23 = 10,772.
Chapter 11, titled "The Determination of the Threefold Reality," being the one hundred forty-eighth chapter.
The illustrious Gajānana said: O King, austerity is also threefold, distinguished as bodily and so forth; it consists of rectitude, straightforwardness, purity, celibacy, and non-violence. 1.
The worship of gurus, the wise, the twice-born, and the enemies of the asuras, as well as the constant observance of one's own dharma—such is physical austerity. || 2 ||
Speech that touches the vital points, is pleasant, free from agitation, beneficial, and truthful;
and the study of the Vedas and the Shastras—such is austerity of speech (vācika-tapas). || 3 ||
Inner serenity, tranquility, silence, restraint of the senses,
and constant purity of intention— such is the austerity of the mind.
That austerity which is performed without desire for reward and with faith is *sāttvika*.

That austerity which is for the sake of ostentation, honor, and worship, being full of hypocrisy, is *rājasa*. (That *rājasa* austerity is for the sake of proving the authority of scriptural injunctions and is full of hypocrisy.
It is unstable and brings about birth and death; of this there is no doubt.
And that austerity which causes pain to oneself and others is said to be tāmasa.

That gift which is given with faith, at the proper time and place, to a worthy recipient, for the sake of the authority of the injunctions— such a gift is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
That which is given by men desiring a return favor or a fruit, or that which is given with difficulty, is said to be of the nature of passion (rājasa). || 8 ||
But that gift which is given at an improper time or place, to an unworthy recipient, with contempt,
or without due respect— that gift is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
And knowledge is threefold, O King; listen with a steady mind.
I shall also speak to you, in passing, of the threefold action and the agent. (10)
But he who perceives Me as the One within various kinds of beings,
and as the Eternal within that which is perishable— O King, that knowledge is sattvic.
That knowledge which perceives within those [beings] a separate and manifold nature, while being attached to it, yet regards Me as the immutable—this is proclaimed as rājasa. || 12 ||
Knowledge that is devoid of cause, untrue, and concerned with the body as the self; or that which has for its object the unreal or the trivial—this is called tamasic knowledge. (13)
O King, know that action has been described by me as being of three kinds according to its divisions;
that which is performed as obligatory duty, free from desire, hatred, and hypocrisy.
Action performed without desire for fruit is said to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
That action which is performed with great distress and that which is performed with a desire for fruit [is of the nature of passion and ignorance].
Action performed by men out of hypocrisy is said to be of the nature of passion (rājasa);
likewise, that which disregards one's own capacity and results in the destruction of wealth is also so described.
Action performed out of ignorance is said to be tāmasa.
Know, O King, that the agent is of three kinds as I describe them. 17.
O King, he who possesses fortitude and enthusiasm, who remains equanimous in failure and unchanging in success, and who is free from egoism—that doer is of the nature of goodness (sāttvika). 18.
He who experiences both joy and sorrow, who commits violence and desires the fruits [of his actions], and who is impure and greedy—he is said to be of the rajasic nature. 19.
The agent who is accompanied by negligence and ignorance, intent on the destruction of others, deceitful, lazy, and argumentative—he is considered to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). || 20 ||
O King, listen now in due order to the threefold nature of happiness and suffering;
I shall describe that which is characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), and darkness (tāmasa).
That which appears at first like poison, yet brings an end to suffering, and which, when pursued through desire and right conduct, becomes like nectar in the end—[that is this]. (22)
That sattvic happiness which is said to arise from the clarity of one's own intellect may at first appear like the enjoyment of sense objects, shining like nectar. (23)
That which is called rajasic pleasure is like deadly poison in its end;
it arises from sloth and negligence, and has its origin in indolence.
Such self-centered pleasure, which is always delusive and characterized by darkness (tamas), does not exist that is free from these three qualities (guṇas). 25.
O King, even Brahmā is threefold according to the distinctions of *om*, *tat*, and *sat*;
O Ruler of the Earth, everything in the three worlds exists as these three forms.
The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are, by their very nature, engaged in different duties;
I shall now state those duties of theirs to you in brief. (27)
Mastery over the internal and external senses, straightforwardness, forgiveness, various austerities, purity—which is twofold—and knowledge of the Self. (28)
Knowledge of the Vedas, the Shastras, the Puranas, and the Smritis, as well as the performance of their prescribed duties—this is declared to be the action pertaining to Brahman. (29)
Firmness, valor, skill, never turning one's back in battle,
protection of those seeking refuge, generosity, fortitude, and energy— these are born of his very nature.
Sovereignty, mental loftiness, sound policy, protection of the world,
and authority over the five types of action— this is declared to be the duty of the Kṣatriya.
The purchase of various goods, the cultivation of land, and the protection of cattle—this threefold authority over work is declared to be the duty of the Vaiśya. (32)
Giving gifts to the twice-born, service, and constant devotion to Śiva—
such, O tiger among men, is declared to be the work of the Śūdra.
Devoted to their respective duties and offering everything to me,
they attain a firm and supreme station through my grace, O King.
Thus, O King, out of favor toward you, I have related this supreme Yoga—along with its ancillaries and in full detail—to you, my beloved, which is established from time immemorial. 35.
Apply the yoga I have declared, which has not been told to anyone else, O King;
guard it, and from that you shall attain the supreme, unsurpassed perfection.
Ka said:
Having heard these words of the gracious and high-souled Gaṇeśa, that most excellent one performed everything exactly as he had been told. 37.
Having abandoned his kingdom and family, he departed swiftly for the Kāntāra forest;
there, by practicing the instructions as prescribed, he attained liberation.
But whoever hears this supreme yoga with faith, || 38 ||
He too attains absolute liberation, just as the yogi does.
The wise man who, having mastered its meaning, should cause this yoga to be heard; || 39 ||
Just as the yogi, so too does he attain supreme nirvāṇa.
Whoever has properly practiced the Gītā and understood its meaning from the mouth of the Guru.
Whoever, having performed worship of Gaṇeśa, recites this every day;
Whoever should recite it once a day, twice a day, or even three times a day; || 41 ||
By seeing even such a person who has become one with Brahman, a man is liberated.
Not by sacrifices, nor by vows, nor by gifts, nor by costly agnihotra rites. || 42 ||
Not by the Vedas thoroughly studied and correctly understood along with their auxiliary limbs, nor by listening to the Purāṇas, nor even by the Śāstras and the reflections of the virtuous; || 43 ||
By means of this [knowledge], the supreme Brahman is attained by men;
even he who is a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of intoxicants, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed attains it. 44.
But he who associates with those four who have committed mortal sins, [is likewise tainted].
Those sinners who are the perpetrators of violence against women, the slaughter of cows, and so forth; || 45 ||
They are all liberated if they recite this song.
He who recites this constantly with a restrained mind is Gaṇeśa himself; of this there is no doubt. || 46 ||
Whoever recites it with devotion on the fourth lunar day, even he is fit for liberation.
Having reached each respective sacred field, one should bathe and worship Gajānana.
Whoever recites this once with devotion is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, a devoted man [should perform this]. || 48 ||
Having fashioned an image of Gaṇeśa out of earth with four arms,
Having worshipped [them] according to the prescribed rite, together with their vehicles and weapons.
Whoever should recite this Gītā with diligence seven times, [attains the supreme goal].
Being pleased with him, Gaṇeśa bestows supreme enjoyment.
Sons, grandsons, wealth, grain, cattle, jewels, and other riches.
One who seeks knowledge shall obtain knowledge; one who seeks happiness shall attain happiness.
A seeker of desires may obtain other desires, yet they ultimately attain liberation. || 52 ||

Om tat sat. Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Creation of the Three Guṇas," in the *Śrīmad-Gaṇeśagītā*, which contains the essence of the Upaniṣads, within the *Yogāmṛtārtha-śāstra*, the *Śrīmad-Ādi-Śrīman-Mahāgāṇeśvara-Mahāpurāṇa*, in its *Uttara-khaṇḍa*, in the *Bālacarita*, within the dialogue between the illustrious Gajānana and Vareṇya. 11.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Creation of the Three Qualities," in the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning: 10,772 + 52 = 10,824.
Chapter 149, titled "The Departure of the Sage," the one hundred and forty-ninth.
Ka said:
Having thus accepted the worship, the Lord dwelt right there in the palace honored by the king, fulfilling the desires of his devotees.
The Sage said:
In the account of Vināyaka’s greatness, various stories have been related;
having descended into the house of Vareṇya, the demon Vighna was slain.
O Four-faced One, the encounter with the demon Gajāsura has been described;
herein, the manifestation from Pārvatī’s womb is also set forth. (3)
O Lord, because of your elephantine face, a doubt has arisen in me;
for there is no one else in the three worlds who can sever this doubt but you.
Ka said:
O Vyāsa, one should not entertain doubt regarding the All-pervading Lord, who is endowed with manifold powers;
He assumes various forms by His own will according to the differences between the kalpas.
O Sage, Gajānana manifested from the mouth and the wrath of Śambhu,
and was born from the luster of Gaurī and from her belly in some accounts.
In some places he is fair-complexioned, and in others two-faced and two-armed;
in some places five-faced, and in others six-faced and ten-armed.
In some places he has twelve hands, and in others he is adorned with a thousand arms;
indeed, various meditations are found in all the Āgamas.
O Sage, you should entertain neither doubt nor wonder regarding the power of Śiva;
for it is described in the Liṅga Purāṇa that both Brahmā and Viṣṇu were born from him.
In the Skanda Purāṇa, the origin of Śiva from the eye of the Creator is described;
furthermore, it is stated that Viṣṇu meditates upon Śiva, and Śiva likewise meditates upon Viṣṇu alone.
The Lord speaks the five-syllabled mantra along with the Tāraka,
and the life-story of Rāma, which consists of one hundred crores and is divided into three parts.
That Śaṅkara established Tāraka in the world of mortals;
in some places creation is said to proceed from Śiva, in others from Brahmā, and in others from Hari.
In some places she is proclaimed as the Bhagavatī, in some from the Sun, and in others from Gaṇeśa;
and in some places she is proclaimed as Brāhmaṇī—all of that is in accordance with the scriptures.
"He who entertains doubt certainly goes to hell.
Ka said: "O Sage, thus has the entire narrative of the Tretā Yuga been told to you."
Now I shall relate a narrative concerning the Kali age;
at the end of the Kali age, O Sage, people will be devoid of proper conduct and likewise untruthful.
Brahmins devoid of the Vedas and abandoned by the ritual baths and twilight prayers will never perform sacrifices, officiate at sacrifices, or give gifts. (16)
And they will accept gifts from the wicked, which is very difficult to avoid;
likewise, they will engage in slandering others, censuring them, and violating the wives of others.
All people will everywhere practice the violation of sacred injunctions, and men will certainly commit treachery against their trust in all places. 18.
O Lord of Sages, when the prescribed rites are neglected, people on this earth will resort to oaths, and the clouds will not bring rain anywhere.
People will practice agriculture in the regions along the banks of great rivers;
even those who are weak will seize by force the wealth of others, including their tribute.
Then two will take [the Veda] from him, and three more from those two by force; Śūdras will recite the Veda, and Brāhmaṇas will perform the duties of Śūdras.
Those of the twice-born caste will perform the duties of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, while Vaiśyas will perform the duties of Śūdras; and the twice-born will accept gifts from outcasts (Caṇḍālas).
They will become impoverished, crying out "Alas! Alas!", and deprived of their senses;
they will say, "Not even the slightest wealth was taken by me."
Moreover, even after receiving wealth from others for the sake of their business,
they accept bribes and give false testimony.
They will revile the virtuous and form friendships only with the wicked;
the twice-born will consume meat in vain.
There would be the destruction of the virtuous and the prosperity of others;
abandoning the gods, all people will become like mere sense-organs. || 26 ||
With their minds attached to the worship of spirits, ghosts, and demons, the Brahmins will assume various kinds of disguises and devour [the people]. (27)
And some Kṣatriyas will wander for alms— a practice unbecoming of their lineage— and they will never at any time observe vows or religious restraints.
In the Kali age, the king will perform actions that cause the intermixture of castes; women who were devoted to their husbands will fall away from their vows.
All the worlds will consist mostly of barbarians, seizing the property of others, merciless, devoted to evil paths, and always devoid of truth. 30.
The earth will be devoid of crops, and trees will be devoid of sap;
furthermore, in the fifth or even the sixth year, a woman shall give birth to a daughter.
Furthermore, at that time in that age, the lifespan will be no more than sixteen years;
the sacred fords and the temples of the deities will exist only in a hidden form.
When evil has thus increased, dharma will consist of merely the welfare of all beings;
at that time, the gods will be devoted solely to fasting.
Deprived of the utterances of Svadhā, Svāhā, and Vaṣaṭ, and overwhelmed by fear,
they will seek refuge with the god who has the face of an elephant, the one free from ailment.
They will offer various kinds of praise and many prostrations to him,
and they will pray to the Lord of Gods, the destroyer of all obstacles.
Having thus reflected upon everything,
he will manifest himself as Gajānana, Śūrpakarṇa, and by name also Dhūmravarṇa.
Mounting his dark-blue horse, sword in hand and blazing with wrath,
he will, by his own will, arrange his army into various formations.
And he will effortlessly fashion weapons and great missiles;
with his own army and his own splendor, he will slay the great Mlecchas.
Then he will slay all the people who have become like Mlecchas,
as well as the Brāhmaṇas living in mountain caves who subsist on forest fare.
Having summoned and honored them, the King of the Gods will bestow the land upon them;
he will establish all those who perform virtuous deeds as true men of integrity.
Then, in the Kṛta age, the universe will consist of righteousness;
having acted thus, Dhūmravarṇa will thereafter disappear.
Thus, O Vyāsa, O sinless one, the names and forms of the high-souled Vighneśa throughout the four yugas have been recounted to you.
And his deeds of wondrous form have been described in their entirety;
by the mere hearing of which all living beings are liberated. 43.
I do not have the power to describe the forms of the One who is without another;
where even the four Vedas are confounded, what need is there to speak further?
"Either for me or even for one like me, in the description of that greatness—go you to carry it out; as for me, I shall make an effort. (45)
Bhṛgu said: Having thus heard from the mouth of Brahmā this story that destroys all sins, Vyāsa, O beloved of Soma, spoke with a heart full of great joy.
The sage said:
"I do not reach satiety hearing this most wonderful narrative.
I am blessed and I am graced, since all my doubts have been [resolved] by you. (47)
Having distanced myself from all other conversation by taking refuge in the life-story of Gaṇeśa, my satisfaction, as if from nectar, does not cease even after hearing it again and again. 48.
Merely by hearing this, the sins accumulated over many successive births go to destruction, and all desires are fulfilled. 49.
Through the power of past merit, this [Purāṇa] comes to be heard by men.
This Purāṇa, which bestows all perfections, must not be recited to a wicked person. 50.
Having spoken thus, and having paid homage and circumambulated the Self-born One,
Vyāsa took his leave and departed for the excellent forest to perform austerities.
There, the fruits and roots were excellent and the waters were pure;
there the wind was not strong, nor was there heat, nor even fire.
There, seated and single-mindedly reciting the single-syllable mantra,
twelve years passed for that sage as he practiced his austerities;
then, Gajānana appeared before him.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Faults of the Kali Age and the Dismissal of the Sages," in the *Krīḍākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
