Chapter One Hundred and Fifty-Two, titled "Description of the Sacred Field of Vyāsa’s Grace," begins with Somakānta saying:
O Bhṛgu, tell me all of that— how the God appeared before that great-souled one— for by hearing it, there shall be a destruction of sins.
Bhṛgu said:
O protector of the earth, I shall relate everything concerning how the elephant-faced god appeared before him; listen with respect. 2.
Wearing red garlands and garments, anointed with red perfumes and unguents,
he has the face of an elephant, lotus-like eyes, and a head as crimson as vermilion.
Resembling many suns, adorned with divine earrings,
he wore armlets and a crown, as well as bracelets upon his remaining arms.
Having thus gazed at him, the sage closed his eyes once more;
trembling, terrified with fear, he remembered the mantra and fell into a swoon.
Then Nāgamukha said, "Do not fear, O best of sages;
I am he whom you contemplate day and night, and I have come before you."
"O Sage, that which is inaccessible even to Brahmā and the other gods, you are able to grant as a boon.
Bhr̥gu said:
"Having heard these sweet words, the bull among sages rejoiced. (7)
Placing his head at their feet, he spoke again and again: "I am blessed, O parents! You are asceticism itself; I am blessed, O Earth and trees! (8)
For he has been seen as possessing all forms, transcending all qualities, the refuge of all,
a mass of consciousness and bliss, infinite, and the cause of all causes.
Having thus praised and petitioned the elephant-faced giver of boons, the sage said:
"Having cast aside all my delusion, grant me firm devotion unto you. (10)
O Lord, act in such a way that I may be capable of composing the eighteen Purāṇas, and likewise possess the power to offer praise to you. || 11 ||
"O Lord of Gods, dwell in my heart; if you are pleased with me, O sinless one.
Gajanana said:
"O child, everything that has been requested by you shall come to pass this very day."
Venerated by all, named Vyāsa, the purifier of all purifiers, and possessing direct knowledge, you shall become the teacher of teachers. 13.
Devoted to Nārāyaṇa, you shall indeed become famous for your virtues and renown, as well as for your prosperity;
you will be the author of the eighteen Purāṇas.
O Lord of Sages, likewise, you previously failed to perform my worship for so many Upapurāṇas due to the influence of hypocrisy. || 15 ||
Or rather, O sinless one, from that recollection there arose this most wonderful paralysis of my speech,
because I have heard his greatness from the mouth of the Creator himself.
"Now that everything has dissolved, I shall enter your belly.
Bhṛgu said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord entered the belly of that sage.
The sage attained incomparable radiance, equal to ten million suns;
then, assuming a physical form, he illuminated all the quarters of the sky.
And he established a great image of Gajānana in the palace,
worshipping it with various offerings individually.
This is a field of accomplishment for all people, purifying to the sight;
it is auspicious, bestowing various perfections of mantra upon those who practice with devotion.
Having spoken thus and having obtained permission, Vyāsa, who was then Nārāyaṇa,
[expounded] that Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa which he had heard from the mouth of Brahmā.
He then spoke it to Vaiśampāyana, and thereafter it spread upon the earth;
all of that has now been recounted by me to you as well, O King. 22.
O best of kings, there exists nothing else in the three worlds equal to this in its sanctity, nor anything that bestows such supreme bliss. (23)
"O Somakānta, you must not speak of this among wicked people;
however, you should speak of it with great effort to those who are disciplined and devoted. (24)
This has been recited and remembered by me incessantly;
out of compassion for you as well, O best of kings, it has been told to you. 25.
Be constantly intent on the meditation of Gajānana and devoted to the recitation of his mantra.
Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "Description of the Siddhikṣetra through Vyāsa’s Grace," in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa. || 150 ||

Chapter One Hundred and Fifty-one, titled "Description of the Attainment of the Moon-Like Radiant Celestial Vehicle," Sūta said:
Having thus constantly heard this story from the lord of sages,
King Somakānta cast that merit into the water at the foot of a withered mango tree.
When a year had passed, the mango tree, exceedingly beautiful due to the merit of ancient sacred texts, shone forth with sprouts, flowers, and fruits.
Somakānta, possessing divine beauty, having abandoned the pain born of leprosy, became unscarred;
and having cast off his foul odor, he became fragrant.
Free from weariness, [he beheld] the king, whose fragrant scent spread through the ten directions,
possessing a divine body with the luster of the sun and resembling ten million moons.
Seeing this, the people were amazed, wondering how such a thing could be so.
By the greatness of the Purāṇa named Gaṇeśa, which removes all defects. || 5 ||
Bhṛgu said:
"O tiger among kings, your success has been achieved through hearing the Purāṇa.
Now you may go to your own son, along with your ministers and the people."
Seeing him after a long year of longing, you will attain great joy.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words, he fell at the feet of the sage.
Immersed in an ocean of bliss, that lover of the moon (Soma) spoke to Bhṛgu.
The King said:
"O Sage, today I have beheld the wonderful majesty of your ascetic power. (8)
"By means of this very hearing of the Purāṇas, my mother and father—who were afflicted with wasting leprosy—have become possessed of divine bodies even though they had fallen [into sin]. (9)
O best of sages, you alone are the creator of this body; even a sapless mango tree became endowed with flowers and fruit because of you. 10.
"Therefore, I do not wish to abandon you; what would be the use of sons born to me?
Having heard those words, Bhṛgu then spoke again.
Bhṛgu said:
"By virtue of merit acquired in a previous birth, the hearing of the Purāṇas has occurred for you through my mouth; it is blessed, for by it your sin has been destroyed. (12)
By whom can the greatness of the Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa be described?
Do not forget me; go now, O Lord of Men, to your own city. 13.
While the two of them were thus conversing, they beheld a great, wondrous, and blazing celestial chariot, possessing a splendor like that of ten million suns.
Bhṛgu said:
"O King, this most wonderful vehicle has arrived for your sake;
having mounted it, go into the presence of Gaṇanātha. (15)
O King, that celestial mansion which the lords of sages do not attain through their religious practices,
has been obtained by you from Gaṇeśvara through the hearing of the Purāṇas.
Even as they were speaking thus, the celestial chariot descended in an instant to the surface of the earth,
accompanied by hosts of Vināyakas and adorned with four arms.
Adorned with ornaments such as crowns, armlets, and necklaces,
they were graced by divine sandalwood paste, garments, and other finery, and shone with lotuses and axes.
Seeing it accompanied by dancing Kinnara maidens with mṛdaṅga drums and cymbals in their hands,
and by singing Kinnaras, the king spoke again.
The king said:
"O lord of sages, I have heard many accounts of celestial chariots;
O Brahmin, those very things have now been seen before me through the power of your ascetic merit."
His greatness is heard in many ways from many mouths;
it has also been experienced by me through hearing the Purāṇas from you. 21.
When the king had spoken thus, all the messengers descended from their vehicles,
prostrated themselves, and then addressed King Somaka.
O pure-souled one, by virtue of your merit, remembrance has been restored to you by the God who is higher than the highest, Gajānana, through the hearing of the Purāṇas and other means. 23.
"We are messengers who have arrived by his command in this celestial chariot;
come, let us lead you, whose fame is meritorious, to the unsurpassed world. (24)
By beholding Him, you will be liberated from birth and death; having come into His presence, you shall attain ultimate bliss there through His grace. || 25 ||
Having heard those words of the messenger, he became as if his body had transcended itself;
with every limb bristling with horripilation, he spoke in a faltering voice.
By that God who is higher than the highest, the creator of the moving and the unmoving,
who is devoid of qualities yet causes the agitation of the qualities, and who is the source of the universe.
O messengers, O sinless ones, I have been remembered with compassion by the Lord of the Wretched;
for neither Brahmā and the others, nor Sanaka and the rest, know Him even through meditation. (28)
Accompanied by an infinite multitude, he sent forth that supreme vehicle;
possessing various forms, he is the master of the highest illusion, manifesting in diverse incarnations.
"Why was such a wondrous remembrance made for me by him?
Having spoken thus and having paid homage to that Bhṛgu, the lord of the earth said: || 30 ||
"By your command, I shall go with the messengers, traveling in a celestial chariot;
and by your grace, O Lord, you ought not to forget me. (31)
Sūta said:
Having heard what he had spoken, Bhṛgu was overwhelmed with agitation;
with tears of joy and his hair standing on end, he clasped the king by the neck.
I said, "O King, I am a brahmin of little fortune, while you possess great merit;
having become a resident of Gaṇeśapura, never forget me. (33)
Having spoken thus, they both went outside; the king, having grasped both their hands and paid homage to that celestial chariot as well as to that best of sages, [departed].
Filled with supreme joy and urged by the words of the messenger, he ascended;
the two ministers, Sudharmā and [the other], also mounted that excellent vehicle.
Then, seeing the splendor of the celestial chariot and hearing the quarters of the sky filled with the sounds of musical instruments from the messengers, Somaka’s son rejoiced.
He considered that this had been obtained through merit from a previous birth;
then, while he was looking at Bhṛgu, he saw a celestial chariot in the sky.
And seeing that the state supreme over all had been attained by means of a mortal body, he was struck with the utmost wonder; having bowed down, he departed from the messengers to his own abode.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of the Somakānta Celestial Vehicle," in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.

Chapter 152, titled "The Vision of Hemakaṇṭha," Sūta said:
Then, from above, the king beheld his own city, Devapura;
he rejoiced upon seeing its golden gate-towers and watchtowers.
Then Sudharmā, beholding that beautiful assembly hall, remembered it;
out of affection for her own son, she spoke to him with a faltering voice.
My son Hemakaṇṭha shall now occupy the auspicious throne,
awaiting the path of his parents once a year has passed since his birth.
"O Lord, O treasure-house of compassion, you ought to grant him an audience.
Having heard these words of the women, the king then fell into deep sorrow.
The king said:
"May my son Hemakaṇṭha be either living or dead;
for I had told him that he would have a vision [of me] after a year."
"Where could I go from untruth? It has never been said that it is possible for me to go there, nor to abandon that supreme state. (6)
"How can this contradiction possibly be reconciled? he cried out, weeping bitterly.
Seeing their grief, the messengers spoke to that best of kings.
Hearing your weeping, compassion has come upon us.
"Let us wait here for a moment; having seen him, go quickly! || 8 ||
Once your composure was restored, our supreme satisfaction would be achieved;
then the messengers brought him up from the depths of the celestial city. 9.
That celestial chariot of Gaṇeśa, which had arrived upon the hearing of the Purāṇa,
pervaded the city with its splendor and resounded with the noise of musical instruments.
Subāhu and Jñānagamyu, having paid homage to the king and his attendants,
departed to report the entire account to Hemakaṇṭha.
In an instant, they beheld Hemakaṇṭha seated upon an auspicious throne,
surrounded by mighty and preeminent heroes clad in armor.
While he was watching an excellent dance accompanied by ministers and citizens,
his two ministers beheld Subala, who is accessible through knowledge.
All the heroes, along with the ministers and Hemakaṇṭhaka, rose up;
they all approached them in great haste to embrace them.
When the embrace with them had taken place, the prince,
filled with great joy and his hair standing on end, departed and spoke to them both.
"Are my mother and father, along with the ministers, anywhere safe?
Having abandoned those two parents, how have you two gone away all alone?"
Having spoken thus, he seated them both on their own seats and honored them with garments,
sandalwood paste, ornaments, fruits, betel, and gold.
Without those two, my life-breaths hang by a mere thread in my throat;
day and night, there is meditation upon them alone in my mind, and nothing else.
"My father previously told me once that he would grant me another audience;
how then could he make such a statement false? (19)
The two of them said:
"O King, do not harbor vain anxiety; your parents are well.
Who in the three worlds knows the power of their merit? (20)
Having obtained your permission, we four have departed from the city; for your father’s gentleness and other virtues were truly great.
Extremely afflicted by hunger, his lotus-feet bled;
yet there was no satisfaction for that king from roots, tubers, or fruits.
Even though your mother’s condition was such, they did not move even a single step;
then, after wandering in many directions, they saw a beautiful, great lake.
There, in the cool shade of trees and creepers, the lord of the earth slept;
Sudharmā, exhausted by fatigue, massaged his feet.
While we two had gone there for the sake of roots and tubers, the sage arrived.
Cyavana, that tiger among sages, saw the two of them there for the purpose of obtaining water.
Taking their heartfelt affection with him, he returned to his own hermitage.
Then we both returned, having gathered much root and fruit.
Then all of them went to that hermitage and were greatly honored by the sage;
fed with foods of six flavors, they attained supreme rest.
Then a conversation ensued between the sage and the king,
and the king related the entire account to the sage at that time.
Then, by the power of meditation, the Sage recounted his previous birth;
filled with compassion, he explained the means for pacifying that misdeed.
And at the mere mention of this misfortune, terror arose within us two, O King;
while he was thus of a doubtful mind, they emerged from his body. (30)
White-colored birds began to devour him;
overwhelmed by the blows of their beaks, the king fell down. || 31 ||
"Protect us! Protect us!"—thus the sage was addressed with a prayer out of compassion;
by his mere glance, the birds vanished in an instant.
Having joined his palms, the king stood facing the sage;
perceiving the great sin of the king, he [the sage] contemplated it with devotion. || 33 ||
The ocean of compassion first poured out one hundred and eight measures of the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, using the names of the deities as the pouring vessels.
Then, having forcibly extracted from his own body a terrible being through the power of his asceticism,
Vyomakeśa— whose tongue lolled out and who was greatly distressed by hunger— stood there.
He requested food from Bhṛgu, and he said to him as he stood before him:
"Eat this great mango tree, which is indeed completely dry. (36)
Touched by him, the mango tree was reduced to ashes in an instant;
then that sage said to the fisherman, "Eat it! (37)
Then the sage said to the king: "O lord of the earth, the hearing of the Purāṇas is a great good; you should constantly cast [your offerings] into this sacred ash."
O King of kings, as soon as the chest of this mango tree becomes like that of another [as it was before],
you too shall possess a divine body.
In that very manner, having bathed and heard many stories,
the king performed his daily rites for spiritual welfare by devoutly casting [the offerings] into those ashes.
O King, at the end of the year, that tree became as it was before;
for when the Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa is completed, it becomes laden with fruits and flowers.
Even Napa, possessing divine splendor, became like the moon and the sun;
meanwhile, as the king was praising the sage, a celestial chariot arrived.
Accompanied by dancing and singing, resounding with the noise of musical instruments,
and joined by the messengers of Gaṇeśa, he arrived at the vicinity of the hermitage.
"O Lord, since our eyes have indeed become fruitful by beholding your splendor, those messengers of your most meritorious father [approached] the king by the command of the gods. (44)
Urged by the gaze of the king, they lowered the boat into the middle of the vehicle;
and Sudharmā, having received the sage’s command, departed, traveling in a celestial chariot.
O King, as soon as the city of the gods was seen, the memory of you returned;
therefore, the vehicle has been brought out from the northern part of the city. 46.
Out of a desire to see you, your two parents have gone to inform them of your whereabouts;
go quickly to meet them, otherwise they will depart.
Having heard those words of theirs, Hemakaṇṭha, filled with haste,
his hair standing on end and his eyes brimming with tears, ran forth after hearing everything.
Then, out of eagerness to see him, he went forth placing those two in front, his collection of ornaments shattered, surrounded by citizens and servants. (49)
With tears falling, he reached in an instant the celestial chariot crowded with hosts.

Chapter 153, titled "Description of Somakānta’s Attainment of the State of a God," begins with Sūta saying:
Then his four ministers went ahead to the city of Somakānta;
having prostrated themselves before everyone, they said, "O King, your son has arrived."
Surrounded by all the heroic citizens as Indra is by the hosts of gods,
he was filled with both joy and sorrow upon seeing the funeral procession of the king.
Thus informed by his ministers, he also arrived quickly,
accompanied by servants including children, women, and the elderly.
Beholding the splendor of the celestial chariot, everyone was filled with overflowing joy;
seeing him, lovely as the moon, in its midst, they bowed down upon the surface of the earth.
Accompanied by the messengers of Gaṇeśa and his exceedingly beautiful consort,
he then alighted from the vehicle and joyfully embraced his son.
Both of them, shedding tears of joy and with their hair standing on end,
remained for a moment like two bodiless beings (Videhas), saying nothing at all.
Then the father spoke with affection to his son who had returned after a year:
"I constantly meditate upon you alone, my virtuous son, the ornament of the lineage;
among all the sons living in the world, I see none equal to you."

Then Sudharmā, running toward her son with affection, embraced him with joy; both of them had tears streaming down their faces. Then the mother said to her son, "O child, it has been a long time since we have seen you."
With my mind longing for you, I was not happy at all;
now, having seen your face, my heart has become filled with joy.
And because of separation from you, my body has become exceedingly emaciated;
therefore, the citizens, bearing your name, embraced one another. (8)
Some performed circumambulations, some then touched his feet, and some, merely by seeing him, returned toward the city.
Then the king said to them all: "By the grace of Bhṛgu, [this has been granted] to me."
That Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa which was narrated, which destroys all sins.
Because of that, I became sinless, possessed of a divine body and traveling in a celestial chariot;
I became visible to all, and I shall go again by means of a vehicle.
"O son, the compassionate Gaṇeśa has sent a vehicle for me to the earth,
and I have enjoyed sovereignty and all riches according to my own will."
"By the grace of the descendant of Bhṛgu, I shall go to the supreme abode.
Thus did they hear those words, spoken with a voice as gentle as the breeze to the moon.
They all wept with piteous voices, and some fell prostrate upon the ground;
then the leaders of the guilds spoke to the beloved of the Somakas, that treasure-house of compassion.
"O protector of the earth, how will you go to that abode without us?
O King, having abandoned our lives, we shall all follow after you."
O King, the guilt of killing you shall fall upon all of us;
we possess no such merit by which we might behold that Lord of Virtues. 13.
"By the grace of Your Majesty, we shall go to the highest world;
for in this cycle of existence there is no happiness at all, as life here is indeed lost in vain. (14)
"Let us have no means whatsoever for the accomplishment of our purpose.
Then Hemakaṇṭha spoke these words with respect to Janaka: || 15 ||

"O father, how can you go to see the elephant-faced god, leaving behind your young son? What is the reason for your desire for the kingdom, and what is the purpose of your command to me, my child? (16)
"O King, you do not wish to hand over even my entire protected kingdom now;
such is your oath, therefore you ought to take me with you. (17)
Somakānta said:
"All of you indeed desire to behold the lotus-feet of the Lord;
however, O people, I am dependent on others in this matter—what should be done by me? (18)
I grieve out of affection for you, and especially out of affection for my son;
for this very reason, having come down from the upward path, I have arrived to see him.
Sūta said:
Then, while the worlds were grieving and even as the moon-faced one was weeping for her son,
compassion arose at that time within the messengers of the gods.
They said to that beloved of Soma: "O King, you are blessed, since these people have dedicated their lives to you just as they do to the Lord of the Universe."
"Therefore, let us take them all and go quickly to Gajānana.
The King said:
"If the entire city is taken, then my fame will be firmly established. (22)
"It shall come to pass in Rasā; it shall not be otherwise.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus regarding the hearing of the ancient Gaṇeśa... (23)
By the king's command, he did not place the merit into their hands or into the water;
when the merit had entered the water and their hands, the people became free from sin and embodiments of merit.
From children, women, and the elderly, all ascended the excellent vehicle;
meanwhile, those who were the messengers of Gaṇeśa departed by way of the sky.
Then some wicked men, who had not even taken water in their hands,
returned to the city and reported on the remaining people.
Then they all beheld a vast city rising upwards;
the remaining ones, gratified by their acquisition of wealth, spoke to one another.
With joyful hearts, they became intent on various endeavors;
meanwhile, messengers carrying staffs struck some who were intent on flight.
Having seized them by force out of curiosity, they threw them into the middle of the vehicle;
likewise, those who had gone there under various pretexts were thrown in as well. || 29 ||
Seated in the central area were the king’s wives, sons, and others;
the ministers and the citizens sat comfortably all around them. || 30 ||
While divine musical instruments resounded and throngs of Apsarases danced, they cried out, "Victory to you, Mayūreśa! Victory to you, Mayūreśa! (31)
Roaring with their echoes even throughout the quarters of the sky,
they reached the auspicious abode of Gaṇeśa with great speed.
Beholding his exquisite beauty, they spoke with wonder:
"Oh, how great is his merit, by which he has beheld the elephant-faced one! (33)
They all attained proximity, and the king attained union (sāyujya).
Sūta said: Thus, O Brahmins, has the ancient narrative of Gaṇeśa been told to you.
This narrative destroys the sins of all who hear it.
O Brahmins, I shall relate to you that entire account which the king questioned the divine messengers while in the celestial chariot. Listen. (35)

Chapter 154, titled "The Description of the Fifty-six Vināyakas. The Sages said:
O sinless one, what was asked by the lover of Soma while he was traveling in his celestial chariot?
We wish to hear that; tell us everything without omission. || 1 ||
Sūta said: As he was traveling along the path of the sky, the high-souled one questioned the messengers regarding the great-souled lords of the Gaṇas who were stationed in Vārāṇasī.
"O sinless ones, hear from us those names of the attendants.
The King said:
'O messengers, please tell me the names of the attendants of the Lord of the Universe.'"
The messengers said: "From the complete remembrance of Gaṇeśa, who bestows all perfections,
we shall describe in brief those who have gone to the enclosure of Viśveśa."
O King, listen now in due order to the Gaṇeśas who remove all fears:
Durgā-Gaṇeśa, Vināyaka, Arka-Gaṇeśa, Bhīma-Gaṇeśa, Caṇḍī-Gaṇeśa, and Vināyaka. 5.
Then Dehalīgaṇa, and likewise Uddaṇḍavināyaka;
then Vināyaka, who holds a noose in his hand and removes all obstacles.
In the first enclosure is Vināyaka in the form of Siddhasiddhi;
[then] Lambodara, Kūṭadanta, and the Vināyaka Śūlaṭaṅka. || 7 ||
The fourth is named Kūṣmāṇḍa, the fifth is designated as Muṇḍa,
and the prince-Vināyaka is known by the name Vikaṭadvija.
The one named Praṇava and another, as well as Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadanta, Trimukha, and Vināyaka, are situated in the second enclosure.
Then there is Vighnarāja as the fourth, and Varada the Vināyaka;
furthermore, there is Pañcāsya and Heramba the Vināyaka. 10.
Those known as Modakapriya reside in the third enclosure; they are Vināyaka, Abhayaprada, and Siṃhatuṇḍa-Vināyaka. 11.
Another is Kuṇitākṣa, and another is known as Kṣipraprasāda;
there is also the one renowned as Cintāmaṇi, and Dantahasta Vināyaka.
Pracaṇḍa, and another, Uddaṇḍamuṇḍavināyaka—these eight Vināyakas are to be known in the fourth enclosure. 13.
The second is Sthūladanta, the Vināyaka fond of strife;
the third is Caturdanta with two trunks, the eldest Gajavināyaka. || 14 ||
Likewise, the one named Kāla and another named Nāgeśa should be known;
these eight Vināyakas are to be known in the fifth enclosure (āvaraṇa). || 15 ||
Maṇikarṇa-Vināyaka, Āśā-sṛṣṭi-Vināyaka, the one named Yakṣa, the one named Gajakarṇa, and Citraghaṇṭa-Vināyaka. || 16 ||
Sumaṅgala and the one named Mitra—these are the Vināyakas in the sixth [month]; Modā, Pramoda, Sumukha, and Durmukha are the Vināyakas. 17.
Furthermore, Gaṇapākhyas, as well as Jñānavināyaka, and likewise Dvāravināyaka, are to be known in the seventh enclosure (saptamāvaraṇa). || 18 ||
Where the eighth is Avimukta, the bestower of liberation, and then Vināyaka; another is indeed named Bhagīratha, and then Hariścandra-Vināyaka. || 19 ||
Kapardin is to be known as the next, as well as Binduvināyaka;
the constant remembrance of these bestows the fruit of all desires. || 20 ||
Whoever, having risen at dawn, recites these with a pure mind,
for him no obstacles shall create hindrance in any of his undertakings.
O Indra among kings, a devoted person should worship these [deities] with the individual names of each, using dūrvā grass, rice grains, sesame seeds, and śamī leaves. || 22 ||
One shall accomplish even an impossible task and be victorious everywhere;
one shall obtain longevity, nourishment, health, and excellent wealth. (23)
"O King, all this that was asked by you has been told to you.
Then the divine messengers departed in joy to their own abode in silence. (24)
Sūta said:
O brahmins, this enclosure of Viśveśa has now been described by me;
I shall now declare the proclamation of the fruits of the Purāṇa.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fifty-six Vināyakas," in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning: 11,026 + 25 = 11,051.
Chapter 155, titled "Description of the Declaration of the Fruit," Sūta said:
By taking refuge in this Purāṇa, O twice-born ones, there shall be neither birth nor death for him, whether he hears it once or many times. || 1 ||
Even Śeṣa and Padmāsana (Brahmā) are unable to fully describe the merit of that man who gives [a gift] at Kurukṣetra during an eclipse of the moon or sun.
A devoted man shall obtain the same merit as that of giving thousands of loads of gold to Brahmins with a spirit of devotion, simply by hearing this. || 3 ||
Who could weigh in a balance the fruit of listening to the Purāṇas against all sacrifices performed with their constituent parts and accompanied by sacrificial fees? 4.
Therefore, the merit of listening to this Purāṇa is particularly distinguished;
what need is there to mention the merit of religious vows or the giving of water there? || 5 ||
The merit that arises from giving away ten million maidens in marriage and thousands of gifts of cows becomes multiplied ten million times by listening to this.
Even from the constant recitation of all four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, or from the exposition of the Śāstras, or even from the constant service of the virtuous; || 7 ||

The merit that would result from hearing the entire Purāṇa of Bhārata multiplied ten million times shall be obtained by hearing this [work]. Whatever merit results from hearing the complete Purāṇa of Bhārata, multiplied ten million times, that shall be obtained by hearing this. 8.
In whosever house the Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa is written, there neither Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, nor Pūtanās and the like shall dwell. || 9 ||
The planets and the spirits that afflict children never cause any harm;
for that house is always protected by Gaṇeśa himself.
Whoever should hear this Purāṇa or worship it with a concentrated mind—by the mere sight of him, even fallen men become purified. 11.
That man becomes worthy of honor by the sages beginning with Brahmā;
when enraged, he may burn the world, and when pleased, he may bestow the highest station.
By listening to this every day, a person attains the eight supernatural powers;
such a man never encounters poverty nor any hardship whatsoever.
One attains one's desired objects as well as the treasures, such as Padma and the others;
likewise, the Kalpa tree, the Kāmadhenu cow, the treasure (Nidhi), and the Cintāmaṇi jewel [are obtained]. 14.
He comes under his control, and he too becomes worthy of worship.
Furthermore, [he attains] the powers of digestion (jāraṇa), killing (māraṇa), immobilization (stambha), and even eradication (uccāṭana). 15.
Merely by remembering this, [all obstacles] shall indeed be dispelled in an instant.
A person should listen to the Purāṇa while standing in the presence of Gaṇeśa. 16.
Freed from even great sins, including the slaughter of women and children,
he shall undoubtedly attain the presence of Gaṇeśa at the end.
Even a Śūdra, having seated Brāhmaṇas in his midst, may listen to this;
he gradually attains the castes known as Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Dvija. || 18 ||
He who, having fallen away from his obligatory and occasional duties, should listen to this, attains the perfection of those rites through the grace of Gaṇeśa. || 19 ||
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, he who has fashioned an image out of clay and,
having worshipped it with supreme devotion in a beautiful pavilion adorned with arches— 20.
If one listens to the Purāṇa immediately, Vināyaka, the Lord of Obstacles, being pleased with him, grants all desires and, at the end, liberation.
If a person recites as many hymns as there are here every single day with devotion, he shall become perfected; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever may be unattainable, a person shall obtain it by reciting those [mantras];
he who performs the ritual application and chants them for just one month. || 23 ||
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion; he too shall attain oneness with That.
The sages said:
O sinless one, how does merit arise from hearing this? By whom was it attained in the past?
"Therefore, O highly blessed son of a Sūta, speak to us who are asking you.
The Sūta said: "Listen, O sages; formerly there was a certain sage who had become mute."
Lomaśa, having unexpectedly gone to the world of Brahmā by chance,
paid homage to the Lord of the World and sat down by his command.
Honored with supreme devotion, Lomaśa then spoke to Brahmā.
Lomaśa said:
"O Lord, this Purāṇa, which increases merit, was told to Vyāsa in the past."
"O illustrious one, you ought to tell me that regarding Gaṇeśa.
Brahmā said:
"Listen attentively, Lomaśa, to this auspicious account which removes all sins. 28.
Indeed, this Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa bestows both worldly desires and liberation upon men.
Sūta said:
Then Brahmā narrated it by means of his own [portion]. 29.
The entire Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa, which bestows both desired objects and liberation,
was heard in its entirety with devotion by Lomaśa from Mūka, who was not greedy for wealth.
Then that sage, like the Lord of Speech himself, spoke the Bhārata;
having mastered it through recitation and composed it, he caused others to hear it as well.
Having enjoyed pleasures according to his desire and having obtained sons and grandsons,
he finally went to the supreme and auspicious abode of Gaṇeśvara.
Furthermore, O sages, listen to this ancient history:
there was a king born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, pure-souled and stainless.
He was a performer of sacrifices, a constant giver of gifts, devoted to the study of the Vedas, and a slayer of his enemies.
He was the expounder of all duties, intent on protecting his subjects, entitled to a sixth share of the world's produce, honored by all, and exceedingly dear to them. (34)
The world-renowned protector named Saṃvaraṇa, famous throughout the three worlds,
being childless, performed the Putrīyā sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son.
Then, despite performing well-ordained sacrifices accompanied by their constituent parts, ritual fees, and gifts of food, the king did not obtain offspring; he subsequently heard of the Harivaṃśa.
Having worshipped the twice-born at the conclusion and having satisfied the reciter with garments, cows, gold, and the like, as well as gems, roots, fruits, and so forth. || 37 ||
Even from him no son was born; by fate, that house remained childless.
However, a renowned scholar of the Purāṇas named Gaṇeśa arrived at their home.
Having been installed and entreated by King Saṃvaraṇa,
the king joyfully heard from his mouth that ancient narrative known as the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa.
At the conclusion of that, he gratified that eminent brahmin Mūka with jewels,
pearls, garments, and ornaments made of gold.
Then he obtained a son, and being devoted to Gaṇeśa, he enjoyed manifold pleasures and attained the supreme station of Gaṇeśa. 41.
His sister had been barren for thirty years, yet she began to menstruate at the proper time; having heard of her offspring, he then [acted]. || 42 ||
And having summoned that sage who had become inspired by hearing the Purāṇa known as the Gaṇeśa,
he listened to that auspicious Purāṇa from his mouth.
Devoted to the worship of Gaṇeśa, she obtained a son who was a great hero;
having attained sons and grandsons, she enjoyed enchanting pleasures. || 44 ||
She departed from her own abode to the realm of Gaṇeśa;
meanwhile, among the sons of Sagara, one son was born lame. 45.
In former times, this ancient merit was also heard by him from Lomaśa with devotion,
being humble and faithful for twelve years.
Having gratified Lomaśa with gifts, he then touched his feet;
being intent on that supreme abode, he attained victory, nourishment, and long life, and at the end of his life, he reached that realm.
Whatever fruit one may obtain from hearing all eighteen Purāṇas, that same fruit shall accrue from hearing this single Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa. 48.
By hearing this, O Brahmins, a woman who has borne only one child becomes the mother of many sons;
a woman whose fetus miscarries becomes one whose fetus is firmly established. 49.
O best of sages, even a mute attains mastery of speech by hearing this;
and even one who is merely venerable becomes a preeminent among the twice-born, perfected through the study of the Vedas. (50)
A Śūdra indeed attains the status of a Vaiśya, a Vaiśya reaches the state of a Kṣatriya, and a Kṣatriya attains the rank of the twice-born simply by remembering him. 51.
Moreover, by merely hearing a single chapter from this, a maiden obtains a husband who is virtuous, of noble lineage, endowed with a large retinue, and possessed of wealth. 52.
By resorting to this ancient [text], one born blind regains his sight—even more so than one who bathes in all sacred fords and gives gifts of every kind. (53)
He who listens to this with devotion attains that same fruit:
the practice of the five fires in summer and dwelling in water during the winter. (54)
A mortal who hears these five chapters obtains that same fruit which one attains by dwelling in the open air for many years during the rainy season. 55.
Whatever fruit is obtained by a devoted man who constantly performs the Agnihotra sacrifice, that very fruit arises from listening to this Purāṇa. 56.
Whatever merit a man might gain by standing on one big toe for ten thousand years,
that same fruit is obtained from hearing ten chapters of this Purāṇa.
A human being who listens constantly from birth until death attains this through devotion; of this there is no doubt. (58)
He who dwells in Kāśī from birth until death shall indeed become a universal emperor (cakravartin) of Gaṇeśa through the Purāṇa. || 59 ||
A mortal obtains that same merit from the Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa which a man gains by bathing at Prayāga for a thousand Māgha months.
A mortal obtains that same fruit from listening to this Purāṇa as he who performs a bath with devotion at the confluence of the Gomatī. || 61 ||
That man who listens with devotion to the Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa shall obtain from its hearing a fruit multiplied ten millionfold. (62)
He has no fear of the trident, nor of the thunderbolt, nor of the discus of Cakra;
all this ancient lore has been told to you in full detail.
O lords of sages, the full majesty cannot be described even in tens of millions of years,
nor by Brahmā, nor by the six-faced Kārttikeya, nor even by Śeṣa.
That which you have asked me concerns the destruction of all sins;
it bestows all desires, grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and increases merit. (65)
What else do you wish to hear that removes the sins of both speaker and listener concerning Gaṇeśa, the Supreme Lord, who assumes manifold divine sports? 66.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Declaration of Fruits," in the Krīḍākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 11,051 + 66 = 11,117 (with 7,021 verses in the Uttara-khaṇḍa).
Thus ends the Uttara-khaṇḍa (the Krīḍā-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Gaṇeśa Mahāpurāṇa. May this be an offering to Śrī Gaṇanātha.
May it be auspicious.
Thus ends the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa.
